It was unknown if the flaw was with the equipment or installation, he said. Karoun Demirjian Niraj Chokshi Hari Raj and Ryley Ober Federal officials said the cascading communications failures that forced the government to shut down flights across the United States on Friday started with a contractor upgrading air traffic control equipment, replacing copper wire with fiber optic cable. The upgrade set off communications failures across the facilities that manage the national air space, the officials said. Alarmed at the scope of the problem, the Federal Aviation Administration decided to issue a rare nationwide ground stop for several hours. Speaking at news conference in Washington, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that the specific problem with the upgrade, which took place in what he called a “remote” facility, was not yet known. The contractor, L3Harris, has worked for the Federal Aviation Administration for decades, he said. Mr. Duffy said his agency was trying to determine whether the problem had been caused by the contractor’s incompetence or faulty equipment. “We haven’t determined what the fault was,” he said. He added, “We’re going to hold people accountable.” At least 3,000 flights scheduled for Saturday were canceled, according to Cirium, an aviation data firm. At Chicago O’Hare International Airport, a ground stop was issued for United Airlines flights. Mr. Duffy again called on lawmakers to fully fund upgrades that he said were needed to prevent similar failures. To upgrade aging air traffic facilities and technology, he said, he wanted another $50 billion from the Republican-controlled Congress, which last year approved $12.5 billion for the project. A key difference, aviation experts say, is that the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration relies on Congress to fund crucial upgrades, while other countries have privatized their air traffic control. That has meant more money, more consistently, to invest in improving systems in places like Canada and the European Union, both considered success stories in aviation management. The F.A.A.’s issuing of a nationwide ground stop on Friday underscored America’s aging infrastructure, which experts have warned for years is in urgent need of modernizing , and which critics say has been chronically underfunded. For decades, U.S. air traffic communications have relied on a system that runs on analog copper wire, floppy disks and alphabetical keyboards so old that the F.A.A. has difficulty sourcing spare parts. Speaking to reporters after the outage, Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, echoed those concerns, describing an air traffic control system stuck in the past, and demanding $50 billion from Congress to improve it. This has allowed both Canada and the European Union to invest billions into updating systems without relying on lawmakers and to make headway on innovations like satellite-based tracking of flights. Although the same upgrade is not entirely complete in Canada, according to NAV Canada, the majority of the work was finished in just 18 months, Mr. Gradek said. The halt grounded or delayed some 10,000 flights from coast to coast and confirmed what experts have been warning for years: that the nation’s flight safety system is perilously fragile. Instead, the president, who remained behind the scenes at the White House, posted messages to social media that night on other topics. They’re our prime contractor. I can’t go somewhere else. They own it. Or was it a faulty router? And we’re going to find that out. And frankly, we’re going to hold people accountable.” In a statement on Saturday, L3Harris said that it was supporting the F.A.A. investigation into what had happened and that it “takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.” The company was formed in 2019, the result of a merger of two defense contractors. It employed about 45,000 people at the start of this year and is based in Florida. L3Harris owns the equipment used to transmit voice communications and data to and from air traffic control facilities, remote radar sites and weather stations, a network known as the F.A.A. Telecommunications Infrastructure. The company is in the midst of upgrading the copper wires used in that network to high-speed fiber optic cable across more than 4,400 sites, with over 70 percent of those lines already replaced. Federal officials said on Saturday that they had halted departing flights a day earlier because of a communications disruption set off by a copper-to-fiber upgrade at a remote site, which they did not identify. A newly installed router began firing more than a thousand connection requests every few seconds, which disrupted voice communications and radar feeds. Ultimately, it took technicians 45 minutes to identify the problem. The F.A.A. is trying to build a modern replacement to its telecommunications network with other partners, including AT&T and Verizon, over the next few years, Secretary Duffy said on Saturday. “Until I can build that, I’m stuck with L3Harris,” he said. Nick Daniels, the president of the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, said that for planes traveling such a large distance over oceanic airspace, “they have process procedures, different standards of separations, than what we do to run the volume of air traffic” in the lower 48 states. At 3 p.m. Pacific Standard Time on Friday, about two hours before the nationwide ground stop was lifted, San Francisco International Airport said that Pacific-bound flights, including to Hawaii and Asia, had been cleared for departure. Why were passengers flying west so fortunate? L3Harris, the federal contractor that was updating air traffic control equipment prior to the nationwide outage, said in a statement that it took the nationwide ground stop seriously. The contractor said it had completed more than 70 percent of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system. The company added it was supporting the F.A.A. in its investigation. The communications failures that prompted Federal Aviation Administration officials to issue a nationwide ground stop started when L3 Harris, a contractor managing the agency’s telecoms network, made a standard upgrade at a remote air traffic location, federal officials said Saturday. The contractor was conducting work on Friday that was needed to replace aging analog copper wire with more modern fiber optic cable, Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, told reporters. The “routine” task was being done at a location remote and small enough that officials assumed a Friday afternoon upgrade would pose no meaningful disruption to the air traffic, he said. That presumption proved wrong, as the changeover from copper to fiber started flooding the system with levels of data it could not handle, triggering a cascade of communications failures across the air traffic facilities that manage the national air space. Officials, alarmed at the scope of the problems, decided to issue a rare nationwide ground stop for hours. As of Saturday morning, administration officials still have not determined whether L3 Harris or shoddy equipment was at fault.

extraction.body: A nationwide US ground stop that caused thousands of flight cancellations and prompted travel chaos was caused by a technical issue following a copper wire upgrade, the transport secretary has said. Sean Duffy told a news conference that the government was trying to find out whether the problem that led to air traffic controllers suspending take-offs for four hours on Friday had been caused by "incompetence" on the part of the company doing the upgrades or faulty equipment. Though the ground stop was lifted on Friday evening, it had a knock-on effect on air travel on Saturday as airlines attempted to clear a backlog of flights. Officials including Duffy had previously attributed the issue to outdated equipment. Maintenance on US air traffic control systems was being carried out to switch from copper wire to fibre-optic cable by a contractor called L3Harris, a technology provider, Duffy said. The US had "an incredibly old telecommunications system", he said, adding: "It was such an old wire that it was being discontinued." The transport secretary explained that a router that was being worked on had started flooding other air traffic control systems and created communication issues with planes, prompting the shutdown on safety grounds. The government was now trying to understand whether the root cause was the wire replacement or a fault with the router. The four-hour suspension from 15:54 EST (19:54 GMT) on Friday was the longest such incident since the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US. More than 15,000 flights in the US were delayed or cancelled that day, according to data from flight tracking sites, affecting an estimated 1.5 million passengers, with more than 5,900 cancelled and 7,000 delayed on Saturday. In some cases, passengers were left stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to the gates. The ground stop also had a knock-on effect on schedules around the world, with some flights out of the UK and Europe cancelled. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said the US flight schedule should return to normal by the end of Sunday. US officials have said they did not believe the issue was as a result of a cyber-attack or a rogue AI agent, though Duffy said an investigation into the exact cause was under way. Bryan Bedford, who heads the FAA, told the same news conference: "We see zero evidence of anything nefarious and zero evidence of anything AI related." L3Harris said on Saturday that it had completed more than 70% of the work it had been tasked to undertake to modernise US air traffic communications infrastructure before the shutdown. The company said it was supporting the FAA in its investigation, adding: "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously." Duffy warned that a similar issue could arise again unless the US Congress approved upgrades to air traffic control infrastructure. US President Donald Trump has requested $30.1bn (£22.8bn) for the upgrades. Both chambers of Congress are currently controlled by the Republican Party. Duffy previously said the system needed a $50bn overhaul. Former TSA Administrator John Pistole told the BBC that "the fact that they were able to get it restarted in four-and-a-half hours is good news - it shows a resilience in the system - but what's to say it's not going to happen tomorrow?" A nationwide ground stop has only been ordered one other time since all flights were banned from take-off for several days following the 11 September 2001 attacks. A failure in the Notice to Air Missions (Notam) system in 2023 prompted a grounding that lasted an hour and 52 minutes, delaying about 9,500 flights and cancelling about 1,300.

Secretary Duffy on the work done by air traffic controllers and pilots to land Americans safely yesterday: “I just want to, again, start off and thank our air traffic controllers and our pilots. They exhibited an amazing performance yesterday. We had 3,500 aircraft in the air. We had a ground stop and they safely landed all of our aircraft which was outstanding. But I also want to thank our flight attendants, our ground crews, our airport authorities. All of them rallied yesterday. A lot of passengers at airports. They all came together and served the American people incredibly well. I also want to thank the passengers. I know a lot of people were disrupted. Whether they were going on vacation, they were coming home from work–they had significant disruption and the patience that they exhibited. We at the DOT and the FAA are grateful for that patience.” Secretary Duffy on what led to the issue: “Now, those of you who are aviation reporters have heard me talk about a decades old air traffic control system. It's not just old equipment. We have an incredibly old telecommunication system. And so, here's what we believe happened yesterday: Secretary Duffy on whether the inconsistencies were caused by a cyber attack: “We don't believe so. Once we were able to isolate the work that was being done at this remote location, all of our systems came back online. So, we don't believe this was cyber at all.” Secretary Duffy on the safety of the national airspace: “To the American traveler, our number one job is their safety and Bryan [Bedford] mentioned this and I’ve mentioned this before but we will keep you on the ground, you won’t get to your destination if we think you can’t get there safely. My first day on the job was the DCA air crash…My heart goes out to those families and everyone who has lost someone in aviation. We do everything we can to keep travelers safe and our airspace is safe. I fly all the time, my kids fly, my wife flies. This is a safe system, evidenced by what happened yesterday. If there is any issue with our telecom…we shut the airspace down. We brought airplanes in, we landed them safely, we figured out what was wrong, our systems came back online and have become fully operational. That’s how seriously we take safety. ” Secretary Duffy on the FAA’s progress modernizing America’s air traffic control system: “The Congress gave me a partial payment. They gave me $12.5 billion. And one of the problems that we had was [Congress] weren't quite sure that we would spend the money well and we'd build with the money. And that's the history of the FAA that goes back from Republicans and Democrats. They haven't spent the money well. So, they want to make sure we're going to spend and spend it well. And we have. And so, in the course of the last year, since I've got that $12.5 billion, I want to talk to you about what we've actually accomplished. Secretary Duffy on the need for Congress to fully fund air traffic control modernization: “I hope that they meet this moment and they invest in what will be the state-of-the-art, the best-in-class, best in the world air traffic control system. When I came in, President Trump, before the DCA air crash, was saying, ‘We have to modernize our airspace. I want you to work on modernizing air traffic control.’...and then if you look at the Congress–that you have both Democrats and Republicans who understand how important this is. For me, it gets to be frustrating where everyone says they want to do it and the president is pushing it but we don't get the resources. And I think this is the moment. If we don't start to switch out our systems, how long are we going to wait? I think this is a sign for [Congress] to lean in. This is bipartisan….We should be able to rely on our air traffic control system—making sure it works… Let’s not let the legacy of the past where investments weren't made, which is why we are here today. Let's make the investments and look forward to a brighter future in aviation , a safer future, a more efficient future in aviation.” FAA Administrator Bedford on how the issue is unrelated to USDOT’s ongoing modernization efforts: “I think we’re conflating ‘Modernization’ with this upgrade at this particular facility. We spend a billion dollars a year maintaining and sustaining the existing 1980’s TDMI telco network—call it 1G, the 1G system that the FAA is on. So we are constantly replacing 2,000 Cisco 600 routers with Juniper routers. So, this is ordinary course-of-business stuff, this is not part of the Peraton-FAA $12.5 billion modernization effort, so let’s not conflate those two things.” Secretary Duffy on the timing of the upgrade: “We're making the transition because it's safer and it's more resilient. But because of the nature of what this switchover was, it was a remote location, we'll do those during the day. Now, if we're going to be at Newark, if we're going to be, you know, in one of our big facilities, those switchovers happen at night and they can have a bigger impact. But these smaller locations don't have that kind of impact—or they shouldn't have that kind of impact which is what we saw yesterday. So, there'll be a reevaluation of when we do this work. But when you look across the country when the work has been done from copper to fiber, going from analog to digital, they've happened at all times of the day, and so we have to drill in a little further about what happened here.”

Alarmed at the scope of the problem, the Federal Aviation Administration decided to issue a rare nationwide ground stop for several hours. Speaking at news conference in Washington, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that the specific problem with the upgrade, which took place in what he called a “remote” facility, was not yet known. The contractor, L3Harris, has worked for the Federal Aviation Administration for decades, he said. At Chicago O’Hare International Airport, a ground stop was issued for United Airlines flights. Mr. Duffy again called on lawmakers to fully fund upgrades that he said were needed to prevent similar failures. To upgrade aging air traffic facilities and technology, he said, he wanted another $50 billion from the Republican-controlled Congress, which last year approved $12.5 billion for the project. A key difference, aviation experts say, is that the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration relies on Congress to fund crucial upgrades, while other countries have privatized their air traffic control. That has meant more money, more consistently, to invest in improving systems in places like Canada and the European Union, both considered success stories in aviation management. The F.A.A.’s issuing of a nationwide ground stop on Friday underscored America’s aging infrastructure, which experts have warned for years is in urgent need of modernizing , and which critics say has been chronically underfunded. For decades, U.S. air traffic communications have relied on a system that runs on analog copper wire, floppy disks and alphabetical keyboards so old that the F.A.A. has difficulty sourcing spare parts. Speaking to reporters after the outage, Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, echoed those concerns, describing an air traffic control system stuck in the past, and demanding $50 billion from Congress to improve it. This has allowed both Canada and the European Union to invest billions into updating systems without relying on lawmakers and to make headway on innovations like satellite-based tracking of flights. In Canada, the changes lowered prices for users and increased productivity, according to a July report by the Reason Foundation , a think tank. America’s “25-year transition from copper wire to fiber is endemic to the type of organization that you have to fight for money every year to move this project one inch at a time,” he said. extraction.body: A nationwide US ground stop that caused thousands of flight cancellations and prompted travel chaos was caused by a technical issue following a copper wire upgrade, the transport secretary has said. Sean Duffy told a news conference that the government was trying to find out whether the problem that led to air traffic controllers suspending take-offs for four hours on Friday had been caused by "incompetence" on the part of the company doing the upgrades or faulty equipment. Though the ground stop was lifted on Friday evening, it had a knock-on effect on air travel on Saturday as airlines attempted to clear a backlog of flights. Officials including Duffy had previously attributed the issue to outdated equipment. Maintenance on US air traffic control systems was being carried out to switch from copper wire to fibre-optic cable by a contractor called L3Harris, a technology provider, Duffy said. The US had "an incredibly old telecommunications system", he said, adding: "It was such an old wire that it was being discontinued." The transport secretary explained that a router that was being worked on had started flooding other air traffic control systems and created communication issues with planes, prompting the shutdown on safety grounds. The government was now trying to understand whether the root cause was the wire replacement or a fault with the router. The four-hour suspension from 15:54 EST (19:54 GMT) on Friday was the longest such incident since the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US. More than 15,000 flights in the US were delayed or cancelled that day, according to data from flight tracking sites, affecting an estimated 1.5 million passengers, with more than 5,900 cancelled and 7,000 delayed on Saturday. In some cases, passengers were left stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to the gates. The ground stop also had a knock-on effect on schedules around the world, with some flights out of the UK and Europe cancelled. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said the US flight schedule should return to normal by the end of Sunday. US officials have said they did not believe the issue was as a result of a cyber-attack or a rogue AI agent, though Duffy said an investigation into the exact cause was under way. Bryan Bedford, who heads the FAA, told the same news conference: "We see zero evidence of anything nefarious and zero evidence of anything AI related." L3Harris said on Saturday that it had completed more than 70% of the work it had been tasked to undertake to modernise US air traffic communications infrastructure before the shutdown. The company said it was supporting the FAA in its investigation, adding: "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously." Duffy warned that a similar issue could arise again unless the US Congress approved upgrades to air traffic control infrastructure. US President Donald Trump has requested $30.1bn (£22.8bn) for the upgrades. Both chambers of Congress are currently controlled by the Republican Party. Duffy previously said the system needed a $50bn overhaul. Former TSA Administrator John Pistole told the BBC that "the fact that they were able to get it restarted in four-and-a-half hours is good news - it shows a resilience in the system - but what's to say it's not going to happen tomorrow?" A nationwide ground stop has only been ordered one other time since all flights were banned from take-off for several days following the 11 September 2001 attacks. A failure in the Notice to Air Missions (Notam) system in 2023 prompted a grounding that lasted an hour and 52 minutes, delaying about 9,500 flights and cancelling about 1,300.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator (FAA) Bryan Bedford provided updates on what led to the FAA’s nationwide ground stop on November 13, 2026, and the restoration efforts the Department took to reopen the airspace safely and quickly. REMINDER: Telecommunications issues that impacted the stability of communications and radar systems utilized by Air Traffic Control led the FAA to issue a nationwide ground stop out of an abundance of caution. FAA’s incredible air traffic controllers and commercial pilots were responsible for safely and efficiently grounding over 3,500 flights swiftly. Once the ground stop lifted, over 8,000 flight operations resumed last night alone. Today, the airspace is open, however, passengers should be prepared for some delays and cancellations as flights resume. Secretary Duffy on the work done by air traffic controllers and pilots to land Americans safely yesterday: “I just want to, again, start off and thank our air traffic controllers and our pilots. They exhibited an amazing performance yesterday. We had 3,500 aircraft in the air. We had a ground stop and they safely landed all of our aircraft which was outstanding. But I also want to thank our flight attendants, our ground crews, our airport authorities. All of them rallied yesterday. A lot of passengers at airports. They all came together and served the American people incredibly well. I also want to thank the passengers. I know a lot of people were disrupted. Whether they were going on vacation, they were coming home from work–they had significant disruption and the patience that they exhibited. We at the DOT and the FAA are grateful for that patience.” Secretary Duffy on what led to the issue: “Now, those of you who are aviation reporters have heard me talk about a decades old air traffic control system. It's not just old equipment. We have an incredibly old telecommunication system. And so, here's what we believe happened yesterday: Secretary Duffy on whether the inconsistencies were caused by a cyber attack: “We don't believe so. Once we were able to isolate the work that was being done at this remote location, all of our systems came back online. So, we don't believe this was cyber at all.” Secretary Duffy on the safety of the national airspace: “To the American traveler, our number one job is their safety and Bryan [Bedford] mentioned this and I’ve mentioned this before but we will keep you on the ground, you won’t get to your destination if we think you can’t get there safely. My first day on the job was the DCA air crash…My heart goes out to those families and everyone who has lost someone in aviation. We do everything we can to keep travelers safe and our airspace is safe. I fly all the time, my kids fly, my wife flies. This is a safe system, evidenced by what happened yesterday. If there is any issue with our telecom…we shut the airspace down. We brought airplanes in, we landed them safely, we figured out what was wrong, our systems came back online and have become fully operational. That’s how seriously we take safety. ” Secretary Duffy on the FAA’s progress modernizing America’s air traffic control system: “The Congress gave me a partial payment. They gave me $12.5 billion. And one of the problems that we had was [Congress] weren't quite sure that we would spend the money well and we'd build with the money. And that's the history of the FAA that goes back from Republicans and Democrats. They haven't spent the money well. So, they want to make sure we're going to spend and spend it well. And we have. And so, in the course of the last year, since I've got that $12.5 billion, I want to talk to you about what we've actually accomplished. Secretary Duffy on the need for Congress to fully fund air traffic control modernization: “I hope that they meet this moment and they invest in what will be the state-of-the-art, the best-in-class, best in the world air traffic control system. When I came in, President Trump, before the DCA air crash, was saying, ‘We have to modernize our airspace. I want you to work on modernizing air traffic control.’...and then if you look at the Congress–that you have both Democrats and Republicans who understand how important this is. For me, it gets to be frustrating where everyone says they want to do it and the president is pushing it but we don't get the resources. And I think this is the moment. If we don't start to switch out our systems, how long are we going to wait? I think this is a sign for [Congress] to lean in. This is bipartisan….We should be able to rely on our air traffic control system—making sure it works… Let’s not let the legacy of the past where investments weren't made, which is why we are here today. extraction.body: State-sponsored hackers from North Korea have taken more than $400 million in cryptocurrency by using fake video calls to steal people's identities, US authorities say. More than 900 victims have fallen prey to the scheme, which the FBI refers to as FaceStealer, in the last 18 months, according to the bureau. "The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," says FBI cyber director Brett Leatherman. This comes a week after the world's largest crypto exchange Binance revealed that hackers had used fake job interviews to steal a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from the company. US law enforcement agencies attributed the Binance hack, thought to be the largest crypto hack to date, to North Korea-linked actors. Pyongyang has denied this claim. Authorities say FaceStealer, the latest scheme, "aggressively targets" those who work in the cryptocurrency and web3 sectors, particularly those who are involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software. According to the FBI and US Justice Department, FaceStealer hackers use fake or hijacked social media accounts to invite potential victims into video calls hosted over "imposter versions" of Zoom, Microsoft Teams, and Google Meet. Next, the hackers play pre-recorded videos of previous victims the target is acquainted with to simulate a legitimate call – except that the audio would appear to malfunction. A message then pops up on the target's screen, asking them to "fix" the audio by clicking on a link. This "fix" would eventually download malware onto the target's device, which allows hackers to access their contact lists and apps, widening their pool of potential victims. Hackers would secretly record these calls and use the recordings as material to scam their new victims, according to the US authorities. The FBI has described FaceStealer as "a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user". "It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships," Patrick Grandy, assistant director in charge of the bureau's Los Angeles field office, said in a statement on Thursday. "If you can't imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough." Police say people are being targeted on WhatsApp with messages pretending to be from Lloyds Bank. Robert Barr directed Sean Favier and Iain Doyle to steal the funds from two houses in Midlothian in 2024. More than 900 victims have fallen prey to the scheme, which the FBI refers to as FaceStealer, in the last 18 months, according to the bureau.

"The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," says FBI cyber director Brett Leatherman.
This comes a week after the world's largest crypto exchange Binance revealed that hackers had used fake job interviews to steal a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from the company.
US law enforcement agencies attributed the Binance hack, thought to be the largest crypto hack to date, to North Korea-linked actors. Pyongyang has denied this claim.

Authorities say FaceStealer, the latest scheme, "aggressively targets" those who work in the cryptocurrency and web3 sectors, particularly those who are involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software.

According to the FBI and US Justice Department, FaceStealer hackers use fake or hijacked social media accounts to invite potential victims into video calls hosted over "imposter versions" of Zoom, Microsoft Teams, and Google Meet.
Next, the hackers play pre-recorded videos of previous victims the target is acquainted with to simulate a legitimate call – except that the audio would appear to malfunction.

A message then pops up on the target's screen, asking them to "fix" the audio by clicking on a link. This "fix" would eventually download malware onto the target's device, which allows hackers to access their contact lists and apps, widening their pool of potential victims.
Hackers would secretly record these calls and use the recordings as material to scam their new victims, according to the US authorities.
The FBI has described FaceStealer as "a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user".

"It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships," Patrick Grandy, assistant director in charge of the bureau's Los Angeles field office, said in a statement on Thursday.
"If you can't imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough."
Police say people are being targeted on WhatsApp with messages pretending to be from Lloyds Bank.
Robert Barr directed Sean Favier and Iain Doyle to steal the funds from two houses in Midlothian in 2024.
The Jersey Cyber Security Centre boss is "challenging whether everyone needs a connected fridge".

extraction.body: The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has established that threat actors tied to the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK aka North Korea) have stolen more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency as part of a social engineering scheme codenamed FaceStealer in the last 18 months. As part of a coordinated set of actions announced by the U.S. government, the cloud-based infrastructure used to pull off the "hard-to-detect" campaign has been seized. In tandem, the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) has announced the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen by the North Korea-linked TraderTraitor actors following the hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance. The plundered digital assets are used to fund Pyongyang's illicit weapons program, the DoJ added. "The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman in a statement. "North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months." According to the Justice Department, FaceStealer relies on surreptitiously recorded videos and deepfakes to facilitate cryptocurrency theft. Some aspects of the activity dovetail with a campaign documented by Kaspersky under the name GhostCall in October 2025. The activity is linked to a prolific North Korea-linked financially motivated threat cluster tracked as BlueNoroff , which is also known by the cryptonyms APT38, CageyChameleon, CryptoCore, DangerousPassword, Nickel Gladstone, Sapphire Sleet, Stardust Chollima, and UNC1069. The campaign involves luring targets with invitations to video meetings delivered from stolen accounts belonging to prior victims. Targets who join the meeting have their video stream recorded, while simultaneously serving an authentic, prerecorded webcam video of a previous victim or victims known to the target to build trust. "The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective," the DoJ said. "Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target's trust." A few seconds into the meeting, a mock technical error is presented to the victim, claiming that they cannot be heard, and they are provided a link to address the non-existent issue. The fix is a ClickFix-style lure that's designed to install malware on the victim's workstation and steal cryptocurrency, as well as abuse the target's privileges to other computer infrastructure. In an extensive report shared with The Hacker News in July 2026, JUMPSEC revealed how the social engineering operation is built atop a phishing kit designed to impersonate videoconferencing platforms like Zoom and Microsoft Teams. The cybersecurity company has characterized FaceStealer as a victim acquisition platform that involves using compromised trusted contacts as a pathway to fuel a self-propagating attack chain via Telegram. This includes hijacking social media and communications accounts such as Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack, and Discord for extended periods of time, and then accessing the victim's contact list to target the victim's personal and professional circles. The goal is to obtain access to the developers' devices and the software repository accounts they control to facilitate software supply chain attacks. Notably, the FaceStealer scheme was put to use in targeting the maintainer of the popular Axios npm package earlier this year to push a trojanized version that delivered a cross-platform remote access trojan (RAT). More than 900 victim webcam video recordings used by the threat actors to impersonate victims in follow-on attacks have been seized by the FBI. The agency said it's "aware of several other attempts by North Korean hackers to target software developers, maintainers, and software libraries with significant download volume." In a report published in April 2026, Arctic Wolf said the targeted social engineering campaign had targeted over 400 victims across more than 20 countries, with most of them concentrated in the U.S., Singapore, the U.K., Hong Kong, South Korea, and the U.A.E. "A full 80% of identified targets operate directly in cryptocurrency/blockchain finance (54%) or adjacent finance and investment sectors (26%)," the cybersecurity company noted at the time. "CEOs and founders alone account for 45% of the target set – nearly half. This underscores BlueNoroff's singular operational focus: individuals with access to cryptocurrency assets, wallet infrastructure, exchange platforms, or investment decision-making authority." The activity has since expanded in scope, with 677 targets identified across 58 countries. More than 80% of the targets are founders and C-suite executives. Besides introducing new lure themes such as a fake Chrome PDF Viewer update, the campaign incorporates generative AI technology from ChatGPT, Google, SpaceXAI Grok, and Wondershare AI Content Generator (AIGC) to supply the attackers with artwork, avatars, and convincing synthetic participant videos. "Upstream, reconnaissance has both widened and become more deliberate," the company added . "Lure material has been scraped not just from profile photos and prior victims' webcam streams, but from YouTube interviews and conference talks, which are screen-recorded by the actor. This allows them to capture a specific person's likeness and voice – a founder perhaps, or a CEO – and then create fake meeting footage without having to directly compromise the target themselves." Each new victim offers a pathway to further the attack. The cyclic modus operandi still remains the beating heart of the social engineering operation. "Combined with their new fake media generation capabilities to produce varied and credible lure content, this presents a significant escalation in BlueNoroff's efforts to compromise high-value individuals who control funds, signing keys, sensitive information, authenticated communications, and trusted professional relationships," Arctic Wolf said. It's worth emphasizing here that the FaceStealer campaign is distinct from ClickFake Interview , an iteration of Contagious Interview that also employs ClickFix-style tactics to trigger the execution of malware as part of recruitment-themed campaigns. Like FaceStealer, this involves the attackers approaching prospective targets by posing as recruiters on platforms like LinkedIn and sharing a "technical assessment" designed to run malware. In a post shared on LinkedIn, Alina Krasavina, an engineering manager at Delivery Hero, detailed how she was targeted in October 2026 by two fake recruiters on the same day, 13 minutes apart. "The first one sent a 'technical assessment': a Next.js project of 113 files. At the end of next.config.js, after 204 spaces, there was a backdoor," Krasavina said . "The second one didn't send any ZIP. On a video call, a 'Member of Technical Staff' asked me to share my whole screen, download a repo, and run it. When I said no, he told me it was 'a requirement to continue.' After the call, I wrote to the recruiter and asked for another interview format. About a minute later she blocked me." "The two attacks were built in opposite ways. The first one put the effort into the code and almost none into the recruiter. The second one put it into the people, and I never even saw its code." According to a joint cybersecurity advisory published by cybersecurity and intelligence agencies from Japan, the U.S., Australia, and Germany in late September 2026, the long-running campaign is estimated to have compromised at least 30,000 devices located in 100 countries. The attacks experiment with multiple delivery methods to convince victims to run malicious code - Last month, Sophos disclosed that an employee's corporate macOS device had been compromised in mid-September 2026 after they cloned a public code repository presented as a job interview coding assignment and opened it as a workspace in VS Code. "The repository contained a weaponized VS Code workspace settings file that replaced the editor's integrated terminal profile," the cybersecurity company said . "When a terminal opened in the workspace, the modified profile silently downloaded and ran a multi-stage payload." The payload in question is BeaverTail, a JavaScript loader that's used to deliver a Python backdoor referred to as InvisibleFerret. Both malware families are attributed to Contagious Interview. Sophos said the malware ran in memory on the device for about 26 hours, right from its execution on September 14, 2026, until it was rebooted a day later. The incident did not affect any of its products or services, or customer data or their systems, it added. What's more, recent research from JFrog has uncovered that the threat actors linked to the campaign have even set up a decoy company named AccuraSoftHire, complete with a careers site, client testimonials, a LinkedIn page, job ads on mainstream boards, and verified recruiters in an attempt to lend credibility and ultimately deceive candidates into running malware through a rigged take-home test and a video verification step. "Our research shows these lures are built to pass the checks people rely on: a professional website, a LinkedIn page, job ads on mainstream boards and recruiters with LinkedIn's verified badge," Guy Korolevski, senior security researcher at JFrog Security Research, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News. "Developers and other employees with system access can't be expected to catch that on their own, so employers need to set the rules. Interview assignments with downloads should only ever run in a disposable virtual machine, never on a work laptop. Security teams should also warn employees about downloading unknown files, even from a source they think they can trust. Developers can also check when a recruiter’s profile was created and whether the company's location is the same on every page." What's more, recent research from JFrog has uncovered that the threat actors linked to the campaign have even set up a decoy company named AccuraSoftHire, complete with a careers site, client testimonials, a LinkedIn page, job ads on mainstream boards, and verified recruiters in an attempt to lend credibility and ultimately deceive candidates into running malware through a rigged take-home test and a video verification step.

"Our research shows these lures are built to pass the checks people rely on: a professional website, a LinkedIn page, job ads on mainstream boards and recruiters with LinkedIn's verified badge," Guy Korolevski, senior security researcher at JFrog Security Research, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

"Developers and other employees with system access can't be expected to catch that on their own, so employers need to set the rules. Interview assignments with downloads should only ever run in a disposable virtual machine, never on a work laptop. Security teams should also warn employees about downloading unknown files, even from a source they think they can trust. Developers can also check when a recruiter’s profile was created and whether the company's location is the same on every page."

extraction.body: The US has seized servers linked to a North Korean scam that used fake video meetings and deepfakes to steal more than $400 million in crypto, and has moved to seize $1.2 billion that was taken from Binance. The United States Justice Department said Thursday it had seized cloud infrastructure used by North Korean hackers in a video-call scam that has stolen more than $400 million (€361 million) in cryptocurrency over 18 months. It also said it had court approval to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion taken in the recent Binance hack. The Federal Bureau of Investigation calls the scam "FaceStealer." According to the Justice Department, hackers sent meeting invitations from accounts taken over from earlier victims. Once a target joins, the hackers record their webcam video and play a prerecorded clip of a previous victim the target knows, so trusted contacts appear to be present. The FBI says hackers are also starting to use AI-generated deepfakes of well-known crypto figures. The hackers then stage a fake technical error and offer a link to "fix" it, which installs malware, the department said. In some cases, they waited months, or over a year, before stealing funds. After that, they use the victim's contacts to find new targets. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Most targets work in crypto and other internet-related fields, and the hackers are increasingly going after open-source software developers, apparently to enable supply-chain attacks, the department said. Under a federal warrant, the FBI seized more than 900 webcam videos of victims. "If you can't imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough," said Patrick Grandy, who heads the FBI's Los Angeles field office. The FBI ties FaceStealer to a hacking cluster known as Sapphire Sleet or UNC1069. It is separate from the North Korean military hackers blamed for the Binance theft. In the Binance case, the FBI said the group known as TraderTraitor stole more than $6 billion (5.4 billion euros) on or around October 29. AP put the figure at about $6.3 billion (5.7 billion euros) and called it the biggest crypto heist on record. US agencies and private firms have since frozen more than $2.7 billion (2.44 billion euros), the department said. Authorities usually file a forfeiture claim in court, after which a judge decides who has a rightful claim to the recovered funds, AP reported. "North Korea's government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft," said M. Scott Proctor, the department's principal deputy assistant attorney general for national security. North Korea has denied involvement in the Binance hack.

extraction.body: State-sponsored hackers from North Korea have taken more than $400 million in cryptocurrency by using fake video calls to steal people's identities, US authorities say. More than 900 victims have fallen prey to the scheme, which the FBI refers to as FaceStealer, in the last 18 months, according to the bureau. "The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," says FBI cyber director Brett Leatherman. This comes a week after the world's largest crypto exchange Binance revealed that hackers had used fake job interviews to steal a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from the company. US law enforcement agencies attributed the Binance hack, thought to be the largest crypto hack to date, to North Korea-linked actors. Pyongyang has denied this claim. Authorities say FaceStealer, the latest scheme, "aggressively targets" those who work in the cryptocurrency and web3 sectors, particularly those who are involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software. According to the FBI and US Justice Department, FaceStealer hackers use fake or hijacked social media accounts to invite potential victims into video calls hosted over "imposter versions" of Zoom, Microsoft Teams, and Google Meet. Next, the hackers play pre-recorded videos of previous victims the target is acquainted with to simulate a legitimate call – except that the audio would appear to malfunction. A message then pops up on the target's screen, asking them to "fix" the audio by clicking on a link. This "fix" would eventually download malware onto the target's device, which allows hackers to access their contact lists and apps, widening their pool of potential victims. Hackers would secretly record these calls and use the recordings as material to scam their new victims, according to the US authorities. The FBI has described FaceStealer as "a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user". "It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships," Patrick Grandy, assistant director in charge of the bureau's Los Angeles field office, said in a statement on Thursday. "If you can't imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough." Police say people are being targeted on WhatsApp with messages pretending to be from Lloyds Bank. passages: State-sponsored hackers from North Korea have taken more than $400 million in cryptocurrency by using fake video calls to steal people's identities, US authorities say.
More than 900 victims have fallen prey to the scheme, which the FBI refers to as FaceStealer, in the last 18 months, according to the bureau.

"The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," says FBI cyber director Brett Leatherman.
This comes a week after the world's largest crypto exchange Binance revealed that hackers had used fake job interviews to steal a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from the company.
US law enforcement agencies attributed the Binance hack, thought to be the largest crypto hack to date, to North Korea-linked actors. Pyongyang has denied this claim.

Authorities say FaceStealer, the latest scheme, "aggressively targets" those who work in the cryptocurrency and web3 sectors, particularly those who are involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software.

According to the FBI and US Justice Department, FaceStealer hackers use fake or hijacked social media accounts to invite potential victims into video calls hosted over "imposter versions" of Zoom, Microsoft Teams, and Google Meet.
Next, the hackers play pre-recorded videos of previous victims the target is acquainted with to simulate a legitimate call – except that the audio would appear to malfunction.

A message then pops up on the target's screen, asking them to "fix" the audio by clicking on a link. This "fix" would eventually download malware onto the target's device, which allows hackers to access their contact lists and apps, widening their pool of potential victims.
Hackers would secretly record these calls and use the recordings as material to scam their new victims, according to the US authorities.
The FBI has described FaceStealer as "a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user".

"It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships," Patrick Grandy, assistant director in charge of the bureau's Los Angeles field office, said in a statement on Thursday.
"If you can't imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough."
Police say people are being targeted on WhatsApp with messages pretending to be from Lloyds Bank.

extraction.body: The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has established that threat actors tied to the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK aka North Korea) have stolen more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency as part of a social engineering scheme codenamed FaceStealer in the last 18 months. As part of a coordinated set of actions announced by the U.S. government, the cloud-based infrastructure used to pull off the "hard-to-detect" campaign has been seized. In tandem, the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) has announced the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen by the North Korea-linked TraderTraitor actors following the hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance. The plundered digital assets are used to fund Pyongyang's illicit weapons program, the DoJ added. "The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman in a statement. "North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months." According to the Justice Department, FaceStealer relies on surreptitiously recorded videos and deepfakes to facilitate cryptocurrency theft. Some aspects of the activity dovetail with a campaign documented by Kaspersky under the name GhostCall in October 2025. The activity is linked to a prolific North Korea-linked financially motivated threat cluster tracked as BlueNoroff , which is also known by the cryptonyms APT38, CageyChameleon, CryptoCore, DangerousPassword, Nickel Gladstone, Sapphire Sleet, Stardust Chollima, and UNC1069. The campaign involves luring targets with invitations to video meetings delivered from stolen accounts belonging to prior victims. Targets who join the meeting have their video stream recorded, while simultaneously serving an authentic, prerecorded webcam video of a previous victim or victims known to the target to build trust. "The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective," the DoJ said. "Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target's trust." A few seconds into the meeting, a mock technical error is presented to the victim, claiming that they cannot be heard, and they are provided a link to address the non-existent issue. The fix is a ClickFix-style lure that's designed to install malware on the victim's workstation and steal cryptocurrency, as well as abuse the target's privileges to other computer infrastructure. In an extensive report shared with The Hacker News in July 2026, JUMPSEC revealed how the social engineering operation is built atop a phishing kit designed to impersonate videoconferencing platforms like Zoom and Microsoft Teams. The cybersecurity company has characterized FaceStealer as a victim acquisition platform that involves using compromised trusted contacts as a pathway to fuel a self-propagating attack chain via Telegram. This includes hijacking social media and communications accounts such as Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack, and Discord for extended periods of time, and then accessing the victim's contact list to target the victim's personal and professional circles. The goal is to obtain access to the developers' devices and the software repository accounts they control to facilitate software supply chain attacks. Notably, the FaceStealer scheme was put to use in targeting the maintainer of the popular Axios npm package earlier this year to push a trojanized version that delivered a cross-platform remote access trojan (RAT). More than 900 victim webcam video recordings used by the threat actors to impersonate victims in follow-on attacks have been seized by the FBI. The agency said it's "aware of several other attempts by North Korean hackers to target software developers, maintainers, and software libraries with significant download volume." In a report published in April 2026, Arctic Wolf said the targeted social engineering campaign had targeted over 400 victims across more than 20 countries, with most of them concentrated in the U.S., Singapore, the U.K., Hong Kong, South Korea, and the U.A.E. "A full 80% of identified targets operate directly in cryptocurrency/blockchain finance (54%) or adjacent finance and investment sectors (26%)," the cybersecurity company noted at the time. "CEOs and founders alone account for 45% of the target set – nearly half. This underscores BlueNoroff's singular operational focus: individuals with access to cryptocurrency assets, wallet infrastructure, exchange platforms, or investment decision-making authority." The activity has since expanded in scope, with 677 targets identified across 58 countries. More than 80% of the targets are founders and C-suite executives. Besides introducing new lure themes such as a fake Chrome PDF Viewer update, the campaign incorporates generative AI technology from ChatGPT, Google, SpaceXAI Grok, and Wondershare AI Content Generator (AIGC) to supply the attackers with artwork, avatars, and convincing synthetic participant videos. "Upstream, reconnaissance has both widened and become more deliberate," the company added . "Lure material has been scraped not just from profile photos and prior victims' webcam streams, but from YouTube interviews and conference talks, which are screen-recorded by the actor. This allows them to capture a specific person's likeness and voice – a founder perhaps, or a CEO – and then create fake meeting footage without having to directly compromise the target themselves." Each new victim offers a pathway to further the attack. The cyclic modus operandi still remains the beating heart of the social engineering operation. "Combined with their new fake media generation capabilities to produce varied and credible lure content, this presents a significant escalation in BlueNoroff's efforts to compromise high-value individuals who control funds, signing keys, sensitive information, authenticated communications, and trusted professional relationships," Arctic Wolf said. It's worth emphasizing here that the FaceStealer campaign is distinct from ClickFake Interview , an iteration of Contagious Interview that also employs ClickFix-style tactics to trigger the execution of malware as part of recruitment-themed campaigns. Like FaceStealer, this involves the attackers approaching prospective targets by posing as recruiters on platforms like LinkedIn and sharing a "technical assessment" designed to run malware. In a post shared on LinkedIn, Alina Krasavina, an engineering manager at Delivery Hero, detailed how she was targeted in October 2026 by two fake recruiters on the same day, 13 minutes apart. "The first one sent a 'technical assessment': a Next.js project of 113 files. At the end of next.config.js, after 204 spaces, there was a backdoor," Krasavina said . "The second one didn't send any ZIP. On a video call, a 'Member of Technical Staff' asked me to share my whole screen, download a repo, and run it. When I said no, he told me it was 'a requirement to continue.' After the call, I wrote to the recruiter and asked for another interview format. About a minute later she blocked me." "The two attacks were built in opposite ways. The first one put the effort into the code and almost none into the recruiter. The second one put it into the people, and I never even saw its code." According to a joint cybersecurity advisory published by cybersecurity and intelligence agencies from Japan, the U.S., Australia, and Germany in late September 2026, the long-running campaign is estimated to have compromised at least 30,000 devices located in 100 countries. The attacks experiment with multiple delivery methods to convince victims to run malicious code - Last month, Sophos disclosed that an employee's corporate macOS device had been compromised in mid-September 2026 after they cloned a public code repository presented as a job interview coding assignment and opened it as a workspace in VS Code. "The repository contained a weaponized VS Code workspace settings file that replaced the editor's integrated terminal profile," the cybersecurity company said . "When a terminal opened in the workspace, the modified profile silently downloaded and ran a multi-stage payload." The payload in question is BeaverTail, a JavaScript loader that's used to deliver a Python backdoor referred to as InvisibleFerret. Both malware families are attributed to Contagious Interview. Sophos said the malware ran in memory on the device for about 26 hours, right from its execution on September 14, 2026, until it was rebooted a day later. The incident did not affect any of its products or services, or customer data or their systems, it added. What's more, recent research from JFrog has uncovered that the threat actors linked to the campaign have even set up a decoy company named AccuraSoftHire, complete with a careers site, client testimonials, a LinkedIn page, job ads on mainstream boards, and verified recruiters in an attempt to lend credibility and ultimately deceive candidates into running malware through a rigged take-home test and a video verification step. "Our research shows these lures are built to pass the checks people rely on: a professional website, a LinkedIn page, job ads on mainstream boards and recruiters with LinkedIn's verified badge," Guy Korolevski, senior security researcher at JFrog Security Research, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News. "Developers and other employees with system access can't be expected to catch that on their own, so employers need to set the rules. Interview assignments with downloads should only ever run in a disposable virtual machine, never on a work laptop. Security teams should also warn employees about downloading unknown files, even from a source they think they can trust. Developers can also check when a recruiter’s profile was created and whether the company's location is the same on every page." extraction.body: A new entity tied to Alice Huang, the Chinese executive at the heart of the scandal that led to the resignation of NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang, disclosed banned NVIDIA GPUs as part of collateral offered by the holding company for financing in 2025, according to a new report from Bloomberg. The new details share another link with Alice Huang, whose firm Megaspeed has already been probed for supplying banned NVIDIA AI chips to China. While reports suggest that the US intelligence community is unconvinced that Alice Huang, the associate of NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang, was a spy, her links to transporting banned GPUs to China are nevertheless present in Bloomberg's analysis of filings with Chinese regulators. In a report , the publication shares that a holding company called Shanghai Longteng Intelligent Computing Data Group Co. ended up gaining access to servers purchased by Aperia Cloud from Dell. Aperia's CEO is facing charges for fraud related to the smuggling of NVIDIA GPUs to China. A Longteng unit (Shanghai Longjie Yaoteng) then used these servers as part of a group of equipment as collateral for financing, says the report, which adds that Alice founded Longteng in 2016 and relinquished shares in 2017. The details about the holding company, which is tied to a Shanghai data center with links to Megaspeed, come as the Southeast Asian nation of Malaysia further tightens GPU rules. Amidst the firestorm created by the former NVIDIA CEO, Minister of Investment, Trade and Industry Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani shared earlier today that his country was evaluating current laws to determine whether they could target GPU re-exports to comply with the US sanctions. US lawmakers are also advancing legislation to prevent Chinese AI companies from accessing restricted chips remotely, with 'footprints' of the banned Blackwell GPUs discovered in forensic analysis of leading Chinese AI models. While Bloomberg also claims that servers manufactured by Super Micro, using the H100 or H200 chips, were also part of the regulatory disclosure, the firm asserted that it did not directly make any such sales. Super Micro has long faced scrutiny for similar shipments. Individuals tied to the firm were charged by the Justice Department in March for diverting restricted chips to China. However, the firm's statement claimed that the actions of the indicted were against its rules and policies and in line with US law. coreStoryFacts.text: A Chinese company with ties to Alice Huang procured NVIDIA AI chips banned in the country, which were then installed at a Shanghai AI facility that also has ties to Alice Huang, according to Bloomberg .

The publication says the documents it has reviewed for its report shows explicit evidence that there's a network of Chinese companies, which have managed to get their hands on NVIDIA chips that weren't supposed to be sold in China, with Huang at the center.
Bloomberg found the hardware details in filings from a company called Shanghai Longteng Intelligent Computing, which was set up by Alice a decade ago.
They were documented as part of the information the company had to submit to the Chinese government, since it was using its servers as a collateral for financing.
The filings also revealed that the company's servers included 52 units made by Super Micro Computer Inc.
Its president is Kang Wei, who is being reported as Alice's husband and the person who introduced her to Jensen Huang .
Former NVIDIA-CEO Jensen Huang is due to testify before Congress this month , and it's likely all of this information will be pored over by officials in the run-up to the event.
To the public, Alice was an executive at Singaporean company Megaspeed, but the reports that had come out since the issue blew up paint a different picture of who she truly was.

Huang stepped down on Thursday following revelations of extramarital affairs, including a reported relationship with a woman suspected by US intelligence of having links to China.

A Chinese company with ties to Alice Huang procured NVIDIA AI chips banned in the country, which were then installed at a Shanghai AI facility that also has ties to Alice Huang, according to Bloomberg . The publication says the documents it has reviewed for its report shows explicit evidence that there's a network of Chinese companies, which have managed to get their hands on NVIDIA chips that weren't supposed to be sold in China, with Huang at the center. To the public, Alice was an executive at Singaporean company Megaspeed, but the reports that had come out since the issue blew up paint a different picture of who she truly was. Bloomberg says the NVIDIA chips listed in the documents it reviewed were sold to Aperia Cloud Services, an NVIDIA Cloud Partner in Singapore. Aperia purchased 22 servers from Dell containing NVIDIA H800 chips, which are banned in China. According to the report, Dell cut off business ties with Aperia in February 2025 due to concerns around the deal. Bloomberg found the hardware details in filings from a company called Shanghai Longteng Intelligent Computing, which was set up by Alice a decade ago. They were documented as part of the information the company had to submit to the Chinese government, since it was using its servers as a collateral for financing. While Alice hasn't been part of Shanghai Longteng since 2017 — and the documents didn't say if she was personally involved in the procurement of the chips — Huang Yu, who was identified as her sister, was the one who took over as majority owner. The filings also revealed that the company's servers included 52 units made by Super Micro Computer Inc. Those units were equipped with NVIDIA's H100 or H200 chips, which can't be sold to Chinese companies without express permission from the US government. The Shanghai AI facility where the smuggled NVIDIA units were installed is called the Yangtze River Delta Project, which Bloomberg says also has ties to Alice Huang. Its president is Kang Wei, who is being reported as Alice's husband and the person who introduced her to Jensen Huang . Alice's company Megaspeed also presented a rendering of the Yangtze River Delta Project to its investors in 2024 and claimed that it was its largest AI facility. Former NVIDIA-CEO Jensen Huang is due to testify before Congress this month , and it's likely all of this information will be pored over by officials in the run-up to the event.

extraction.body: A new entity tied to Alice Huang, the Chinese executive at the heart of the scandal that led to the resignation of NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang, disclosed banned NVIDIA GPUs as part of collateral offered by the holding company for financing in 2025, according to a new report from Bloomberg. The new details share another link with Alice Huang, whose firm Megaspeed has already been probed for supplying banned NVIDIA AI chips to China. While reports suggest that the US intelligence community is unconvinced that Alice Huang, the associate of NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang, was a spy, her links to transporting banned GPUs to China are nevertheless present in Bloomberg's analysis of filings with Chinese regulators. In a report , the publication shares that a holding company called Shanghai Longteng Intelligent Computing Data Group Co. ended up gaining access to servers purchased by Aperia Cloud from Dell. Aperia's CEO is facing charges for fraud related to the smuggling of NVIDIA GPUs to China. A Longteng unit (Shanghai Longjie Yaoteng) then used these servers as part of a group of equipment as collateral for financing, says the report, which adds that Alice founded Longteng in 2016 and relinquished shares in 2017. The details about the holding company, which is tied to a Shanghai data center with links to Megaspeed, come as the Southeast Asian nation of Malaysia further tightens GPU rules. Amidst the firestorm created by the former NVIDIA CEO, Minister of Investment, Trade and Industry Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani shared earlier today that his country was evaluating current laws to determine whether they could target GPU re-exports to comply with the US sanctions. US lawmakers are also advancing legislation to prevent Chinese AI companies from accessing restricted chips remotely, with 'footprints' of the banned Blackwell GPUs discovered in forensic analysis of leading Chinese AI models. While Bloomberg also claims that servers manufactured by Super Micro, using the H100 or H200 chips, were also part of the regulatory disclosure, the firm asserted that it did not directly make any such sales. Super Micro has long faced scrutiny for similar shipments. Individuals tied to the firm were charged by the Justice Department in March for diverting restricted chips to China. However, the firm's statement claimed that the actions of the indicted were against its rules and policies and in line with US law. extraction.body: Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has drawn a range of responses across Asia, with some governments moving to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations. On Sunday, November 8, Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation after reports that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation; Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed. Nvidia’s influence extends far beyond the United States. The chip giant has built close ties with companies worldwide, particularly in Asia, where many of its key partners play important roles in the global AI industry. China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing. On Friday , a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang. Huang’s exit has also raised uncertainty over more than $3 billion in Chinese AI computing projects reliant on Nvidia’s restricted processors, according to Reuters. Many of these chips are subject to U.S. export controls, making them difficult for Chinese companies to obtain. In Singapore, authorities seized the passport of Alice Huang, former CEO of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, in June 2025 as part of an investigation into possible false declarations regarding server purchases, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs. The Singapore ministry said police took her passport to ensure she remained available for questioning, as she was not based in Singapore. The investigation examined whether servers shipped from Singapore to Malaysia were later sent to other countries without proper declaration. In February 2026, police found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang had committed offenses related to the suspected false declarations, according to the ministry. However, authorities said she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed. She was issued a warning and barred from re-entering Singapore. Her passport was returned that month. Singapore also said it received limited assistance from U.S. authorities despite repeated requests for information about U.S. server maker Supermicro. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said its investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals remains ongoing. The ministry did not identify the six individuals or specify their alleged roles in the case. South Korea has close ties to Nvidia, with major chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix playing important roles in supplying memory chips used in its AI processors. Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects. Apart from that, South Korea’s government AI strategy council held an emergency meeting on Friday to assess the potential impact of Huang’s departure on the country’s AI industry, per a local media report. Taiwan’s Economy Minister Kung Ming-shin said Huang’s departure was unlikely to significantly change the growth of the global AI industry, according to local media . Meanwhile, Taipei’s city government said Nvidia’s planned overseas headquarters in the city remained on track despite the leadership change. The company has met its contractual obligations so far, and officials said they would continue to support the project. In Japan, the Industry Ministry said the government would closely monitor Nvidia following Huang’s resignation, describing the chipmaker as an important player in Japan’s AI semiconductor industry, Reuters reported. Deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki said it was too early to assess the impact on the global AI industry, while stressing Japan’s commitment to ensuring a stable supply of semiconductors. passages: [BEIJING] Nvidia has said US export controls have effectively shut it out of China’s artificial intelligence data centre market, but a Reuters review has identified more than US$3 billion in Chinese computing projects built around the American chipmaker’s restricted processors.

The findings come a day after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive amid a scandal over his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by US authorities of intelligence ties to Beijing .
Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation , saying it had no reason to believe company secrets or US national security were compromised.
There has been no public finding that Jensen Huang violated export-control laws.
But an IDC report cited by Reuters in October estimated Nvidia still accounted for 34 per cent of Chinese AI-accelerator shipments in the first half of 2026.
Huang, a vocal advocate of easing export restrictions, said in 2025 Nvidia’s market share in China had fallen from 95 per cent to zero.
Inside Jensen Huang’s last hours as Nvidia CEO

The projects, stretching from China’s wealthy coastal technology hubs to remote western provinces, reveal the scale of continuing demand for Nvidia hardware even as Washington seeks to curb Beijing’s access to the technology powering the global AI boom .
The estimate includes planned investments and signed contracts as well as completed installations.
It covers buildings, power systems and other infrastructure, and does not reflect spending on Nvidia chips alone.
Huang’s departure could deepen these vulnerabilities by weakening Nvidia’s lobbying leverage as US lawmakers press for tighter controls.

The scrutiny has intensified since Huang’s resignation on Thursday (Nov 12), following allegations involving Alice Huang, a former executive associated with Singapore-based Nvidia cloud partner Megaspeed .
Across China, developers and institutions are advancing billions of dollars in AI data centre projects designed around restricted Nvidia H100, H200, and H800 processors.

These range from massive regional computing hubs to retrofitted commercial sites – such as a facility in northwestern Gansu province that was expected to install thousands of Nvidia chips before end-2026, though it remains unclear if those processors ever arrived.
Washington began restricting Nvidia’s advanced AI processors in 2022 and subsequently tightened controls on modified chips developed for China, including the H800.
Megaspeed has denied illegally diverting Nvidia chips to China.
The Chinese projects identified by Reuters have not been linked to Megaspeed or the allegations involving Huang.
The findings paint a detailed picture of how deeply Nvidia technology remains embedded in China’s AI expansion.
China’s commerce ministry and Nvidia did not immedietely respond to Reuters request for comment.

The company has also excluded China data centre computing revenue from its forecasts, citing regulatory uncertainty. That does not mean Chinese demand has disappeared. Sunny Cheung, an analyst at the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation, said Reuters’ findings reinforce his own view on enforcement.

Across China, developers and institutions are advancing billions of dollars in AI data centre projects designed around restricted Nvidia H100, H200, and H800 processors.

These range from massive regional computing hubs to retrofitted commercial sites – such as a facility in northwestern Gansu province that was expected to install thousands of Nvidia chips before end-2026, though it remains unclear if those processors ever arrived.
