Huang’s departure could deepen these vulnerabilities by weakening Nvidia’s lobbying leverage as US lawmakers press for tighter controls.
Washington began restricting Nvidia’s advanced AI processors in 2022 and subsequently tightened controls on modified chips developed for China, including the H800.
In January, the Trump administration moved to review H200 export licences for eligible Chinese customers individually , subject to conditions.

Nvidia’s August filing said it was effectively excluded from China’s data centre computing market. But an IDC report cited by Reuters in October estimated Nvidia still accounted for 34 per cent of Chinese AI-accelerator shipments in the first half of 2026.
The figures measure different things and do not establish how the restricted hardware identified in the Reuters investigation reached Chinese users.

The scrutiny has intensified since Huang’s resignation on Thursday (Nov 12), following allegations involving Alice Huang, a former executive associated with Singapore-based Nvidia cloud partner Megaspeed .
Megaspeed has denied illegally diverting Nvidia chips to China.

Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation , saying it had no reason to believe company secrets or US national security were compromised. There has been no public finding that Jensen Huang violated export-control laws.

passages: The intersection of Jensen Huang's sudden resignation as Nvidia's CEO, intense U.S. regulatory scrutiny, and fresh investigative findings regarding restricted semiconductor flows has created a massive compliance and political crisis for the tech giant.

A comprehensive investigation by Reuters revealed a pipeline of over $3 billion in Chinese computing projects—embedded across local government-backed ventures, regional cloud data centers, state-owned engineering groups, and universities—that rely directly on restricted Nvidia processors (such as the H100 and H200 series).

The Resignation: Jensen Huang stepped down as chief executive following intense scrutiny surrounding his personal relationships—specifically involving a businesswoman (Alice Huang) alleged by U.S. authorities to have intelligence ties to Beijing.

The Reuters review examined more than 150 Chinese procurement notices, investment plans, construction contracts and corporate disclosures, identifying projects and equipment agreements with a combined reported value exceeding 23 billion yuan ($3.2 billion).

The projects, stretching from China's wealthy coastal technology hubs to remote western provinces, reveal the scale of continuing demand for Nvidia hardware even as Washington seeks to curb Beijing's access to the technology powering the global artificial-intelligence (AI) boom.

coreStoryFacts.text: Intelligence agencies worried that she was a spy, helping the Chinese government gain information from Nvidia and Jensen Huang, and fretted that Nvidia's CEO had access to President Donald Trump.

The Nvidia spokesperson pushed back on the story in a statement to CNBC, saying that Singapore-based Megaspeed is another one of the company's regional cloud customers, and that Jensen Huang's interactions with its officials are not unusual, because he speaks with thousands of customers every year.
Earlier this year the U.S. government cleared Nvidia's H200 chip to be shipped to China, but Chinese regulators prevented their imports.
H200s are Nvidia's Hopper generation chip, not the current faster Blackwell generation currently used by American AI developers.
Last year, Nvidia wrote off about $4.5 billion in Chinese-tuned AI chips.
Nvidia said that Megaspeed had already been investigated for evading export controls.
The spokesperson added that customers don't get access to Nvidia trade secrets or relevant national security information.
Nvidia has had to walk a tightrope in Washington as its AI chips have become a powerful tool for all AI developers and a bargaining chip in economic competition with China.
China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing.

On Friday , a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang.
Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects.

Meanwhile, Taipei’s city government said Nvidia’s planned overseas headquarters in the city remained on track despite the leadership change.

extraction.body: An Nvidia spokesperson on Thursday pushed back on a New York Times report that detailed American intelligence agencies surveilling a person close to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang because they thought she could be a Chinese intelligence asset. According to the Times report , which cited people briefed on intelligence surveillance, Alice Huang, who is linked to the Singapore-based cloud Megaspeed, developed a close relationship with Nvidia's Jensen Huang. Intelligence agencies worried that she was a spy, helping the Chinese government gain information from Nvidia and Jensen Huang, and fretted that Nvidia's CEO had access to President Donald Trump. The Nvidia spokesperson pushed back on the story in a statement to CNBC, saying that Singapore-based Megaspeed is another one of the company's regional cloud customers, and that Jensen Huang's interactions with its officials are not unusual, because he speaks with thousands of customers every year. The spokesperson added that customers don't get access to Nvidia trade secrets or relevant national security information. The report also alleged that Megaspeed was previously suspected of helping companies evade U.S. export controls on Nvidia's AI chips, which aren't allowed to be shipped to China. Nvidia said that Megaspeed had already been investigated for evading export controls. "The diversion allegations against this regional cloud were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year," the spokesperson said in a statement. Nvidia implied that the U.S. government had not briefed Nvidia on Alice Huang. "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know," the spokesperson said. Nvidia has had to walk a tightrope in Washington as its AI chips have become a powerful tool for all AI developers and a bargaining chip in economic competition with China. Politicians and analysts say that Nvidia's AI chips could be used to create Chinese military AI models, or commercial AI models that could compete and eventually surpass American technology. As AI has become more important to the government, Nvidia's Huang has befriended Trump and has given pro-American speeches about building U.S. AI infrastructure. Huang has appeared with Trump at state dinners, AI summits, and international trips, all while pushing for certain Nvidia chips to get a green light to be shipped to China. Earlier this year the U.S. government cleared Nvidia's H200 chip to be shipped to China, but Chinese regulators prevented their imports. H200s are Nvidia's Hopper generation chip, not the current faster Blackwell generation currently used by American AI developers. The Nvidia spokesperson said the Chinese government is not looking for Nvidia products from regional clouds like Megaspeed. "Instead, the PRC government blocked U.S. AI chips, protecting its own industry and resulting in the largest write-offs in U.S. tech history," the Nvidia spokesperson said. extraction.body: Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has drawn a range of responses across Asia, with some governments moving to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations. On Sunday, November 8, Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation after reports that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation; Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed. Nvidia’s influence extends far beyond the United States. The chip giant has built close ties with companies worldwide, particularly in Asia, where many of its key partners play important roles in the global AI industry. China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing. On Friday , a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang. Huang’s exit has also raised uncertainty over more than $3 billion in Chinese AI computing projects reliant on Nvidia’s restricted processors, according to Reuters. Many of these chips are subject to U.S. export controls, making them difficult for Chinese companies to obtain. In Singapore, authorities seized the passport of Alice Huang, former CEO of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, in June 2025 as part of an investigation into possible false declarations regarding server purchases, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs. The Singapore ministry said police took her passport to ensure she remained available for questioning, as she was not based in Singapore. The investigation examined whether servers shipped from Singapore to Malaysia were later sent to other countries without proper declaration. In February 2026, police found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang had committed offenses related to the suspected false declarations, according to the ministry. However, authorities said she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed. She was issued a warning and barred from re-entering Singapore. Her passport was returned that month. Singapore also said it received limited assistance from U.S. authorities despite repeated requests for information about U.S. server maker Supermicro. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said its investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals remains ongoing. The ministry did not identify the six individuals or specify their alleged roles in the case. South Korea has close ties to Nvidia, with major chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix playing important roles in supplying memory chips used in its AI processors. Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects. Apart from that, South Korea’s government AI strategy council held an emergency meeting on Friday to assess the potential impact of Huang’s departure on the country’s AI industry, per a local media report. Taiwan’s Economy Minister Kung Ming-shin said Huang’s departure was unlikely to significantly change the growth of the global AI industry, according to local media . Meanwhile, Taipei’s city government said Nvidia’s planned overseas headquarters in the city remained on track despite the leadership change. The company has met its contractual obligations so far, and officials said they would continue to support the project. In Japan, the Industry Ministry said the government would closely monitor Nvidia following Huang’s resignation, describing the chipmaker as an important player in Japan’s AI semiconductor industry, Reuters reported. Deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki said it was too early to assess the impact on the global AI industry, while stressing Japan’s commitment to ensuring a stable supply of semiconductors. Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation , saying it had no reason to believe company secrets or US national security were compromised.
There has been no public finding that Jensen Huang violated export-control laws.
But an IDC report cited by Reuters in October estimated Nvidia still accounted for 34 per cent of Chinese AI-accelerator shipments in the first half of 2026.
Huang, a vocal advocate of easing export restrictions, said in 2025 Nvidia’s market share in China had fallen from 95 per cent to zero.
Inside Jensen Huang’s last hours as Nvidia CEO

The projects, stretching from China’s wealthy coastal technology hubs to remote western provinces, reveal the scale of continuing demand for Nvidia hardware even as Washington seeks to curb Beijing’s access to the technology powering the global AI boom .
The estimate includes planned investments and signed contracts as well as completed installations.
It covers buildings, power systems and other infrastructure, and does not reflect spending on Nvidia chips alone.
Huang’s departure could deepen these vulnerabilities by weakening Nvidia’s lobbying leverage as US lawmakers press for tighter controls.

The scrutiny has intensified since Huang’s resignation on Thursday (Nov 12), following allegations involving Alice Huang, a former executive associated with Singapore-based Nvidia cloud partner Megaspeed .
Across China, developers and institutions are advancing billions of dollars in AI data centre projects designed around restricted Nvidia H100, H200, and H800 processors.

These range from massive regional computing hubs to retrofitted commercial sites – such as a facility in northwestern Gansu province that was expected to install thousands of Nvidia chips before end-2026, though it remains unclear if those processors ever arrived.
Washington began restricting Nvidia’s advanced AI processors in 2022 and subsequently tightened controls on modified chips developed for China, including the H800.
Megaspeed has denied illegally diverting Nvidia chips to China.
The Chinese projects identified by Reuters have not been linked to Megaspeed or the allegations involving Huang.
The findings paint a detailed picture of how deeply Nvidia technology remains embedded in China’s AI expansion.
China’s commerce ministry and Nvidia did not immedietely respond to Reuters request for comment.

The projects, stretching from China’s wealthy coastal technology hubs to remote western provinces, reveal the scale of continuing demand for Nvidia hardware even as Washington seeks to curb Beijing’s access to the technology powering the global AI boom . The Reuters review examined more than 150 Chinese procurement notices, investment plans, construction contracts and corporate disclosures, identifying projects and equipment agreements with a combined reported value exceeding 23 billion yuan (US$3.2 billion). The findings paint a detailed picture of how deeply Nvidia technology remains embedded in China’s AI expansion. They reveal the company’s technology reaches well beyond China’s largest tech firms, into local government-backed ventures, universities and regional computing centres. The company has also excluded China data centre computing revenue from its forecasts, citing regulatory uncertainty. That does not mean Chinese demand has disappeared. While Nvidia’s statements address its own ability to compete and sell directly in China, the documents Reuters reviewed show Chinese customers continuing to plan purchases and, in some cases, operating restricted processors. Sunny Cheung, an analyst at the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation, said Reuters’ findings reinforce his own view on enforcement. “Washington must stop focusing solely on who buys the chips on the surface and start examining who ultimately uses the computing power – and for what purpose,” said Cheung. sources.title: Jensen Huang’s exit and US scrutiny imperil $3 billion in Chinese AI projects reliant on Nvidia - The News International
passages: The intersection of Jensen Huang's sudden resignation as Nvidia's CEO, intense U.S. regulatory scrutiny, and fresh investigative findings regarding restricted semiconductor flows has created a massive compliance and political crisis for the tech giant.

A comprehensive investigation by Reuters revealed a pipeline of over $3 billion in Chinese computing projects—embedded across local government-backed ventures, regional cloud data centers, state-owned engineering groups, and universities—that rely directly on restricted Nvidia processors (such as the H100 and H200 series).

The Resignation: Jensen Huang stepped down as chief executive following intense scrutiny surrounding his personal relationships—specifically involving a businesswoman (Alice Huang) alleged by U.S. authorities to have intelligence ties to Beijing.

The Reuters review examined more than 150 Chinese procurement notices, investment plans, construction contracts and corporate disclosures, identifying projects and equipment agreements with a combined reported value exceeding 23 billion yuan ($3.2 billion).

The projects, stretching from China's wealthy coastal technology hubs to remote western provinces, reveal the scale of continuing demand for Nvidia hardware even as Washington seeks to curb Beijing's access to the technology powering the global artificial-intelligence (AI) boom.
The exposure of these projects coincides with unprecedented turbulence at the top of Nvidia:
The estimate includes planned investments and signed contracts as well as completed installations.
It covers buildings, power systems and other infrastructure, and does not reflect spending on Nvidia chips alone
Following a historic leadership exit, explosive findings reveal a sprawling multi-billion-dollar network of restricted U.S. processors embedded across Beijing's AI ecosystem

While Nvidia’s official filings have long maintained that U.S. export controls and licensing restrictions have effectively frozen or excluded the company from China’s data-center market, local planning and procurement documents prove that hardware continues to reach Chinese end-users.

Industry estimates (including IDC data) show Nvidia maintaining a notable presence via secondary or indirect routes, highlighting how difficult it is for Washington to completely sever high-end computing supply chains.

While Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation concluding that no company secrets or national security parameters were compromised, and no legal finding of export-control violations has been leveled against Huang directly, the political shockwaves are immense.
The findings paint a detailed picture of how deeply Nvidia technology remains embedded in China's AI expansion.

extraction.body: Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security. U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported. The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. coreStoryFacts.text: Nov 11 (Reuters) - A controversy surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and the chipmaker's China business has spiraled into a national-security and political storm, drawing scrutiny from lawmakers, the company's board ‌and investors.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
The fallout has also intensified a long-running debate in Washington over whether the US ‌should allow its most advanced AI chips to be sold to China.
U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security.
This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times.

Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him.
Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report.
Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up.
Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said .
The company’s current CFO, Colette Kress , will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties.

The chairmen of the House Select Committee on China, the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and the House Intelligence Committee formally requested a closed-door briefing from Jensen Huang, with the request reported around November 5, 2026.
No public response from Huang or Nvidia was identified in the cited reporting at that time.
During 2024 and into 2025 , media reports said Jensen Huang and Alice Huang were photographed or observed socializing in Taiwan, where Jensen Huang was born.
The memo allegedly stated she had been recruited to gather information about Jensen Huang .
It also alleged she was tasked with influencing Nvidia’s commercial position on advanced chip sales to China.
Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has led it since.
Alice Huang , also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen and former senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data-center company that rents computing capacity built on Nvidia processors.
Nvidia responded by characterizing Jensen Huang’s interactions with her as ordinary customer-related contact.

Public reporting has not established what information Alice Huang allegedly obtained, whether any Nvidia proprietary information was transferred, or whether export-control violations involving Megaspeed occurred.

Congressional committees have requested access to Jensen Huang ; no hearing date has been announced, and until investigators publish conclusions or authorities bring formal charges, the espionage allegations remain unproven.

In October 2025 , U.S. and Singapore authorities reportedly examined whether Megaspeed had helped Chinese firms, including Alibaba, obtain Nvidia processors in potential violation of U.S. export restrictions.

extraction.body: Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security. U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported. The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up. By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. More reports continue to roll out that illustrate the shock and severity of Huang’s resignation from Nvidia. Bloomberg reported that Huang looked “broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted” by the time he surrendered his role on Wednesday night, uttering phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care.” Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported that Huang had been critical of his CFO and current interim CEO, Colette Kress. Huang is said to have described Kress as “a deer in the headlights” during a presentation this summer, and he had described Kress as someone who could not help him steer strategy or decision-making. In a scathing letter sent to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Representative Richard Neal (D-MA) and Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) said they will investigate how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China, especially after Trump was briefed about Huang’s relationship with a purported Chinese spy. “Although [Lutnick] and President Trump were reportedly briefed on this intelligence, the Administration did not appear to acknowledge this evident national security threat. On the contrary: despite reportedly learning of Mr. Huang’s compromising relationship last fall, President Trump granted Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales,” the letter states. Nvidia said its board had accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. The company’s current CFO, Colette Kress , will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang. Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia’s board since 1993. Later in the day, Huang confirmed that he would testify in Congress at some point before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26. “Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.” The testimony is expected to take place behind closed doors, but Mast believes the briefing will be recorded and transcribed. After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per The Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days. Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said . The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO. According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year. Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressmen to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China Committee Chairman John Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed . The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum. Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported . The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips. Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported . Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang. An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary. “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.” U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times. Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo. Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service. Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born. These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. Nvidia’s board launched an independent probe after a classified U.S. memo alleged Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to target Jensen Huang Nvidia makes the processors that power large-scale artificial intelligence systems. U.S. export controls restrict the most advanced of those chips from reaching China, a country competing directly with the United States in AI development. Those rules reflect bipartisan concern that advanced AI processors could accelerate China’s military and surveillance capabilities, which is what transforms the following sequence of events from a corporate personnel matter into a national-security concern. Jensen Huang leads Nvidia; Alice Huang ran operations at a firm built on Nvidia’s technology. Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has led it since. Alice Huang , also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen and former senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data-center company that rents computing capacity built on Nvidia processors. She is not related to Jensen Huang. Media accounts placed the pair together in Taiwan multiple times before any investigation became public. During 2024 and into 2025 , media reports said Jensen Huang and Alice Huang were photographed or observed socializing in Taiwan, where Jensen Huang was born. Those encounters later became relevant to intelligence reporting about the alleged operation, according to the cited reporting. No public statement about the relationship was identified in that reporting from either Nvidia or U.S. officials at the time. U.S. and Singapore authorities opened parallel inquiries into whether Nvidia chips reached China through a third-party operator. In October 2025 , U.S. and Singapore authorities reportedly examined whether Megaspeed had helped Chinese firms, including Alibaba, obtain Nvidia processors in potential violation of U.S. export restrictions. Export controls are rules that restrict the sale of certain advanced technology to designated countries, entities, or uses, sometimes requiring government licensing. Officials also questioned the disposition of Nvidia equipment observed at a Malaysian facility, according to the supplied reporting, as AI is making enforcement of such controls increasingly complex. The president learned of the intelligence months before it became public. The New York Times reported that in late 2025, President Trump was informed about intelligence concerning Alice Huang’s alleged activities and her relationship with Jensen Huang. No publicly announced action was identified in the cited reporting at that time. The briefing was not disclosed until reporting on the broader story emerged in late October 2026. U.S. officials reportedly concluded Alice Huang was working for Chinese intelligence, though that assessment has not been independently verified. In spring 2026 , U.S. officials reportedly circulated a classified memo alleging that Alice Huang was an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security , the country’s primary civilian intelligence agency. The memo allegedly stated she had been recruited to gather information about Jensen Huang . It also alleged she was tasked with influencing Nvidia’s commercial position on advanced chip sales to China. This is an intelligence assessment reported by news organizations citing unnamed officials; it is not an established legal or investigative finding. Such government restrictions on technology access echo broader debates over how authorities worldwide handle sensitive data, as seen when Europe restricts major cloud providers from handling sensitive public-sector information. A New York Times report in October 2026 brought the relationship and the investigation into public view. On October 29, 2026 , the New York Times disclosed that U.S. officials had been investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed for more than a year and that she had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. Nvidia responded by characterizing Jensen Huang’s interactions with her as ordinary customer-related contact. A rapid sequence of corporate and political responses followed that disclosure. Three House committee chairmen asked Jensen Huang to appear before a closed-door session. The chairmen of the House Select Committee on China, the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and the House Intelligence Committee formally requested a closed-door briefing from Jensen Huang, with the request reported around November 5, 2026. The letter cited concerns about Chinese access to sensitive U.S. technology and possible infiltration of American technology companies. No public response from Huang or Nvidia was identified in the cited reporting at that time. The CEO issued a public apology on November 8 without naming Alice Huang. On November 8, 2026 , Jensen Huang publicly acknowledged that he had been unfaithful, apologizing to his wife, children, Nvidia employees, and the company. He linked his statement to national-security concerns described in media coverage but did not identify Alice Huang by name. He also withdrew from planned appearances at the ElevenLabs Summit and the Anthropic CEO Forum. The board acted the following day, saying it had no immediate evidence of compromised secrets. On November 9, 2026 , Nvidia’s board announced an independent investigation into whether Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The board said it had no reason at that stage to believe Nvidia secrets or U.S. national security had been compromised. President Trump said Jensen Huang should remain CEO. Trump later added that Huang had told him he did not know Alice Huang was allegedly a spy. Beijing’s Foreign Ministry called the espionage claim “groundless speculation.” On November 10, 2026 , China’s Foreign Ministry characterized the allegation that Alice Huang was working for Chinese intelligence as a smear and rejected it as unsubstantiated. Corporate records, as reported by media, separately identified her as a Megaspeed director from March to November 2023. The supplied reporting does not identify her current status or whereabouts. The investigation is ongoing, and several core questions have no public answers yet. Public reporting has not established what information Alice Huang allegedly obtained, whether any Nvidia proprietary information was transferred, or whether export-control violations involving Megaspeed occurred. Nvidia’s independent board investigation has not released findings. Congressional committees have requested access to Jensen Huang ; no hearing date has been announced, and until investigators publish conclusions or authorities bring formal charges, the espionage allegations remain unproven. extraction.body: For more on Jensen Huang’s resignation and the fallout from Nvidia’s leadership crisis, follow Terrence O’Brien. How it started On October 29th, The New York Times reported that Nvidia co-founder and showman CEO Jensen Huang appeared to be the target of a Chinese spy plot. Any major tech CEO potentially being compromised by the Chinese government is concerning — especially Jensen Huang. “If you could draw the network diagram of the entire US AI ecosystem, Nvidia would be at the center of that,” Kyle Chan, a foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. “If you could draw the diagram of the entire Nvidia ecosystem, a single man is standing at the heart of all of that.” The Times reported that Jensen Huang had developed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. Alice Huang had been on the American government’s radar for some time, perhaps as early as 2024. Her company was investigated by the US Commerce Department over suspicions it was illegally smuggling Nvidia’s AI chips into China in violation of US government trade restrictions. Singapore authorities confiscated her passport back in June of 2025, eventually barring her from the country, after she reportedly gave “inaccurate information” to police. And perhaps more concerningly, some US officials believed she was passing information, possibly about Nvidia’s designs or the White House’s deliberations over trade restrictions, directly back to Beijing. This made her relationship with Jensen Huang concerning for multiple reasons. Nvidia’s chips are considered crucial to America’s AI superiority and a matter of national security by the White House. The government has restricted the sale of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China since the Biden administration. But Jensen Huang has routinely pushed to loosen those trade restrictions. On Friday, November 6th, the Times reported that Alice Huang was specifically recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia’s CEO. Though, there is some disagreement among US intelligence officials over the strength of evidence tying Alice Huang to Beijing. While the paper did not confirm it at the time, rumors suggested the “close relationship” between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang was romantic in nature. On Sunday, November 8th, Jensen Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair, but did not name the Megaspeed exec and alleged Chinese spy specifically. Nvidia’s board announced that it was launching an investigation into its CEO shortly after. Many believed that Jensen Huang would survive the scandal. His company’s importance to America’s booming AI industry and his crucial role at the company seemed to make him nearly untouchable. He was, after all, the only CEO the company had ever known with no clear and obvious succession plan in place, and he sat atop an unusual corporate structure with around 60 direct reports. (These numbers are slightly outdated, but according to the Harvard Business Review, 10 to 20 is far more common among Fortune 500 companies, and Tim Cook reportedly had 17 in 2015, which was deemed “a lot” by Business Insider.) Then on Wednesday, November 11th, The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had a second affair — this one with one of his direct reports, Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care. Whether that was the last straw or if they were afraid it would be merely the tip of the iceberg, the board was ready to push Jensen Huang out, according to reports circulating that evening. According to Bloomberg, he had accepted his fate Wednesday evening reportedly looking “broken and shattered” and telling people, “I’m a piece of shit.” On Thursday, November 12th, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang had resigned as CEO of Nvidia. How it’s going CFO Colette Kress was immediately named interim CEO, and acknowledged to employees that this has been an “extraordinarily difficult period.” Harvey Jones was also named the first board chair in the company’s history, already signaling there would be some changes to the corporate structure. In a memo to employees, Jones said the company would “search for a permanent successor looking at both internal and external candidates.” But the destabilizing impact was immediate. Nvidia’s stock closed at an all-time high of $239.24 on October 6th. It’s hard to overstate the importance of Nvidia to the US’s AI arms race with China, and the industry in general. The company has invested $99 billion in various AI labs, startups, and neo clouds. Plus has announced plans to mobilize over $500 billion in financing for building out AI data centers and other infrastructure. Even before Jensen Huang had resigned, Nvidia was already facing a shareholder lawsuit claiming the company had deceived investors. Jensen Huang and the company’s spokespeople insisted that the relationship with Alice Huang and Megaspeed was “completely normal and not unusual.” Only days later, Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair that raised “national security concerns” without naming anyone specifically. According to Reuters, Jensen Huang misled several Nvidia leaders, “including general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld” about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang. Many in the AI industry and Silicon Valley jumped to Jensen Huang’s defense. Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney called it a “sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity,” in a particularly hyperbolic post. Elon Musk said on X that it would “be an honor” to hire Jensen Huang. Many of Nvidia’s employees even voiced their support to “bring back THE boss,” on an internal post.

extraction.body: We’re getting some extraordinary reporting on what it has been like inside Nvidia during Huang’s last days. Before his forced resignation, Huang had given up, Bloomberg says , and was heard saying things like “whatever,” “I don’t care,” and referring to himself as a “piece of sh--.” That, of course, was in stark contrast to how Huang historically ran the company. Huang had “imperial control,” and ran it like a “feudal system,” according to the FT . “I can’t tell you what a cult this place is,” a source told the paper. General counsel Tim Teter wore a leather jacket just like Huang’s, the source said: “Jensen is a god, and that’s how he’s worshipped.” Noteworthy: In addition to having no board chair, the company also did not have a compliance officer, the FT says. Interim CEO Colette Kress and whoever replaces her as permanent CEO will have messy office politics to deal with, according to the FT . Huang’s daughter Madison Huang is a senior director of marketing at the company, but she acts like her father’s de facto chief of staff, the FT says. Nvidia also employs her husband Nico Caprez and Huang’s son Spencer. Kress, meanwhile, sometimes did not get Huang’s respect, the WSJ reported . He once called her “a deer in the headlights” and a “reporting CFO” (as opposed to a strategic leader) during a meeting in which they were discussing Nvidia’s agreements “to provide billions of dollars of guarantees to companies that couldn’t afford its chips,” the WSJ said. Kress struggled to rein in Caprez, who had made multiple offers of financing to cloud providers and data-center builders in return for shares of revenue. Lenders relied on the Huang family's backing for AI financing when structuring deals with AI providers. Without Huang at the top, “that Nvidia guarantee is not worth what it was worth a week ago, that puts those neocloud businesses at risk,” Joe Kaiser of Switchyard Partners, an AI financing company, told Fortune’s Catherina Gioino . Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and commerce secretary Howard Lutnick have been called by Sen. Tim Scott (R-South Carolina) to testify in front of the Senate Banking Committee, the NYT reports . The hearing will be conducted next month. “Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology,” Scott said. That’s a reference to Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy who ran a company that bought Nvidia chips and is suspected of smuggling them into China in violation of U.S. export controls. As for Lutnick, Republicans are furious at what they perceive was the special treatment he gave Nvidia in terms of its access to the Chinese market and in his foot-dragging on the enforcement of export bans to China, the FT says . Lutnick shielded Nvidia from the White House’s attempts to restrict export of the U.S.’s best technology to China, the NYT reported . All matters related to Nvidia were routed through a deputy to Lutnick, Jeff Kessler, who rarely took action without Lutnick’s approval, the NYT said . Inside the White House, senior Trump administration figures largely blame Lutnick for being asleep at the wheel in terms of the threat Nvidia posed to national security, given its ties to Chinese importers, the WSJ reported . ​​Alice Huang: Those concerns will get extra momentum on the news that Jensen Huang’s affair partner, suspected spy Alice Huang (no relation) of Megaspeed, had a relationship with Huawei, China’s biggest competitor in China, according to CNBC . Alice Huang allegedly ran a complicated network of companies to do deals with Nvidia that resulted in its chips ending up at Chinese companies, per Bloomberg . Congress needs to catch up - Andrew M. Cuomo One central question about the Anthropic IPO is: how can this company grow revenue if its product prices—as measured via tokens—are in a race to the bottom? Turns out that piling it high and selling it cheap works in AI the same way it works in groceries, as these charts from Alpine Macro’s Noah Ramos show. “While token prices have declined dramatically, overall customer spending continues to scale. This reflects both users extracting more intelligence per unit of compute and inference optimizations that make it economically viable to consume substantially more tokens. Lower token prices are expanding consumption rather than reducing spending,” he said in a note. —Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives, expressing the head-spinning pace at which Jensen Huang went from indispensable founder to excess baggage at his own company, Nvidia. “The old Jensen, the black leather jacket, the Godfather of AI, the rock star viewed as the face of the AI boom, is over and in the past; his value to the company pre and post this week is dramatically different, and the board did what we said it needed to do, which is rip off the band-aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter without him after this dark moment for Jensen and Nvidia.” Ives also has an eyebrow-raising suggestion for who could replace Huang as CEO: Apple’s Tim Cook. He could be “a dark horse candidate in our view given the global importance of Nvidia to the overall U.S. tech industry.” The proposal makes sense given that Cook just retired as CEO of Apple, and although he is now its chairman, he does, in theory, have time on his hands. And frankly, who knows more than Cook about stewarding the most important tech company of its day to further success following the loss of an “irreplaceable” founder? It goes without saying that the stakes are high. Remember what happened at HP and Intel, warn Wedbush’s Matt Bryson and Tuo Ma: “Both [HP’s] Mark Hurd and [Intel’s] Brian Krzanich departed their posts relatively abruptly following affairs with no clear successors in place. And for both Intel and HP, we believe these transitions played some role in disastrous periods that saw the companies lose their respective leadership positions in technology, with HP eventually breaking apart and Intel still struggling to prove it can regain the fab and chip design expertise it seemingly lost during its failed 10nm transition.” Ouch! New analysis of Federal Reserve data points to a subtler one: a third child. Mike Konczal, vice president of policy and research at the Economic Security Project and a former White House economist, studied households headed by 45- to 64-year-olds in his analysis of the Fed’s Survey of Consumer Finances, pooling five surveys from 2013 through 2025. He found that 49% of top-1% earners have three or more children, compared with about 40% of the rest of the top 10%. Families with four or more kids are about as common in both groups, so the gap comes down to the third child: 34% of the 1% stop at exactly three, versus 24% of the merely affluent. That’s a reference to Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy who ran a company that bought Nvidia chips and is suspected of smuggling them into China in violation of U.S. export controls.

Lutnick shielded Nvidia from the White House’s attempts to restrict export of the U.S.’s best technology to China, the NYT reported .
All matters related to Nvidia were routed through a deputy to Lutnick, Jeff Kessler, who rarely took action without Lutnick’s approval, the NYT said .

Inside the White House, senior Trump administration figures largely blame Lutnick for being asleep at the wheel in terms of the threat Nvidia posed to national security, given its ties to Chinese importers, the WSJ reported .

One central question about the Anthropic IPO is: how can this company grow revenue if its product prices—as measured via tokens—are in a race to the bottom? Turns out that piling it high and selling it cheap works in AI the same way it works in groceries, as these charts from Alpine Macro’s Noah Ramos show.

“While token prices have declined dramatically, overall customer spending continues to scale. This reflects both users extracting more intelligence per unit of compute and inference optimizations that make it economically viable to consume substantially more tokens. Lower token prices are expanding consumption rather than reducing spending,” he said in a note.

—Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives, expressing the head-spinning pace at which Jensen Huang went from indispensable founder to excess baggage at his own company, Nvidia. “The old Jensen, the black leather jacket, the Godfather of AI, the rock star viewed as the face of the AI boom, is over and in the past; his value to the company pre and post this week is dramatically different, and the board did what we said it needed to do, which is rip off the band-aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter without him after this dark moment for Jensen and Nvidia.”

Ives also has an eyebrow-raising suggestion for who could replace Huang as CEO: Apple’s Tim Cook. He could be “a dark horse candidate in our view given the global importance of Nvidia to the overall U.S. tech industry.” The proposal makes sense given that Cook just retired as CEO of Apple, and although he is now its chairman, he does, in theory, have time on his hands. And frankly, who knows more than Cook about stewarding the most important tech company of its day to further success following the loss of an “irreplaceable” founder?

And for both Intel and HP, we believe these transitions played some role in disastrous periods that saw the companies lose their respective leadership positions in technology, with HP eventually breaking apart and Intel still struggling to prove it can regain the fab and chip design expertise it seemingly lost during its failed 10nm transition.” Ouch!

Fanatics CEO Michael Rubin engaged to model girlfriend Camille Fishel after 10 years of dating - NY Post
For decades, the markers of extreme wealth were easy to spot: the second home, the fancy cars, the Ivy League education. New analysis of Federal Reserve data points to a subtler one: a third child.

Mike Konczal, vice president of policy and research at the Economic Security Project and a former White House economist, studied households headed by 45- to 64-year-olds in his analysis of the Fed’s Survey of Consumer Finances, pooling five surveys from 2013 through 2025. He found that 49% of top-1% earners have three or more children, compared with about 40% of the rest of the top 10%.
Families with four or more kids are about as common in both groups, so the gap comes down to the third child: 34% of the 1% stop at exactly three, versus 24% of the merely affluent.

He was, after all, the only CEO the company had ever known with no clear and obvious succession plan in place, and he sat atop an unusual corporate structure with around 60 direct reports. Then on Wednesday, November 11th, The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had a second affair — this one with one of his direct reports, Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care.
Many in the AI industry and Silicon Valley jumped to Jensen Huang’s defense.
Any major tech CEO potentially being compromised by the Chinese government is concerning — especially Jensen Huang.
Elon Musk said on X that it would “be an honor” to hire Jensen Huang.
But Jensen Huang has routinely pushed to loosen those trade restrictions.
Huang has offloaded 1,00,000 shares in the span of two days as part of a trading plan which allows him to sell up to $856 million worth shares by the end of 2025.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has started the sale of his company’s stock.
Apart from Huang, Mark Stevens a board member of Nvidia also sold over 600,000 shares worth $88 million recently.
Huang still has more than 900 million shares.This sale of stockers by Huang comes at a time when Nvidia is dominating the AI chip market and its stock value witnessed 25% surge over the past year.
This pre-arranged structure ensures transparency and compliance with regulatory standards.The plan mentioned in Nvidia’s quarterly report was adopted in March 2025.

extraction.body: For more on Jensen Huang’s resignation and the fallout from Nvidia’s leadership crisis, follow Terrence O’Brien. How it started On October 29th, The New York Times reported that Nvidia co-founder and showman CEO Jensen Huang appeared to be the target of a Chinese spy plot. Any major tech CEO potentially being compromised by the Chinese government is concerning — especially Jensen Huang. “If you could draw the network diagram of the entire US AI ecosystem, Nvidia would be at the center of that,” Kyle Chan, a foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. “If you could draw the diagram of the entire Nvidia ecosystem, a single man is standing at the heart of all of that.” The Times reported that Jensen Huang had developed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. Alice Huang had been on the American government’s radar for some time, perhaps as early as 2024. Her company was investigated by the US Commerce Department over suspicions it was illegally smuggling Nvidia’s AI chips into China in violation of US government trade restrictions. Singapore authorities confiscated her passport back in June of 2025, eventually barring her from the country, after she reportedly gave “inaccurate information” to police. And perhaps more concerningly, some US officials believed she was passing information, possibly about Nvidia’s designs or the White House’s deliberations over trade restrictions, directly back to Beijing. This made her relationship with Jensen Huang concerning for multiple reasons. Nvidia’s chips are considered crucial to America’s AI superiority and a matter of national security by the White House. The government has restricted the sale of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China since the Biden administration. But Jensen Huang has routinely pushed to loosen those trade restrictions. On Friday, November 6th, the Times reported that Alice Huang was specifically recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia’s CEO. Though, there is some disagreement among US intelligence officials over the strength of evidence tying Alice Huang to Beijing. While the paper did not confirm it at the time, rumors suggested the “close relationship” between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang was romantic in nature. On Sunday, November 8th, Jensen Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair, but did not name the Megaspeed exec and alleged Chinese spy specifically. Nvidia’s board announced that it was launching an investigation into its CEO shortly after. Many believed that Jensen Huang would survive the scandal. His company’s importance to America’s booming AI industry and his crucial role at the company seemed to make him nearly untouchable. He was, after all, the only CEO the company had ever known with no clear and obvious succession plan in place, and he sat atop an unusual corporate structure with around 60 direct reports. (These numbers are slightly outdated, but according to the Harvard Business Review, 10 to 20 is far more common among Fortune 500 companies, and Tim Cook reportedly had 17 in 2015, which was deemed “a lot” by Business Insider.) Then on Wednesday, November 11th, The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had a second affair — this one with one of his direct reports, Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care. Whether that was the last straw or if they were afraid it would be merely the tip of the iceberg, the board was ready to push Jensen Huang out, according to reports circulating that evening. According to Bloomberg, he had accepted his fate Wednesday evening reportedly looking “broken and shattered” and telling people, “I’m a piece of shit.” On Thursday, November 12th, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang had resigned as CEO of Nvidia. How it’s going CFO Colette Kress was immediately named interim CEO, and acknowledged to employees that this has been an “extraordinarily difficult period.” Harvey Jones was also named the first board chair in the company’s history, already signaling there would be some changes to the corporate structure. In a memo to employees, Jones said the company would “search for a permanent successor looking at both internal and external candidates.” But the destabilizing impact was immediate. Nvidia’s stock closed at an all-time high of $239.24 on October 6th. It’s hard to overstate the importance of Nvidia to the US’s AI arms race with China, and the industry in general. The company has invested $99 billion in various AI labs, startups, and neo clouds. Plus has announced plans to mobilize over $500 billion in financing for building out AI data centers and other infrastructure. Even before Jensen Huang had resigned, Nvidia was already facing a shareholder lawsuit claiming the company had deceived investors. Jensen Huang and the company’s spokespeople insisted that the relationship with Alice Huang and Megaspeed was “completely normal and not unusual.” Only days later, Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair that raised “national security concerns” without naming anyone specifically. According to Reuters, Jensen Huang misled several Nvidia leaders, “including general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld” about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang. Many in the AI industry and Silicon Valley jumped to Jensen Huang’s defense. Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney called it a “sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity,” in a particularly hyperbolic post. Elon Musk said on X that it would “be an honor” to hire Jensen Huang. Many of Nvidia’s employees even voiced their support to “bring back THE boss,” on an internal post.

extraction.body: We’re getting some extraordinary reporting on what it has been like inside Nvidia during Huang’s last days. Before his forced resignation, Huang had given up, Bloomberg says , and was heard saying things like “whatever,” “I don’t care,” and referring to himself as a “piece of sh--.” That, of course, was in stark contrast to how Huang historically ran the company. Huang had “imperial control,” and ran it like a “feudal system,” according to the FT . “I can’t tell you what a cult this place is,” a source told the paper. General counsel Tim Teter wore a leather jacket just like Huang’s, the source said: “Jensen is a god, and that’s how he’s worshipped.” Noteworthy: In addition to having no board chair, the company also did not have a compliance officer, the FT says. Interim CEO Colette Kress and whoever replaces her as permanent CEO will have messy office politics to deal with, according to the FT . Huang’s daughter Madison Huang is a senior director of marketing at the company, but she acts like her father’s de facto chief of staff, the FT says. Nvidia also employs her husband Nico Caprez and Huang’s son Spencer. Kress, meanwhile, sometimes did not get Huang’s respect, the WSJ reported . He once called her “a deer in the headlights” and a “reporting CFO” (as opposed to a strategic leader) during a meeting in which they were discussing Nvidia’s agreements “to provide billions of dollars of guarantees to companies that couldn’t afford its chips,” the WSJ said. Kress struggled to rein in Caprez, who had made multiple offers of financing to cloud providers and data-center builders in return for shares of revenue. Lenders relied on the Huang family's backing for AI financing when structuring deals with AI providers. Without Huang at the top, “that Nvidia guarantee is not worth what it was worth a week ago, that puts those neocloud businesses at risk,” Joe Kaiser of Switchyard Partners, an AI financing company, told Fortune’s Catherina Gioino . Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and commerce secretary Howard Lutnick have been called by Sen. Tim Scott (R-South Carolina) to testify in front of the Senate Banking Committee, the NYT reports . The hearing will be conducted next month. “Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology,” Scott said. That’s a reference to Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy who ran a company that bought Nvidia chips and is suspected of smuggling them into China in violation of U.S. export controls. As for Lutnick, Republicans are furious at what they perceive was the special treatment he gave Nvidia in terms of its access to the Chinese market and in his foot-dragging on the enforcement of export bans to China, the FT says . Lutnick shielded Nvidia from the White House’s attempts to restrict export of the U.S.’s best technology to China, the NYT reported . All matters related to Nvidia were routed through a deputy to Lutnick, Jeff Kessler, who rarely took action without Lutnick’s approval, the NYT said . Inside the White House, senior Trump administration figures largely blame Lutnick for being asleep at the wheel in terms of the threat Nvidia posed to national security, given its ties to Chinese importers, the WSJ reported . ​​Alice Huang: Those concerns will get extra momentum on the news that Jensen Huang’s affair partner, suspected spy Alice Huang (no relation) of Megaspeed, had a relationship with Huawei, China’s biggest competitor in China, according to CNBC . Alice Huang allegedly ran a complicated network of companies to do deals with Nvidia that resulted in its chips ending up at Chinese companies, per Bloomberg . Turns out that piling it high and selling it cheap works in AI the same way it works in groceries, as these charts from Alpine Macro’s Noah Ramos show. “While token prices have declined dramatically, overall customer spending continues to scale. This reflects both users extracting more intelligence per unit of compute and inference optimizations that make it economically viable to consume substantially more tokens. Lower token prices are expanding consumption rather than reducing spending,” he said in a note. —Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives, expressing the head-spinning pace at which Jensen Huang went from indispensable founder to excess baggage at his own company, Nvidia. “The old Jensen, the black leather jacket, the Godfather of AI, the rock star viewed as the face of the AI boom, is over and in the past; his value to the company pre and post this week is dramatically different, and the board did what we said it needed to do, which is rip off the band-aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter without him after this dark moment for Jensen and Nvidia.” Ives also has an eyebrow-raising suggestion for who could replace Huang as CEO: Apple’s Tim Cook. He could be “a dark horse candidate in our view given the global importance of Nvidia to the overall U.S. tech industry.” The proposal makes sense given that Cook just retired as CEO of Apple, and although he is now its chairman, he does, in theory, have time on his hands. And frankly, who knows more than Cook about stewarding the most important tech company of its day to further success following the loss of an “irreplaceable” founder? It goes without saying that the stakes are high. Remember what happened at HP and Intel, warn Wedbush’s Matt Bryson and Tuo Ma: “Both [HP’s] Mark Hurd and [Intel’s] Brian Krzanich departed their posts relatively abruptly following affairs with no clear successors in place. And for both Intel and HP, we believe these transitions played some role in disastrous periods that saw the companies lose their respective leadership positions in technology, with HP eventually breaking apart and Intel still struggling to prove it can regain the fab and chip design expertise it seemingly lost during its failed 10nm transition.” Ouch! New analysis of Federal Reserve data points to a subtler one: a third child. Mike Konczal, vice president of policy and research at the Economic Security Project and a former White House economist, studied households headed by 45- to 64-year-olds in his analysis of the Fed’s Survey of Consumer Finances, pooling five surveys from 2013 through 2025. He found that 49% of top-1% earners have three or more children, compared with about 40% of the rest of the top 10%. Families with four or more kids are about as common in both groups, so the gap comes down to the third child: 34% of the 1% stop at exactly three, versus 24% of the merely affluent. sources.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's 'spy' affair could spark Congress crackdown on AI export controls: 'Massive earthquake' - New York Post
passages: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy has sparked fears of a major clampdown on the AI industry – pitting China hawks against those who warn that an overreaction will put the US at a disadvantage versus Beijing, The Post has learned.

Lawmakers from both parties are scrutinizing past remarks from Jensen, who was the most influential voice pushing US officials to curb export controls on Nvidia chips — even as they assess whether his affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang compromised national security.

Meanwhile, Bloomberg reported Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter directly called Kessler, who oversees chip export controls, in the summer of 2025 to ask about the department’s investigation into Megaspeed.

Ousting Huang himself, the source added, would be a “massive earthquake” during a fragile moment for the AI sector, which is already facing questions on Wall Street over whether it’s a giant bubble ready to burst.

However, there are real concerns about Huang’s ability to remain at the helm of Nvidia – despite the fact that many consider him irreplaceable to the company and the lack of any obvious successor within its ranks.
That argument seems unlikely to satisfy key lawmakers who were already concerned about China gaining access to Nvidia’s best hardware – even before Huang’s embarrassing misstep.

Some DC sources believe the scandal will result in a bipartisan push for even stronger curbs on chip sales — with proponents concerned that Nvidia’s cutting-edge chips will fuel greater inroads into AI by Chinese companies.
“Republican chairs are reaching out to speak to Jensen and get some more details,” a Senate Democratic aide told The Post.
One key loophole currently under the microscope is China’s well-documented practice of accessing high-end Nvidia hardware housed in data centers based in Southeast Asia.

Nvidia initially replied that all of its chip sales were accurately recorded – even though Megaspeed had imported 50,000 more computer chips than what Nvidia linked to its data centers, Bloomberg reported.
Rush Doshi, a China policy expert and Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, expects Democrats to push hard to close the “remote access” loophole.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy has sparked fears of a major clampdown on the AI industry – pitting China hawks against those who warn that an overreaction will put the US at a disadvantage versus Beijing, The Post has learned. Lawmakers from both parties are scrutinizing past remarks from Jensen, who was the most influential voice pushing US officials to curb export controls on Nvidia chips — even as they assess whether his affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang compromised national security. Some DC sources believe the scandal will result in a bipartisan push for even stronger curbs on chip sales — with proponents concerned that Nvidia’s cutting-edge chips will fuel greater inroads into AI by Chinese companies. At the same time, some of them warn that ordering such a crackdown – for example banning a loophole allowing Chinese companies to rent access to Nvidia’s high-end hardware through data centers located in Southeast Asia – would play right into China’s hands, a source close to the situation said. “If they do that, it will just drive those foreign clouds to Huawei,” the source told The Post, referring to the Chinese telecom giant that is aggressively pursuing AI business. “Ultimately, over time, those clouds will choose what’s available to them. It becomes an economic question – do you want foreign clouds to have American technology or Huawei technology?” Ousting Huang himself, the source added, would be a “massive earthquake” during a fragile moment for the AI sector, which is already facing questions on Wall Street over whether it’s a giant bubble ready to burst. “Nvidia is at the center of the AI buildout and he’s the central figure in the company,” the source said of Jensen Huang. That argument seems unlikely to satisfy key lawmakers who were already concerned about China gaining access to Nvidia’s best hardware – even before Huang’s embarrassing misstep. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) said he “strongly supports” adding tougher chip controls to an annual year-end defense spending bill, while Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) called for legislation targeting “various pathways through which China accesses advanced chips.” “Republican chairs are reaching out to speak to Jensen and get some more details,” a Senate Democratic aide told The Post. “This is not, at this point, a partisan mud fight. This is bipartisan. We need answers about what happened here, what the FBI is looking into or already knew . We are in a bipartisan gathering phase.” One key loophole currently under the microscope is China’s well-documented practice of accessing high-end Nvidia hardware housed in data centers based in Southeast Asia. US officials have suspected Singapore-based Megaspeed – and alleged Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang – of exploiting the loophole to smuggle AI chips to China. Nvidia has long resisted efforts to crack down on so-called “remote access,” while key Commerce Department figures like Howard Lutnick and undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler, who oversees the Bureau of Industry and Security, have been reluctant to take action. Rush Doshi, a China policy expert and Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, expects Democrats to push hard to close the “remote access” loophole. “If the reporting is right, it potentially reveals corruption and compromise in American China policy on one of the most important issues of our time, including in ways that undermine AI safety for Americans,” Doshi said. “Democrats and Republicans alike are going to want to investigate what they see as the decision to sell off American national security and economic advantage and AI safety for profit.” In October, White House officials nudged Congressional staffers to tack on a provision that would direct the Commerce Department to close the loophole as part of the AI Overwatch Act, a measure cosponsored by Warren and Banks and set to be included in the year-end defense bill, The Information reported. Nvidia declined to comment. Representatives for the White House and Commerce Department did not immediately return questions for comment. Aside from pursuing answers about Huang’s personal conduct, lawmakers from both parties are sure to seek answers about the Trump administration’s handling of the situation – specifically, its delay in taking action despite warnings months ago that the Nvidia boss was tangled up with an alleged Chinese spy, and the Commerce Department’s dealings with Nvidia, Doshi added. Last year, US officials grew concerned that Megaspeed, the largest buyer of Nvidia chips in southeast Asia, was involved in chip smuggling and asked Nvidia to audit its dealings with the firm. Nvidia initially replied that all of its chip sales were accurately recorded – even though Megaspeed had imported 50,000 more computer chips than what Nvidia linked to its data centers, Bloomberg reported. Meanwhile, Bloomberg reported Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter directly called Kessler, who oversees chip export controls, in the summer of 2025 to ask about the department’s investigation into Megaspeed. The report added that Commerce staffers were subsequently “muzzled in their ability to look into the company” and told to route requests on the matter through Kessler. “BIS conducts all enforcement strictly by the book,” a spokesperson told the outlet. “BIS enforces aggressively across the board, including with respect to chip smuggling, and enforcement is at an all-time high.” While the scandal is a major black eye for Nvidia, it’s unlikely to completely upend the company’s role as the linchpin of the AI movement, according to Daniel Newman, CEO of Futurum Group.
