Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy has sparked fears of a major clampdown on the AI industry – pitting China hawks against those who warn that an overreaction will put the US at a disadvantage versus Beijing, The Post has learned.

Lawmakers from both parties are scrutinizing past remarks from Jensen, who was the most influential voice pushing US officials to curb export controls on Nvidia chips — even as they assess whether his affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang compromised national security.

Some DC sources believe the scandal will result in a bipartisan push for even stronger curbs on chip sales — with proponents concerned that Nvidia’s cutting-edge chips will fuel greater inroads into AI by Chinese companies.

At the same time, some of them warn that ordering such a crackdown – for example banning a loophole allowing Chinese companies to rent access to Nvidia’s high-end hardware through data centers located in Southeast Asia – would play right into China’s hands, a source close to the situation said.
“If they do that, it will just drive those foreign clouds to Huawei,” the source told The Post, referring to the Chinese telecom giant that is aggressively pursuing AI business.
“Ultimately, over time, those clouds will choose what’s available to them. It becomes an economic question – do you want foreign clouds to have American technology or Huawei technology?”

Ousting Huang himself, the source added, would be a “massive earthquake” during a fragile moment for the AI sector, which is already facing questions on Wall Street over whether it’s a giant bubble ready to burst.
“Nvidia is at the center of the AI buildout and he’s the central figure in the company,” the source said of Jensen Huang.
That argument seems unlikely to satisfy key lawmakers who were already concerned about China gaining access to Nvidia’s best hardware – even before Huang’s embarrassing misstep.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) said he “strongly supports” adding tougher chip controls to an annual year-end defense spending bill, while Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) called for legislation targeting “various pathways through which China accesses advanced chips.”

“Republican chairs are reaching out to speak to Jensen and get some more details,” a Senate Democratic aide told The Post. “This is not, at this point, a partisan mud fight. This is bipartisan. We need answers about what happened here, what the FBI is looking into or already knew . We are in a bipartisan gathering phase.”

One key loophole currently under the microscope is China’s well-documented practice of accessing high-end Nvidia hardware housed in data centers based in Southeast Asia. US officials have suspected Singapore-based Megaspeed – and alleged Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang – of exploiting the loophole to smuggle AI chips to China.

Nvidia has long resisted efforts to crack down on so-called “remote access,” while key Commerce Department figures like Howard Lutnick and undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler, who oversees the Bureau of Industry and Security, have been reluctant to take action.
Rush Doshi, a China policy expert and Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, expects Democrats to push hard to close the “remote access” loophole.

“If the reporting is right, it potentially reveals corruption and compromise in American China policy on one of the most important issues of our time, including in ways that undermine AI safety for Americans,” Doshi said.
“Democrats and Republicans alike are going to want to investigate what they see as the decision to sell off American national security and economic advantage and AI safety for profit.”

In October, White House officials nudged Congressional staffers to tack on a provision that would direct the Commerce Department to close the loophole as part of the AI Overwatch Act, a measure cosponsored by Warren and Banks and set to be included in the year-end defense bill, The Information reported.
Nvidia declined to comment. Representatives for the White House and Commerce Department did not immediately return questions for comment.

Aside from pursuing answers about Huang’s personal conduct, lawmakers from both parties are sure to seek answers about the Trump administration’s handling of the situation – specifically, its delay in taking action despite warnings months ago that the Nvidia boss was tangled up with an alleged Chinese spy, and the Commerce Department’s dealings with Nvidia, Doshi added.

Last year, US officials grew concerned that Megaspeed, the largest buyer of Nvidia chips in southeast Asia, was involved in chip smuggling and asked Nvidia to audit its dealings with the firm. Nvidia initially replied that all of its chip sales were accurately recorded – even though Megaspeed had imported 50,000 more computer chips than what Nvidia linked to its data centers, Bloomberg reported.

Meanwhile, Bloomberg reported Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter directly called Kessler, who oversees chip export controls, in the summer of 2025 to ask about the department’s investigation into Megaspeed.
The report added that Commerce staffers were subsequently “muzzled in their ability to look into the company” and told to route requests on the matter through Kessler.

“BIS conducts all enforcement strictly by the book,” a spokesperson told the outlet. “BIS enforces aggressively across the board, including with respect to chip smuggling, and enforcement is at an all-time high.”

While the scandal is a major black eye for Nvidia, it’s unlikely to completely upend the company’s role as the linchpin of the AI movement, according to Daniel Newman, CEO of Futurum Group. The company’s deal roadmap is already largely set through 2028, and companies can’t easily find a replacement for Nvidia’s advanced hardware even if they were inclined to.

However, there are real concerns about Huang’s ability to remain at the helm of Nvidia – despite the fact that many consider him irreplaceable to the company and the lack of any obvious successor within its ranks.

“The big question is on the continuum of, is he a CEO that committed infidelity? I think he can survive that. That doesn’t mean it’s good,” Newman said. “All the risks around intelligence stuff is not survivable. If any line was crossed beyond him just having an affair, the board is going to have to move.”

extraction.body: The chip-smuggling controversy swirling around Nvidia centers on one company : Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing provider that, according to several media reports, is suspected of funneling advanced AI processors to Chinese companies. While details of what Megaspeed is alleged to have done remain murky, experts say the case shows how Chinese firms rely on Southeast Asia to skirt U.S. trade controls. “Chinese firms can access data centers in Singapore and Malaysia—and their computing capacity—without having to import restricted semiconductors,” Ja Ian Chong, a political science expert from the National University of Singapore (NUS), tells Fortune . “But the ease of shipping [chips] through Singapore and Malaysia also makes them attractive for firms and people who wish to circumvent U.S. controls.” Washington restricts the export of Nvidia’s top-end Blackwell and Rubin chips to China, out of fear Beijing could use them to supercharge its AI ambitions . According to The Information , Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, used her personal relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to move at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips through Megaspeed and its Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix. Singapore says it is investigating Megaspeed for “suspected breaches of our domestic laws,” but it separately rejected reports that its authorities were investigating Alice Huang over the espionage allegations. U.S. officials had also been investigating Megaspeed for potential export-control violations. Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing; Nvidia has previously claimed that it found no evidence of illicit chip transfers. Nvidia’s board said in a Nov. 8 statement that it was initiating an independent investigation into whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, though it added it had no reason to believe “either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” The board said it “prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders.” Following reports that Huang conducted a second affair, this time with an Nvidia executive, the chipmaker’s board is now considering removing Huang as CEO, the Wall Street Journal reports. Megaspeed is a Singapore-based neocloud that supplies AI computing power. Originally incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International, a Chinese gaming firm with ties to state-backed investors, the company changed its name to Megaspeed in early 2023, the same year that Alice Huang joined the company. Another Singapore-registered firm, Swiftdata, acquired Megaspeed in November 2023. Alice Huang stepped down as Megaspeed’s managing director, while Singaporean businessman Tan Yong Pong—who owns Swiftdata —became its sole director. (Tan owns another Singapore-registered company, Monster Investment.) In 2024, Tan established Speedmatrix, a Malaysia-based subsidiary of Megaspeed, which was reportedly used to receive shipments of Nvidia chips. According to the New York Times , between June 2024 and June 2025, Speedmatrix received over 200 shipments of restricted Nvidia technology. These chips—which are subject to U.S. restrictions on sales to China—were eventually used to power data centers built by Shanghai Century Litong, a Chinese firm in which Alice’s younger sister, Huang Yu, is a founding shareholder, according to The Information . The firm, which builds data centers in the Chinese cities of Shanghai and Shenzhen, then provides high-performance AI computing capacity to Chinese tech giants including Alibaba and Tencent . “AI chip distributors and resellers often spend too little effort vetting customers, usually relying on paperwork the customer provides,” notes Erich Grunewald, a senior researcher at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy (IAPS), a U.S. nonpartisan think tank. Malaysia has been one of Southeast Asia’s biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom, drawing $94 billion in data center investments between 2021 and mid-2026, including from global tech hyperscalers like Google, AWS and Microsoft . “Malaysia has ample land and relatively cheap electricity and water, at least for now,” Chong notes. “The fact that it sits next to key submarine cables also makes it attractive as a spot for data centers.” Singapore, on the other hand, is favored by multinationals for its open economy, stable political environment and business-friendly policies. Many AI firms, including U.S. firms Anthropic and OpenAI , have chosen to house their APAC headquarters there. Companies like Megaspeed typically offer two routes to restricted silicon. The first is renting out chips already housed in data centers in Singapore and Malaysia—which, under current rules, is legal. The second is buying chips through front companies and shipping them to China, potentially in violation of U.S. export controls. (Megaspeed reportedly did both: it set up data center operations in Sedenak Tech Park in the Malaysian state of Johor , and according to the reports , also shuttled chips to Shanghai Century Litong’s facilities in China.) Under current U.S. export rules, it is legal to give Chinese companies access to AI processors housed outside of China—though previous deals have invited regulatory scrutiny. On Nov. 3, The Financial Times reported that Oracle had canceled a $7 billion deal to grant Tencent access to 100,000 AI chips in data centers across Southeast Asia after U.S. officials raised concerns. The FT also reported that Nvidia is telling cloud computing clients they must sell at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese companies. The U.S. House of Representatives passed a law—the Remote Access Security Act —that would close the loophole allowing Chinese companies to use AI processors housed in other countries; the bill is now before the U.S. Senate. Both Singapore and Malaysia have cracked down on chip smuggling. In addition to its investigation of Megaspeed, the Singaporean government last year charged three individuals with fraud after they diverted AI servers bound for Singapore to Malaysia instead. In October, Malaysian customs officials seized $12.1 million worth of advanced AI chips at Kuala Lumpur International Airport. Initial investigations found the 30 servers—falsely declared as electronic components—were being transferred from one Asian country to another, though officials declined to say which. Megaspeed, however, has denied the allegations . “There has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities, and this demonstrates that we are a compliant and legitimate company,” it wrote in a statement last December. “We operate fully within the bounds of all applicable export control regulations and maintain the highest standards of legal and ethical conduct.” Chong says the escalating AI arms race between the U.S. and China means both Beijing and Washington will subject third parties like Singapore and Malaysia to deeper scrutiny to keep their own technology from leaking. “Both Singapore and Malaysia will want to continue to benefit from trust by Beijing and Washington for as long as they can,” concludes Chong. “But they may face greater suspicion, scrutiny, restrictions and even punishment from one or both major powers going forward, and perceptions that they are unreliable or duplicitous partners will only increase such pressure.” Angelica Ang is a Singapore-based journalist who covers the Asia-Pacific region.

coreStoryFacts.text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy has sparked fears of a major clampdown on the AI industry – pitting China hawks against those who warn that an overreaction will put the US at a disadvantage versus Beijing, The Post has learned.

Lawmakers from both parties are scrutinizing past remarks from Jensen, who was the most influential voice pushing US officials to curb export controls on Nvidia chips — even as they assess whether his affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang compromised national security.

Meanwhile, Bloomberg reported Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter directly called Kessler, who oversees chip export controls, in the summer of 2025 to ask about the department’s investigation into Megaspeed.

Ousting Huang himself, the source added, would be a “massive earthquake” during a fragile moment for the AI sector, which is already facing questions on Wall Street over whether it’s a giant bubble ready to burst.

However, there are real concerns about Huang’s ability to remain at the helm of Nvidia – despite the fact that many consider him irreplaceable to the company and the lack of any obvious successor within its ranks.
That argument seems unlikely to satisfy key lawmakers who were already concerned about China gaining access to Nvidia’s best hardware – even before Huang’s embarrassing misstep.

Some DC sources believe the scandal will result in a bipartisan push for even stronger curbs on chip sales — with proponents concerned that Nvidia’s cutting-edge chips will fuel greater inroads into AI by Chinese companies.
“Republican chairs are reaching out to speak to Jensen and get some more details,” a Senate Democratic aide told The Post.
One key loophole currently under the microscope is China’s well-documented practice of accessing high-end Nvidia hardware housed in data centers based in Southeast Asia.

Nvidia initially replied that all of its chip sales were accurately recorded – even though Megaspeed had imported 50,000 more computer chips than what Nvidia linked to its data centers, Bloomberg reported.
Rush Doshi, a China policy expert and Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, expects Democrats to push hard to close the “remote access” loophole.

“Chinese firms can access data centers in Singapore and Malaysia—and their computing capacity—without having to import restricted semiconductors,” Ja Ian Chong, a political science expert from the National University of Singapore (NUS), tells Fortune .

According to The Information , Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, used her personal relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to move at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips through Megaspeed and its Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix.

The chip-smuggling controversy swirling around Nvidia centers on one company : Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing provider that, according to several media reports, is suspected of funneling advanced AI processors to Chinese companies.
Companies like Megaspeed typically offer two routes to restricted silicon.
The second is buying chips through front companies and shipping them to China, potentially in violation of U.S. export controls.
3, The Financial Times reported that Oracle had canceled a $7 billion deal to grant Tencent access to 100,000 AI chips in data centers across Southeast Asia after U.S. officials raised concerns.
In addition to its investigation of Megaspeed, the Singaporean government last year charged three individuals with fraud after they diverted AI servers bound for Singapore to Malaysia instead.

Originally incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International, a Chinese gaming firm with ties to state-backed investors, the company changed its name to Megaspeed in early 2023, the same year that Alice Huang joined the company.

“But they may face greater suspicion, scrutiny, restrictions and even punishment from one or both major powers going forward, and perceptions that they are unreliable or duplicitous partners will only increase such pressure.”
“Malaysia has ample land and relatively cheap electricity and water, at least for now,” Chong notes.
“The fact that it sits next to key submarine cables also makes it attractive as a spot for data centers.”

Singapore says it is investigating Megaspeed for “suspected breaches of our domestic laws,” but it separately rejected reports that its authorities were investigating Alice Huang over the espionage allegations.
Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing; Nvidia has previously claimed that it found no evidence of illicit chip transfers.

While details of what Megaspeed is alleged to have done remain murky, experts say the case shows how Chinese firms rely on Southeast Asia to skirt U.S. trade controls. “Chinese firms can access data centers in Singapore and Malaysia—and their computing capacity—without having to import restricted semiconductors,” Ja Ian Chong, a political science expert from the National University of Singapore (NUS), tells Fortune . “But the ease of shipping [chips] through Singapore and Malaysia also makes them attractive for firms and people who wish to circumvent U.S. controls.” Washington restricts the export of Nvidia’s top-end Blackwell and Rubin chips to China, out of fear Beijing could use them to supercharge its AI ambitions . According to The Information , Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, used her personal relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to move at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips through Megaspeed and its Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix. Singapore says it is investigating Megaspeed for “suspected breaches of our domestic laws,” but it separately rejected reports that its authorities were investigating Alice Huang over the espionage allegations. U.S. officials had also been investigating Megaspeed for potential export-control violations. Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing; Nvidia has previously claimed that it found no evidence of illicit chip transfers. Nvidia’s board said in a Nov. 8 statement that it was initiating an independent investigation into whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, though it added it had no reason to believe “either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” The board said it “prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders.” Following reports that Huang conducted a second affair, this time with an Nvidia executive, the chipmaker’s board is now considering removing Huang as CEO, the Wall Street Journal reports. Megaspeed is a Singapore-based neocloud that supplies AI computing power. Originally incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International, a Chinese gaming firm with ties to state-backed investors, the company changed its name to Megaspeed in early 2023, the same year that Alice Huang joined the company. Another Singapore-registered firm, Swiftdata, acquired Megaspeed in November 2023. Alice Huang stepped down as Megaspeed’s managing director, while Singaporean businessman Tan Yong Pong—who owns Swiftdata —became its sole director. (Tan owns another Singapore-registered company, Monster Investment.) In 2024, Tan established Speedmatrix, a Malaysia-based subsidiary of Megaspeed, which was reportedly used to receive shipments of Nvidia chips. According to the New York Times , between June 2024 and June 2025, Speedmatrix received over 200 shipments of restricted Nvidia technology. These chips—which are subject to U.S. restrictions on sales to China—were eventually used to power data centers built by Shanghai Century Litong, a Chinese firm in which Alice’s younger sister, Huang Yu, is a founding shareholder, according to The Information . The firm, which builds data centers in the Chinese cities of Shanghai and Shenzhen, then provides high-performance AI computing capacity to Chinese tech giants including Alibaba and Tencent . “AI chip distributors and resellers often spend too little effort vetting customers, usually relying on paperwork the customer provides,” notes Erich Grunewald, a senior researcher at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy (IAPS), a U.S. nonpartisan think tank. Malaysia has been one of Southeast Asia’s biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom, drawing $94 billion in data center investments between 2021 and mid-2026, including from global tech hyperscalers like Google, AWS and Microsoft . “Malaysia has ample land and relatively cheap electricity and water, at least for now,” Chong notes. “The fact that it sits next to key submarine cables also makes it attractive as a spot for data centers.” Singapore, on the other hand, is favored by multinationals for its open economy, stable political environment and business-friendly policies. Many AI firms, including U.S. firms Anthropic and OpenAI , have chosen to house their APAC headquarters there. Companies like Megaspeed typically offer two routes to restricted silicon. The first is renting out chips already housed in data centers in Singapore and Malaysia—which, under current rules, is legal. The second is buying chips through front companies and shipping them to China, potentially in violation of U.S. export controls. (Megaspeed reportedly did both: it set up data center operations in Sedenak Tech Park in the Malaysian state of Johor , and according to the reports , also shuttled chips to Shanghai Century Litong’s facilities in China.) Under current U.S. export rules, it is legal to give Chinese companies access to AI processors housed outside of China—though previous deals have invited regulatory scrutiny. On Nov. 3, The Financial Times reported that Oracle had canceled a $7 billion deal to grant Tencent access to 100,000 AI chips in data centers across Southeast Asia after U.S. officials raised concerns. The FT also reported that Nvidia is telling cloud computing clients they must sell at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese companies. The U.S. House of Representatives passed a law—the Remote Access Security Act —that would close the loophole allowing Chinese companies to use AI processors housed in other countries; the bill is now before the U.S. Senate. Both Singapore and Malaysia have cracked down on chip smuggling. In addition to its investigation of Megaspeed, the Singaporean government last year charged three individuals with fraud after they diverted AI servers bound for Singapore to Malaysia instead. In October, Malaysian customs officials seized $12.1 million worth of advanced AI chips at Kuala Lumpur International Airport. Initial investigations found the 30 servers—falsely declared as electronic components—were being transferred from one Asian country to another, though officials declined to say which. While details of what Megaspeed is alleged to have done remain murky, experts say the case shows how Chinese firms rely on Southeast Asia to skirt U.S. trade controls.

“Chinese firms can access data centers in Singapore and Malaysia—and their computing capacity—without having to import restricted semiconductors,” Ja Ian Chong, a political science expert from the National University of Singapore (NUS), tells Fortune . “But the ease of shipping [chips] through Singapore and Malaysia also makes them attractive for firms and people who wish to circumvent U.S. controls.”
Washington restricts the export of Nvidia’s top-end Blackwell and Rubin chips to China, out of fear Beijing could use them to supercharge its AI ambitions .

According to The Information , Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, used her personal relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to move at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips through Megaspeed and its Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix.

Singapore says it is investigating Megaspeed for “suspected breaches of our domestic laws,” but it separately rejected reports that its authorities were investigating Alice Huang over the espionage allegations. U.S. officials had also been investigating Megaspeed for potential export-control violations.
Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing; Nvidia has previously claimed that it found no evidence of illicit chip transfers.

Nvidia’s board said in a Nov. 8 statement that it was initiating an independent investigation into whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, though it added it had no reason to believe “either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” The board said it “prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders.”

Another Singapore-registered firm, Swiftdata, acquired Megaspeed in November 2023. (Tan owns another Singapore-registered company, Monster Investment.)

In October, Malaysian customs officials seized $12.1 million worth of advanced AI chips at Kuala Lumpur International Airport. Megaspeed, however, has denied the allegations . “There has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities, and this demonstrates that we are a compliant and legitimate company,” it wrote in a statement last December. “We operate fully within the bounds of all applicable export control regulations and maintain the highest standards of legal and ethical conduct.”

extraction.body: US HOUSE Speaker Mike Johnson said on Thursday (Nov 12) there was growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China after a spy scandal forced out Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Huang stepped down after reports of a romantic relationship with a businesswoman whom US authorities suspect of spying for the Chinese government. Lawmakers from both parties have since called for tougher restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips, threatening access to chips that underpin China’s surging AI development. And senior White House officials were discussing whether Commerce ​Secretary Howard Lutnick should be pushed out, two people familiar with the situation said, as the desire to take action rose across Washington. A growing number of lawmakers have criticised Lutnick for the administration’s refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a key US trade blacklist, and over whether the government was properly overseeing Nvidia’s exports to China. Nvidia’s advanced AI chips are widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company key to the US race against China to build superior AI systems. The US has sought for years to limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips because it does not want the Chinese military to benefit from them. “The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here,” Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, told reporters at the US Capitol, adding he favoured limiting China’s access to the advanced technology. “I think there’s a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take.” The Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, was an executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner the US government suspects of helping China obtain advanced AI chips restricted under US export controls. Beijing has denied Alice Huang is a spy. The case has revived claims among China critics in Washington that US export policies are too weak, boosting calls for more restrictions. Reuters reported that Chinese AI companies are trying to rent ​Nvidia-powered computing capacity outside China because they are worried the Jensen Huang allegations could spur Washington to tighten restrictions on their ability to access the company’s chips remotely. Congressional Republicans are keen to attach new restrictions on exporting advanced AI chips to China in the annual defence authorisation Bill, a must-pass measure that funds the military and typically ​attracts bipartisan support, according to a Senate aide, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Lawmakers are pressing their colleagues to pass at least four Bills on chip exports, according to statements since Monday. The AI Overwatch Act would give Congress more power over advanced AI chip exports. The Chip Security Act would require ​companies to track the location of advanced AI processors to prevent smuggling. The Match Act would pressure US allies to restrict sales and maintenance of advanced chipmaking equipment destined for China. The Remote Access Security Act would give the Commerce Department the tools to stop Chinese firms from renting overseas data centres to access Nvidia chips. Huang’s resignation is unlikely to end congressional scrutiny of Nvidia and could leave the former chief executive more exposed to investigation, said Sunny Cheung, an analyst at the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation. “Congress can still subpoena him and Nvidia should conduct an independent investigation to determine whether the problems extend beyond Huang,” Cheung said. Cheung said Huang’s departure could weaken Nvidia’s influence in Washington and create additional momentum for legislation that tightens restrictions on advanced chip exports. He said Nvidia’s new leadership could also reconsider the company’s China strategy as it seeks to rebuild trust with US policymakers. Jensen Huang is separately expected to testify before Congress before Thanksgiving, which falls on Nov 26. House Foreign Affairs chairman Brian Mast, a Florida Republican, told reporters on Thursday that congressional staff spoke with Nvidia on Wednesday night about a date and location for his testimony. Mast and two other leading House Republicans asked Huang last week to brief them behind closed doors about his relationship with Alice Huang. Less than two weeks ago, billionaire Jensen Huang was a gainfully employed CEO whose personal life the general public knew very little about; today, he’s out at Nvidia, the multitrillion-dollar company he co-founded in 1993, following revelations that he had an affair with (1) a woman accused of being a Chinese spy and (2) an Nvidia subordinate. On Wednesday Nvidia’s board met for hours to decide Huang’s fate, and, despite the CEO reportedly “fighting hard to hang onto his role with the company he founded,” Huang resigned Thursday morning and chief financial officer Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO. Incredibly, Nvidia had no successor in place prior to the scandal that took down its leader because Huang didn’t believe in succession planning ; he was also apparently a micromanager with 60 direct reports and said last year that he reads thousands of employee emails a day. According to The Information, Huang told colleagues in the past several years that he would run Nvidia until he is 120 years old. Which is all well and good if you’re planning to both (a) live that long and (b) not have an affair with an accused Chinese spy. Otherwise it’s pretty risky! The stunning downfall will undoubtedly have reverberations far beyond Nvidia’s Silicon Valley campus, given Huang’s position as one of the most powerful, if not the most powerful, figures in the AI industry and his close proximity to Donald Trump. On Wall Street, the company’s stock was down 11 percent on the news of his departure, which translates to a loss of roughly $1 trillion just this month. In Washington, the New York Times notes that few tech executives “have had as much sway as Huang over Trump’s approach to A.I. and China.” He reportedly “persuaded the president to roll back a ban on chip sales to China and Nvidia has donated at least $20 million to a fund for Trump’s White House ballroom project.” On Thursday morning, Trump — who spent the prior days telling reporters how wonderful Huang is — recommended former Apple CEO Tim Cook for the job. Trump has gushed in the past about “Tim Apple,” who visited the White House last year bearing gifts . “A Legend replaces a Legend!” the president wrote . If you’re just catching up to the sex-spy-AI scandal, here’s everything that’s happened so far. In a bombshell story, the New York Times reports that after concluding that Alice Huang (no relation), the chief executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed, was a “Chinese intelligence asset,” U.S. intelligence officials made an even more startling discovery: that Huang “had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang.” The Times story also reveals that Donald Trump had been “briefed about the intelligence findings” a year ago and “chose not to do anything with the information.” In fairness, the president may have been preoccupied with ballroom renovations; at the time, he was fighting with his architect . In an interview with Bloomberg, the CEO insists his interactions with Ms. Huang were strictly professional. “Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual,” Huang says . He will regret this statement ! GOP representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford — who lead the House’s Committee on Foreign Affairs, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the Select Committee on Intelligence, respectively — send a letter to Huang telling him they want a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Ms. Huang. “Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” they write. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk.” Democratic senator Chris Coons, who is expected to chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee come January, writes on X: “The more I learn about the insane relationship between the Trump Administration, Chinese spies, and AI billionaires, the more I’m convinced there is nothing this administration does that isn’t corrupt. Congress will investigate and get answers.” In a letter to Nvidia employees, Huang — who denied the affair less than two weeks prior — writes : “I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. On Wednesday Nvidia’s board met for hours to decide Huang’s fate, and, despite the CEO reportedly “fighting hard to hang onto his role with the company he founded,” Huang resigned Thursday morning and chief financial officer Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO. Incredibly, Nvidia had no successor in place prior to the scandal that took down its leader because Huang didn’t believe in succession planning ; he was also apparently a micromanager with 60 direct reports and said last year that he reads thousands of employee emails a day. According to The Information, Huang told colleagues in the past several years that he would run Nvidia until he is 120 years old. Which is all well and good if you’re planning to both (a) live that long and (b) not have an affair with an accused Chinese spy. Otherwise it’s pretty risky!

The stunning downfall will undoubtedly have reverberations far beyond Nvidia’s Silicon Valley campus, given Huang’s position as one of the most powerful, if not the most powerful, figures in the AI industry and his close proximity to Donald Trump. On Wall Street, the company’s stock was down 11 percent on the news of his departure, which translates to a loss of roughly $1 trillion just this month. In Washington, the New York Times notes that few tech executives “have had as much sway as Huang over Trump’s approach to A.I. and China.” He reportedly “persuaded the president to roll back a ban on chip sales to China and Nvidia has donated at least $20 million to a fund for Trump’s White House ballroom project.”

On Thursday morning, Trump — who spent the prior days telling reporters how wonderful Huang is — recommended former Apple CEO Tim Cook for the job. Trump has gushed in the past about “Tim Apple,” who visited the White House last year bearing gifts . “A Legend replaces a Legend!” the president wrote .

In an interview with Bloomberg, the CEO insists his interactions with Ms. Huang were strictly professional. “Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual,” Huang says . He will regret this statement !

GOP representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford — who lead the House’s Committee on Foreign Affairs, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the Select Committee on Intelligence, respectively — send a letter to Huang telling him they want a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Ms. Huang. “Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” they write. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. Democratic senator Chris Coons, who is expected to chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee come January, writes on X: “The more I learn about the insane relationship between the Trump Administration, Chinese spies, and AI billionaires, the more I’m convinced there is nothing this administration does that isn’t corrupt. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s bravado had evaporated this week by the time it became clear his scandalous affairs including one with an alleged Chinese spy would cost him his job — and he chastised himself as a “piece of s–t,” according to reports. On Wednesday, in his final hours in charge of the chipmaker he had grown into a $4 trillion giant, Huang had started using phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care,” and calling himself a “piece of s–t,” Bloomberg reported, citing unnamed sources. It was a quick fall from grace for the billionaire and face of the AI boom, who had repeatedly denied that his relationship with Alice Huang – an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed , who’s of no relation – was anything but an ordinary business relationship. After news outlets reported that the relationship with the suspected Chinese spy was a romantic one, Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, rushed to Huang’s house to confront him and Huang confessed, according to Bloomberg and The Information. The board was reportedly wary of taking action, but Teter urged them to make an announcement. On Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang had a second affair with Kimberly Powell , Nvidia’s vice president of health care. The board gathered for an emergency late-night meeting, and Huang was forced to resign, according to reports. On Thursday, Reuters reported that Huang had a third affair — with yet another Nvidia employee, who remains unidentified. The Information reported the same day that Huang has hired Paul Weiss, a major law firm. Huang has claimed not to care about what happens to himself, and that his main concern is his wife and not “ruining the lives” of the multiple women now linked to him, according to the Information. Just months ago, business was booming for Nvidia. The stock hit an all-time high in October and Huang’s personal fortune surpassed $200 billion, according to Forbes. Huang had cultivated a close relationship with President Trump and was seen as somewhat of a celebrity in his native Taiwan. Trouble started brewing in late October, when the New York Times reported that Huang had been the target of a Chinese spy plot involving Alice Huang. Days later, the Financial Times revealed that a secret, months-old government memo had found the relationship was a romantic one. On Sunday, Nvidia’s board announced it would investigate the reports. It hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz – the law firm that previously probed sexual harassment allegations against former Gov. Andrew Cuomo – to lead the investigation. That same day, Huang sent an email blast to the entire company admitting to the affair and apologizing to shareholders and business partners. Morning Report delivers the latest news, videos, photos and more. Huang has been married to his wife Lori for over 40 years , and his two children and son-in-law work at Nvidia. Behind closed doors, Huang assured Nvidia’s senior executives that the affair with Alice was his only instance of marital infidelity, according to Bloomberg. But reports later identified two more affairs with two executives at Nvidia. Huang – who co-founded Nvidia 33 years ago – managed 60 direct reports, had a hand in day-to-day operations and managed decisions as small as the compensation of junior employees, according to reports. He typically responded to emails immediately at all times of day and night – but his responses had slowed, according to Bloomberg. His close hold on the company is part of the reason investors panicked that the firm might not survive without him – causing the stock to shed over $450 billion in market value. The ousted Nvidia boss hasn’t been without defenders. Trump has repeatedly praised Huang since news of the first affair. Most recently, Trump told Stephen A. Smith on Thursday that Huang should only step down if Alice was truly a Chinese spy, and that Huang is “going through hell” and “feels most badly [about] his wife and family.” In the meantime, Huang is gearing up to testify before Congress .

extraction.body: Biographer Stephen Witt wonders whether the former tech chief can – or even wants to – lead again [SINGAPORE] At 63, Jensen Huang may no longer have it in him to start or lead another tech company, speculates Stephen Witt, who wrote Huang’s best-selling biography The Thinking Machine in 2025. Here for the Singapore Writers Festival, Witt says: “In the time that I was with him, I saw him slow down just a step. That’s just age. It’s time. It happens.” Witt worked on the book over several months, speaking with Huang as well as over 200 employees, customers, rivals and friends. The book built a picture of a brilliant, demanding workaholic who had made Nvidia the centre of his life. “But I just don’t know if he can be a CEO again or if he wants to be a CEO again,” Witt tells the festival audience in his keynote speech at Victoria Theatre. “I think his motivation might be shot after this.” Huang’s next task will probably be more personal: trying to save his marriage. Witt says: “I think he will beg his wife not to divorce him.” Although Huang had lovers, including businesswoman Alice Huang and Nvidia’s vice-president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, his love for his wife was genuine, Witt suggests. “Jensen talked about his wife all the time. All the time. He praised her constantly,” Witt says. “He never overlooked that sacrifice she made (leaving engineering to raise their two children). He acknowledged it constantly in conversation.” At the same time, “Nvidia consumed him, it was his life”, Witt adds. “I can see him having almost an identity crisis now… and he may reassess everything. I can see a world where Jensen leaves and just does philanthropic giving, believe it or not.” The biographer’s doubts about a comeback coexist with considerable admiration for the abilities that make Huang so difficult to replace . “Jensen’s a world-class computer scientist. He’s a world-class deal maker. And he’s a world-class ops guy.” Witt describes how Huang could draw an exploded diagram of a graphics chip from memory, explain what each component did and cost, and identify the various suppliers to call for a better price. “He didn’t know anything about business. He just knew about microchips. But he educated himself. He re-engineered himself to be the CEO of the company.” In an anecdote from Witt’s book, retold at the festival, Huang challenged an Nvidia executive with a Masters in Business Administration to name his three favourite books on pricing. The man could not name one, so Huang supplied three. “I want you to read these three books. And when you’re done, we’ll continue this conversation,” he told the executive. Even Huang’s public charisma, Witt suggests, had been painstakingly developed. extraction.body: We live in the age of artificial intelligence — an age that Jensen Huang, perhaps more than any other single person, has made possible. The systems we are building with Nvidia’s equipment will transform our society and culture in ways we can’t imagine. But Mr. Huang’s unraveling is not a technology story. It is a timeless tale of masculine hubris, of a man undone by reckless overconfidence. Some things never change. When I wrote my biography of Mr. Huang, I titled it “The Thinking Machine”. The name referred to the microchips that powered A.I., but also to Mr. Huang’s marauding, relentless intellect, which never slowed down or turned off. In the wake of his stunning departure, spurred by revelations that he carried on at least two affairs, one with a woman who U.S. intelligence determined is a Chinese spy and another with one of his direct reports, I should write a sequel: “The What-Were-You-Thinking?! Machine”. Let’s start with Mr. Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, an executive who managed a Singapore-based company that owns data centers in Southeast Asia. These data centers are suspected of helping Chinese A.I. developers circumvent U.S. restrictions on sales of Nvidia equipment. A recent report in The Information suggests they were used as a way station to illicitly smuggle some $7 billion of equipment into China. Since U.S. intelligence captured evidence of Mr. Huang in a romantic relationship with Ms. Huang, it’s hard to believe that he did not understand what was going on. Now consider Mr. Huang’s reported involvement with Kimberly Powell, an executive in the health care group at his company and his direct subordinate. A former Nvidia employee told me this affair was common knowledge in the company — the same company that employs both of Mr. Huang’s children in executive roles. It’s a stunning and disrespectful display of arrogance. I asked the former employee why Mr. Huang would behave this way, right in front of his kids. The former employee said that it got him high — a narcissist’s high. I started hearing rumors of Mr. Huang’s infidelities earlier but was unable to confirm them. Inside Nvidia, there was a culture of omertà that was difficult to break, and this enabled Mr. Huang to be his worst self. I sensed this deference, at times, in the sycophantic laughter of his subordinates when he was around, and the little things they muttered once he left the room. Ultimately, it took government intelligence to pierce Nvidia’s culture of silence — along with reporters at this newspaper. But now that containment is shattered, and I will not be surprised if more women come forward. No one will be surprised. Mr. Huang went to considerable lengths to cloak his arrogance. When I first met him in 2023, he and his handlers were pushing the idea that he was a humble man. In our conversations, Mr. Huang was constantly deflecting attention away from his success, always quick to assign credit to his employees and executive staff members. He also liked to glad-hand service people. He was a dishwasher once, a point he never let you forget. He loved visiting small, hole-in-the-wall restaurants and leaving extravagant tips. I’d met him for breakfast at Denny’s, and he tipped our waitress $1,000 in $100 bills. He didn’t make a show of it, either. I had to track her down to ask. Over time, though, I began to suspect that this was an act, one performed not for the observer but to flatter himself. In truth, Mr. Huang was quite arrogant. He had little tolerance for disagreement and almost no capacity for open discourse. When you contradicted him, even over the most trivial matter, it was like lighting a fuse. Stick to your position, and soon he exploded, screaming at you for your idiocy. A harangue from Mr. Huang could last an hour or more; his executive staff appeared genuinely afraid of him. Listening to their stories, I was reminded of the abusive music instructor from the movie “Whiplash”. Mr. Huang went to even greater lengths to present himself as a family man. Here, the act was harder to detect and must have involved a great deal of self-deception. He spoke of his wife, Lori, and his kids, Madison and Spencer, all the time. Unlike his flimsy man-of-the-people shtick, this affection for his family seemed genuine. He traveled with them often, all over the world. He encouraged his kids to leave careers in unrelated fields to join him at his microchip company. Several weeks ago, at a wedding in Hawaii, he gave away his daughter, Madison, to Nico Caprez, another Nvidia executive. Mr. Huang met his future wife when he was 17. The two were lab partners in an electrical engineering course, and Mr. Huang was so shy, it took him six months to ask her out. She was his first girlfriend, and they married in their early 20s. She left the work force to raise their kids so Mr. Huang could pursue his dream of founding a company. He has spoken often of the sacrifices she made for him. His betrayal of her is absolute. While reporting his biography, I spoke to some of the Huangs’ oldest friends. These were people they knew in their 20s, long before the money and the fame. I sometimes dropped little hints: Was there any chance of infidelity, perhaps? Any rumors of marital friction? Any arrangements? The response I got was that the Huangs’ marriage was happy, even ideal — something to be emulated. In a divorce, Lori Huang could become one of the richest women in America. It’s possible the Huangs signed a prenuptial agreement, or have some other agreement, but I doubt it. When they married, in the mid-1980s, neither had much in assets. The hundreds of millions of Nvidia shares they jointly own are held in family trusts. They recently donated $75 million toward a flagship building at Vanderbilt University’s new campus in San Francisco. Another building they helped fund at Oregon State University, where they met, is nearing completion. The hypocrisy is almost overwhelming. In the early days — the 1990s — Nvidia was a boys’ club. The staff played video games and drank beer in the office, and almost no women worked there. Their mascot, for a time, was Dawn, an underdressed, large-breasted C.G.I. pixie. Dawn was memory-holed in 2020, around the time Mr. Huang started to talk about empowering women within the company. In 2023, while at Nvidia’s campus, I saw Mr. Huang make an impassioned call for gender parity at Nvidia, where men still account for 80 percent of its employees. Maybe he had an ulterior motive. I was surprised — and, frankly, amazed — when Mr. Huang became President Trump’s close ally in 2025. He’d never shown much interest in politics and had limited Washington connections. He didn’t attend Mr. Trump’s inauguration. But soon, in a masterly display of social engineering, he’d gained the president’s trust, mostly by flattering him. By the time of the president’s tech summit at the White House this September, Mr. Huang was seated at Mr. Trump’s right arm. Mr. Trump and Mr. Huang have a fair amount in common — the bluster, the narcissism and, I suppose, the womanizing. But it was politics that triggered Mr. Huang’s downfall. He persuaded the president to lift export restrictions on Nvidia chips to China, and this put him in conflict with the more hawkish members of the president’s staff — especially Secretary of State Marco Rubio, whose sharp criticisms of China at one point got him barred from that country. It was Mr. Rubio who oversaw the memo that exposed Mr. Huang. Now Nvidia must find a successor. That’s going to be difficult: Mr. Huang never groomed one and has no second in command. Colette Kress will serve as interim chief executive, but she comes from the world of finance, not electrical engineering, so I don’t think she can provide a long-term solution. Whoever replaces Mr. Huang must be a world-class computer scientist, someone who can close deals with powerful customers and someone who can get on the phone to Taiwan and start screaming when the chips are delayed. Nvidia without Jensen Huang is like the Bulls without Michael Jordan. Mr. Huang built Nvidia from nothing, but through his arrogance and toxic self-regard, he has left an empty space that might be impossible to fill. coreStoryFacts.text: Less than two weeks ago, billionaire Jensen Huang was a gainfully employed CEO whose personal life the general public knew very little about; today, he’s out at Nvidia, the multitrillion-dollar company he co-founded in 1993, following revelations that he had an affair with (1) a woman accused of being a Chinese spy and (2) an Nvidia subordinate.

The stunning downfall will undoubtedly have reverberations far beyond Nvidia’s Silicon Valley campus, given Huang’s position as one of the most powerful, if not the most powerful, figures in the AI industry and his close proximity to Donald Trump.
On Wall Street, the company’s stock was down 11 percent on the news of his departure, which translates to a loss of roughly $1 trillion just this month.

In Washington, the New York Times notes that few tech executives “have had as much sway as Huang over Trump’s approach to A.I. and China.” He reportedly “persuaded the president to roll back a ban on chip sales to China and Nvidia has donated at least $20 million to a fund for Trump’s White House ballroom project.”

On Wednesday Nvidia’s board met for hours to decide Huang’s fate, and, despite the CEO reportedly “fighting hard to hang onto his role with the company he founded,” Huang resigned Thursday morning and chief financial officer Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO.

Incredibly, Nvidia had no successor in place prior to the scandal that took down its leader because Huang didn’t believe in succession planning ; he was also apparently a micromanager with 60 direct reports and said last year that he reads thousands of employee emails a day.

On Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang had a second affair with Kimberly Powell , Nvidia’s vice president of health care.
Huang has been married to his wife Lori for over 40 years , and his two children and son-in-law work at Nvidia.
But reports later identified two more affairs with two executives at Nvidia.
On Sunday, Nvidia’s board announced it would investigate the reports.
The ousted Nvidia boss hasn’t been without defenders.

The stunning downfall will undoubtedly have reverberations far beyond Nvidia’s Silicon Valley campus, given Huang’s position as one of the most powerful, if not the most powerful, figures in the AI industry and his close proximity to Donald Trump.
On Wall Street, the company’s stock was down 11 percent on the news of his departure, which translates to a loss of roughly $1 trillion just this month.

In Washington, the New York Times notes that few tech executives “have had as much sway as Huang over Trump’s approach to A.I. and China.” He reportedly “persuaded the president to roll back a ban on chip sales to China and Nvidia has donated at least $20 million to a fund for Trump’s White House ballroom project.”

On Wednesday Nvidia’s board met for hours to decide Huang’s fate, and, despite the CEO reportedly “fighting hard to hang onto his role with the company he founded,” Huang resigned Thursday morning and chief financial officer Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO.

Incredibly, Nvidia had no successor in place prior to the scandal that took down its leader because Huang didn’t believe in succession planning ; he was also apparently a micromanager with 60 direct reports and said last year that he reads thousands of employee emails a day.
I support the investigation and will cooperate fully.
I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security.

But reports later identified two more affairs with two executives at Nvidia.
On Sunday, Nvidia’s board announced it would investigate the reports.
The ousted Nvidia boss hasn’t been without defenders.
Days later, the Financial Times revealed that a secret, months-old government memo had found the relationship was a romantic one.
[SINGAPORE] At 63, Jensen Huang may no longer have it in him to start or lead another tech company, speculates Stephen Witt, who wrote Huang’s best-selling biography The Thinking Machine in 2025.
Witt worked on the book over several months, speaking with Huang as well as over 200 employees, customers, rivals and friends.
The book built a picture of a brilliant, demanding workaholic who had made Nvidia the centre of his life.
In an anecdote from Witt’s book, retold at the festival, Huang challenged an Nvidia executive with a Masters in Business Administration to name his three favourite books on pricing.
The man could not name one, so Huang supplied three.
In 2019, Tesla replaced its in-car driving computer developed by Nvidia with its own hardware.
“I don’t think Jensen ever completely forgave him,” Witt says.
Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang carried a secret for more than a year.
At the same time, “Nvidia consumed him, it was his life”, Witt adds.
“I can see him having almost an identity crisis now… and he may reassess everything.
“So Marco Rubio took it to The New York Times and showed it to them instead.
The people who broke this story were the White House reporters at the Times .
They did not cover Nvidia, like all of us Nvidia chumps over here trying to break the story.
Although Huang had lovers, including businesswoman Alice Huang and Nvidia’s vice-president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, his love for his wife was genuine, Witt suggests.
In Witt’s reading, Nvidia’s directors had to weigh the value of keeping Huang – an undoubtedly formidable leader – against the prospect of further damaging disclosures.
According to news agency Anadolu, Musk had earlier responded to a suggestion that he should hire Huang by writing on X: “That would be an honour” – without actually announcing a formal offer.
He cultivated US President Donald Trump partly to preserve Nvidia’s access to China.
We live in the age of artificial intelligence — an age that Jensen Huang, perhaps more than any other single person, has made possible.
Stephen Witt is the author of The Thinking Machine , a biography of Jensen Huang.
Nvidia without Jensen Huang is like the Bulls without Michael Jordan.
While reporting his biography, I spoke to some of the Huangs’ oldest friends.

Less than two weeks ago, billionaire Jensen Huang was a gainfully employed CEO whose personal life the general public knew very little about; today, he’s out at Nvidia, the multitrillion-dollar company he co-founded in 1993, following revelations that he had an affair with (1) a woman accused of being a Chinese spy and (2) an Nvidia subordinate. On Wednesday Nvidia’s board met for hours to decide Huang’s fate, and, despite the CEO reportedly “fighting hard to hang onto his role with the company he founded,” Huang resigned Thursday morning and chief financial officer Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO. Incredibly, Nvidia had no successor in place prior to the scandal that took down its leader because Huang didn’t believe in succession planning ; he was also apparently a micromanager with 60 direct reports and said last year that he reads thousands of employee emails a day. According to The Information, Huang told colleagues in the past several years that he would run Nvidia until he is 120 years old. Which is all well and good if you’re planning to both (a) live that long and (b) not have an affair with an accused Chinese spy. Otherwise it’s pretty risky! The stunning downfall will undoubtedly have reverberations far beyond Nvidia’s Silicon Valley campus, given Huang’s position as one of the most powerful, if not the most powerful, figures in the AI industry and his close proximity to Donald Trump. On Wall Street, the company’s stock was down 11 percent on the news of his departure, which translates to a loss of roughly $1 trillion just this month. In Washington, the New York Times notes that few tech executives “have had as much sway as Huang over Trump’s approach to A.I. and China.” He reportedly “persuaded the president to roll back a ban on chip sales to China and Nvidia has donated at least $20 million to a fund for Trump’s White House ballroom project.” On Thursday morning, Trump — who spent the prior days telling reporters how wonderful Huang is — recommended former Apple CEO Tim Cook for the job. Trump has gushed in the past about “Tim Apple,” who visited the White House last year bearing gifts . “A Legend replaces a Legend!” the president wrote . If you’re just catching up to the sex-spy-AI scandal, here’s everything that’s happened so far. In a bombshell story, the New York Times reports that after concluding that Alice Huang (no relation), the chief executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed, was a “Chinese intelligence asset,” U.S. intelligence officials made an even more startling discovery: that Huang “had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang.” The Times story also reveals that Donald Trump had been “briefed about the intelligence findings” a year ago and “chose not to do anything with the information.” In fairness, the president may have been preoccupied with ballroom renovations; at the time, he was fighting with his architect . In an interview with Bloomberg, the CEO insists his interactions with Ms. Huang were strictly professional. “Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual,” Huang says . Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s bravado had evaporated this week by the time it became clear his scandalous affairs including one with an alleged Chinese spy would cost him his job — and he chastised himself as a “piece of s–t,” according to reports. On Wednesday, in his final hours in charge of the chipmaker he had grown into a $4 trillion giant, Huang had started using phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care,” and calling himself a “piece of s–t,” Bloomberg reported, citing unnamed sources. It was a quick fall from grace for the billionaire and face of the AI boom, who had repeatedly denied that his relationship with Alice Huang – an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed , who’s of no relation – was anything but an ordinary business relationship. After news outlets reported that the relationship with the suspected Chinese spy was a romantic one, Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, rushed to Huang’s house to confront him and Huang confessed, according to Bloomberg and The Information. The board was reportedly wary of taking action, but Teter urged them to make an announcement. On Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang had a second affair with Kimberly Powell , Nvidia’s vice president of health care. The board gathered for an emergency late-night meeting, and Huang was forced to resign, according to reports. On Thursday, Reuters reported that Huang had a third affair — with yet another Nvidia employee, who remains unidentified. The Information reported the same day that Huang has hired Paul Weiss, a major law firm. Huang has claimed not to care about what happens to himself, and that his main concern is his wife and not “ruining the lives” of the multiple women now linked to him, according to the Information. Just months ago, business was booming for Nvidia. The stock hit an all-time high in October and Huang’s personal fortune surpassed $200 billion, according to Forbes. Huang had cultivated a close relationship with President Trump and was seen as somewhat of a celebrity in his native Taiwan. Trouble started brewing in late October, when the New York Times reported that Huang had been the target of a Chinese spy plot involving Alice Huang. Days later, the Financial Times revealed that a secret, months-old government memo had found the relationship was a romantic one. On Sunday, Nvidia’s board announced it would investigate the reports. It hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz – the law firm that previously probed sexual harassment allegations against former Gov. Andrew Cuomo – to lead the investigation. That same day, Huang sent an email blast to the entire company admitting to the affair and apologizing to shareholders and business partners. Morning Report delivers the latest news, videos, photos and more. Huang has been married to his wife Lori for over 40 years , and his two children and son-in-law work at Nvidia. Behind closed doors, Huang assured Nvidia’s senior executives that the affair with Alice was his only instance of marital infidelity, according to Bloomberg. But reports later identified two more affairs with two executives at Nvidia. Huang – who co-founded Nvidia 33 years ago – managed 60 direct reports, had a hand in day-to-day operations and managed decisions as small as the compensation of junior employees, according to reports. He typically responded to emails immediately at all times of day and night – but his responses had slowed, according to Bloomberg. His close hold on the company is part of the reason investors panicked that the firm might not survive without him – causing the stock to shed over $450 billion in market value. The ousted Nvidia boss hasn’t been without defenders. Trump has repeatedly praised Huang since news of the first affair. Most recently, Trump told Stephen A. Smith on Thursday that Huang should only step down if Alice was truly a Chinese spy, and that Huang is “going through hell” and “feels most badly [about] his wife and family.” In the meantime, Huang is gearing up to testify before Congress .

extraction.body: Biographer Stephen Witt wonders whether the former tech chief can – or even wants to – lead again [SINGAPORE] At 63, Jensen Huang may no longer have it in him to start or lead another tech company, speculates Stephen Witt, who wrote Huang’s best-selling biography The Thinking Machine in 2025. Here for the Singapore Writers Festival, Witt says: “In the time that I was with him, I saw him slow down just a step. That’s just age. It’s time. It happens.” Witt worked on the book over several months, speaking with Huang as well as over 200 employees, customers, rivals and friends. The book built a picture of a brilliant, demanding workaholic who had made Nvidia the centre of his life. “But I just don’t know if he can be a CEO again or if he wants to be a CEO again,” Witt tells the festival audience in his keynote speech at Victoria Theatre. “I think his motivation might be shot after this.” Huang’s next task will probably be more personal: trying to save his marriage. Witt says: “I think he will beg his wife not to divorce him.” Although Huang had lovers, including businesswoman Alice Huang and Nvidia’s vice-president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, his love for his wife was genuine, Witt suggests. “Jensen talked about his wife all the time. All the time. He praised her constantly,” Witt says. “He never overlooked that sacrifice she made (leaving engineering to raise their two children). He acknowledged it constantly in conversation.” At the same time, “Nvidia consumed him, it was his life”, Witt adds. “I can see him having almost an identity crisis now… and he may reassess everything. extraction.body: We live in the age of artificial intelligence — an age that Jensen Huang, perhaps more than any other single person, has made possible. The systems we are building with Nvidia’s equipment will transform our society and culture in ways we can’t imagine. But Mr. Huang’s unraveling is not a technology story. It is a timeless tale of masculine hubris, of a man undone by reckless overconfidence. Some things never change. When I wrote my biography of Mr. Huang, I titled it “The Thinking Machine”. The name referred to the microchips that powered A.I., but also to Mr. Huang’s marauding, relentless intellect, which never slowed down or turned off. In the wake of his stunning departure, spurred by revelations that he carried on at least two affairs, one with a woman who U.S. intelligence determined is a Chinese spy and another with one of his direct reports, I should write a sequel: “The What-Were-You-Thinking?! Machine”. Let’s start with Mr. Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, an executive who managed a Singapore-based company that owns data centers in Southeast Asia. These data centers are suspected of helping Chinese A.I. developers circumvent U.S. restrictions on sales of Nvidia equipment. A recent report in The Information suggests they were used as a way station to illicitly smuggle some $7 billion of equipment into China. Since U.S. intelligence captured evidence of Mr. Huang in a romantic relationship with Ms. Huang, it’s hard to believe that he did not understand what was going on. Now consider Mr. Huang’s reported involvement with Kimberly Powell, an executive in the health care group at his company and his direct subordinate. A former Nvidia employee told me this affair was common knowledge in the company — the same company that employs both of Mr. Huang’s children in executive roles. It’s a stunning and disrespectful display of arrogance. I asked the former employee why Mr. Huang would behave this way, right in front of his kids. The former employee said that it got him high — a narcissist’s high. I started hearing rumors of Mr. Huang’s infidelities earlier but was unable to confirm them. Inside Nvidia, there was a culture of omertà that was difficult to break, and this enabled Mr. Huang to be his worst self. I sensed this deference, at times, in the sycophantic laughter of his subordinates when he was around, and the little things they muttered once he left the room. Ultimately, it took government intelligence to pierce Nvidia’s culture of silence — along with reporters at this newspaper. But now that containment is shattered, and I will not be surprised if more women come forward. No one will be surprised. Mr. Huang went to considerable lengths to cloak his arrogance. When I first met him in 2023, he and his handlers were pushing the idea that he was a humble man. In our conversations, Mr. Huang was constantly deflecting attention away from his success, always quick to assign credit to his employees and executive staff members. He also liked to glad-hand service people. He was a dishwasher once, a point he never let you forget. He loved visiting small, hole-in-the-wall restaurants and leaving extravagant tips. I’d met him for breakfast at Denny’s, and he tipped our waitress $1,000 in $100 bills. He didn’t make a show of it, either. I had to track her down to ask. Over time, though, I began to suspect that this was an act, one performed not for the observer but to flatter himself. In truth, Mr. Huang was quite arrogant. He had little tolerance for disagreement and almost no capacity for open discourse. When you contradicted him, even over the most trivial matter, it was like lighting a fuse. Stick to your position, and soon he exploded, screaming at you for your idiocy. A harangue from Mr. Huang could last an hour or more; his executive staff appeared genuinely afraid of him. Listening to their stories, I was reminded of the abusive music instructor from the movie “Whiplash”. Mr. Huang went to even greater lengths to present himself as a family man. Here, the act was harder to detect and must have involved a great deal of self-deception. He spoke of his wife, Lori, and his kids, Madison and Spencer, all the time. Unlike his flimsy man-of-the-people shtick, this affection for his family seemed genuine. He traveled with them often, all over the world. He encouraged his kids to leave careers in unrelated fields to join him at his microchip company. Several weeks ago, at a wedding in Hawaii, he gave away his daughter, Madison, to Nico Caprez, another Nvidia executive. Mr. Huang met his future wife when he was 17. The two were lab partners in an electrical engineering course, and Mr. Huang was so shy, it took him six months to ask her out. She was his first girlfriend, and they married in their early 20s. She left the work force to raise their kids so Mr. Huang could pursue his dream of founding a company. He has spoken often of the sacrifices she made for him. His betrayal of her is absolute. While reporting his biography, I spoke to some of the Huangs’ oldest friends. These were people they knew in their 20s, long before the money and the fame. I sometimes dropped little hints: Was there any chance of infidelity, perhaps? Any rumors of marital friction? Any arrangements? The response I got was that the Huangs’ marriage was happy, even ideal — something to be emulated. In a divorce, Lori Huang could become one of the richest women in America. It’s possible the Huangs signed a prenuptial agreement, or have some other agreement, but I doubt it. When they married, in the mid-1980s, neither had much in assets. The hundreds of millions of Nvidia shares they jointly own are held in family trusts. They recently donated $75 million toward a flagship building at Vanderbilt University’s new campus in San Francisco. Another building they helped fund at Oregon State University, where they met, is nearing completion. The hypocrisy is almost overwhelming. In the early days — the 1990s — Nvidia was a boys’ club. The staff played video games and drank beer in the office, and almost no women worked there. Their mascot, for a time, was Dawn, an underdressed, large-breasted C.G.I. pixie. Dawn was memory-holed in 2020, around the time Mr. Huang started to talk about empowering women within the company. In 2023, while at Nvidia’s campus, I saw Mr. Huang make an impassioned call for gender parity at Nvidia, where men still account for 80 percent of its employees. Maybe he had an ulterior motive. I was surprised — and, frankly, amazed — when Mr. Huang became President Trump’s close ally in 2025. He’d never shown much interest in politics and had limited Washington connections. He didn’t attend Mr. Trump’s inauguration. But soon, in a masterly display of social engineering, he’d gained the president’s trust, mostly by flattering him. By the time of the president’s tech summit at the White House this September, Mr. Huang was seated at Mr. Trump’s right arm. Mr. Trump and Mr. Huang have a fair amount in common — the bluster, the narcissism and, I suppose, the womanizing. But it was politics that triggered Mr. Huang’s downfall. He persuaded the president to lift export restrictions on Nvidia chips to China, and this put him in conflict with the more hawkish members of the president’s staff — especially Secretary of State Marco Rubio, whose sharp criticisms of China at one point got him barred from that country. It was Mr. Rubio who oversaw the memo that exposed Mr. Huang. Now Nvidia must find a successor. That’s going to be difficult: Mr. Huang never groomed one and has no second in command. Colette Kress will serve as interim chief executive, but she comes from the world of finance, not electrical engineering, so I don’t think she can provide a long-term solution. Whoever replaces Mr. Huang must be a world-class computer scientist, someone who can close deals with powerful customers and someone who can get on the phone to Taiwan and start screaming when the chips are delayed. Nvidia without Jensen Huang is like the Bulls without Michael Jordan. Mr. Huang built Nvidia from nothing, but through his arrogance and toxic self-regard, he has left an empty space that might be impossible to fill.
