extraction.body: A nationwide US ground stop that caused thousands of flight cancellations and prompted travel chaos was caused by a technical issue following a copper wire upgrade, the transport secretary has said. Sean Duffy told a news conference that the government was trying to find out whether the problem that led to air traffic controllers suspending take-offs for four hours on Friday had been caused by "incompetence" on the part of the company doing the upgrades or faulty equipment. Though the ground stop was lifted on Friday evening, it had a knock-on effect on air travel on Saturday as airlines attempted to clear a backlog of flights. Officials including Duffy had previously attributed the issue to outdated equipment. Maintenance on US air traffic control systems was being carried out to switch from copper wire to fibre-optic cable by a contractor called L3Harris, a technology provider, Duffy said. The US had "an incredibly old telecommunications system", he said, adding: "It was such an old wire that it was being discontinued." The transport secretary explained that a router that was being worked on had started flooding other air traffic control systems and created communication issues with planes, prompting the shutdown on safety grounds. The government was now trying to understand whether the root cause was the wire replacement or a fault with the router. The four-hour suspension from 15:54 EST (19:54 GMT) on Friday was the longest such incident since the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US. More than 15,000 flights in the US were delayed or cancelled that day, according to data from flight tracking sites, affecting an estimated 1.5 million passengers, with more than 5,900 cancelled and 7,000 delayed on Saturday. In some cases, passengers were left stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to the gates. The ground stop also had a knock-on effect on schedules around the world, with some flights out of the UK and Europe cancelled. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said the US flight schedule should return to normal by the end of Sunday. US officials have said they did not believe the issue was as a result of a cyber-attack or a rogue AI agent, though Duffy said an investigation into the exact cause was under way. Bryan Bedford, who heads the FAA, told the same news conference: "We see zero evidence of anything nefarious and zero evidence of anything AI related." L3Harris said on Saturday that it had completed more than 70% of the work it had been tasked to undertake to modernise US air traffic communications infrastructure before the shutdown. The company said it was supporting the FAA in its investigation, adding: "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously." Duffy warned that a similar issue could arise again unless the US Congress approved upgrades to air traffic control infrastructure. US President Donald Trump has requested $30.1bn (£22.8bn) for the upgrades. Both chambers of Congress are currently controlled by the Republican Party. Duffy previously said the system needed a $50bn overhaul. Former TSA Administrator John Pistole told the BBC that "the fact that they were able to get it restarted in four-and-a-half hours is good news - it shows a resilience in the system - but what's to say it's not going to happen tomorrow?" A nationwide ground stop has only been ordered one other time since all flights were banned from take-off for several days following the 11 September 2001 attacks. A failure in the Notice to Air Missions (Notam) system in 2023 prompted a grounding that lasted an hour and 52 minutes, delaying about 9,500 flights and cancelling about 1,300.

Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator (FAA) Bryan Bedford provided updates on what led to the FAA’s nationwide ground stop on November 13, 2026, and the restoration efforts the Department took to reopen the airspace safely and quickly. REMINDER: Telecommunications issues that impacted the stability of communications and radar systems utilized by Air Traffic Control led the FAA to issue a nationwide ground stop out of an abundance of caution. FAA’s incredible air traffic controllers and commercial pilots were responsible for safely and efficiently grounding over 3,500 flights swiftly. Once the ground stop lifted, over 8,000 flight operations resumed last night alone. Today, the airspace is open, however, passengers should be prepared for some delays and cancellations as flights resume. Secretary Duffy on the work done by air traffic controllers and pilots to land Americans safely yesterday: “I just want to, again, start off and thank our air traffic controllers and our pilots. They exhibited an amazing performance yesterday. We had 3,500 aircraft in the air. We had a ground stop and they safely landed all of our aircraft which was outstanding. But I also want to thank our flight attendants, our ground crews, our airport authorities. All of them rallied yesterday. A lot of passengers at airports. They all came together and served the American people incredibly well. I also want to thank the passengers. I know a lot of people were disrupted. Whether they were going on vacation, they were coming home from work–they had significant disruption and the patience that they exhibited. We at the DOT and the FAA are grateful for that patience.” Secretary Duffy on what led to the issue: “Now, those of you who are aviation reporters have heard me talk about a decades old air traffic control system. It's not just old equipment. We have an incredibly old telecommunication system. And so, here's what we believe happened yesterday: Secretary Duffy on whether the inconsistencies were caused by a cyber attack: “We don't believe so. Once we were able to isolate the work that was being done at this remote location, all of our systems came back online. So, we don't believe this was cyber at all.” Secretary Duffy on the safety of the national airspace: “To the American traveler, our number one job is their safety and Bryan [Bedford] mentioned this and I’ve mentioned this before but we will keep you on the ground, you won’t get to your destination if we think you can’t get there safely. My first day on the job was the DCA air crash…My heart goes out to those families and everyone who has lost someone in aviation. We do everything we can to keep travelers safe and our airspace is safe. I fly all the time, my kids fly, my wife flies. This is a safe system, evidenced by what happened yesterday. If there is any issue with our telecom…we shut the airspace down. We brought airplanes in, we landed them safely, we figured out what was wrong, our systems came back online and have become fully operational. That’s how seriously we take safety. ” Secretary Duffy on the FAA’s progress modernizing America’s air traffic control system: “The Congress gave me a partial payment. They gave me $12.5 billion. And one of the problems that we had was [Congress] weren't quite sure that we would spend the money well and we'd build with the money. And that's the history of the FAA that goes back from Republicans and Democrats. They haven't spent the money well. So, they want to make sure we're going to spend and spend it well. And we have. And so, in the course of the last year, since I've got that $12.5 billion, I want to talk to you about what we've actually accomplished. Secretary Duffy on the need for Congress to fully fund air traffic control modernization: “I hope that they meet this moment and they invest in what will be the state-of-the-art, the best-in-class, best in the world air traffic control system. When I came in, President Trump, before the DCA air crash, was saying, ‘We have to modernize our airspace. I want you to work on modernizing air traffic control.’...and then if you look at the Congress–that you have both Democrats and Republicans who understand how important this is. For me, it gets to be frustrating where everyone says they want to do it and the president is pushing it but we don't get the resources. And I think this is the moment. If we don't start to switch out our systems, how long are we going to wait? I think this is a sign for [Congress] to lean in. This is bipartisan….We should be able to rely on our air traffic control system—making sure it works… Let’s not let the legacy of the past where investments weren't made, which is why we are here today. Let's make the investments and look forward to a brighter future in aviation , a safer future, a more efficient future in aviation.” FAA Administrator Bedford on how the issue is unrelated to USDOT’s ongoing modernization efforts: “I think we’re conflating ‘Modernization’ with this upgrade at this particular facility. We spend a billion dollars a year maintaining and sustaining the existing 1980’s TDMI telco network—call it 1G, the 1G system that the FAA is on. So we are constantly replacing 2,000 Cisco 600 routers with Juniper routers. So, this is ordinary course-of-business stuff, this is not part of the Peraton-FAA $12.5 billion modernization effort, so let’s not conflate those two things.” Secretary Duffy on the timing of the upgrade: “We're making the transition because it's safer and it's more resilient. But because of the nature of what this switchover was, it was a remote location, we'll do those during the day. Now, if we're going to be at Newark, if we're going to be, you know, in one of our big facilities, those switchovers happen at night and they can have a bigger impact. But these smaller locations don't have that kind of impact—or they shouldn't have that kind of impact which is what we saw yesterday. So, there'll be a reevaluation of when we do this work. But when you look across the country when the work has been done from copper to fiber, going from analog to digital, they've happened at all times of the day, and so we have to drill in a little further about what happened here.”

extraction.body: State-sponsored hackers from North Korea have taken more than $400 million in cryptocurrency by using fake video calls to steal people's identities, US authorities say. More than 900 victims have fallen prey to the scheme, which the FBI refers to as FaceStealer, in the last 18 months, according to the bureau. "The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," says FBI cyber director Brett Leatherman. This comes a week after the world's largest crypto exchange Binance revealed that hackers had used fake job interviews to steal a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from the company. US law enforcement agencies attributed the Binance hack, thought to be the largest crypto hack to date, to North Korea-linked actors. Pyongyang has denied this claim. Authorities say FaceStealer, the latest scheme, "aggressively targets" those who work in the cryptocurrency and web3 sectors, particularly those who are involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software. According to the FBI and US Justice Department, FaceStealer hackers use fake or hijacked social media accounts to invite potential victims into video calls hosted over "imposter versions" of Zoom, Microsoft Teams, and Google Meet. Next, the hackers play pre-recorded videos of previous victims the target is acquainted with to simulate a legitimate call – except that the audio would appear to malfunction. A message then pops up on the target's screen, asking them to "fix" the audio by clicking on a link. This "fix" would eventually download malware onto the target's device, which allows hackers to access their contact lists and apps, widening their pool of potential victims. Hackers would secretly record these calls and use the recordings as material to scam their new victims, according to the US authorities. The FBI has described FaceStealer as "a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user". "It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships," Patrick Grandy, assistant director in charge of the bureau's Los Angeles field office, said in a statement on Thursday. "If you can't imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough." Police say people are being targeted on WhatsApp with messages pretending to be from Lloyds Bank. Robert Barr directed Sean Favier and Iain Doyle to steal the funds from two houses in Midlothian in 2024. extraction.body: The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has established that threat actors tied to the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK aka North Korea) have stolen more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency as part of a social engineering scheme codenamed FaceStealer in the last 18 months. As part of a coordinated set of actions announced by the U.S. government, the cloud-based infrastructure used to pull off the "hard-to-detect" campaign has been seized. In tandem, the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) has announced the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen by the North Korea-linked TraderTraitor actors following the hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance. The plundered digital assets are used to fund Pyongyang's illicit weapons program, the DoJ added. "The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman in a statement. "North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months." According to the Justice Department, FaceStealer relies on surreptitiously recorded videos and deepfakes to facilitate cryptocurrency theft. Some aspects of the activity dovetail with a campaign documented by Kaspersky under the name GhostCall in October 2025. The activity is linked to a prolific North Korea-linked financially motivated threat cluster tracked as BlueNoroff , which is also known by the cryptonyms APT38, CageyChameleon, CryptoCore, DangerousPassword, Nickel Gladstone, Sapphire Sleet, Stardust Chollima, and UNC1069. The campaign involves luring targets with invitations to video meetings delivered from stolen accounts belonging to prior victims. Targets who join the meeting have their video stream recorded, while simultaneously serving an authentic, prerecorded webcam video of a previous victim or victims known to the target to build trust. "The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective," the DoJ said. "Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target's trust." A few seconds into the meeting, a mock technical error is presented to the victim, claiming that they cannot be heard, and they are provided a link to address the non-existent issue. The fix is a ClickFix-style lure that's designed to install malware on the victim's workstation and steal cryptocurrency, as well as abuse the target's privileges to other computer infrastructure. In an extensive report shared with The Hacker News in July 2026, JUMPSEC revealed how the social engineering operation is built atop a phishing kit designed to impersonate videoconferencing platforms like Zoom and Microsoft Teams. The cybersecurity company has characterized FaceStealer as a victim acquisition platform that involves using compromised trusted contacts as a pathway to fuel a self-propagating attack chain via Telegram. This includes hijacking social media and communications accounts such as Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack, and Discord for extended periods of time, and then accessing the victim's contact list to target the victim's personal and professional circles. The goal is to obtain access to the developers' devices and the software repository accounts they control to facilitate software supply chain attacks. Notably, the FaceStealer scheme was put to use in targeting the maintainer of the popular Axios npm package earlier this year to push a trojanized version that delivered a cross-platform remote access trojan (RAT). More than 900 victim webcam video recordings used by the threat actors to impersonate victims in follow-on attacks have been seized by the FBI. The agency said it's "aware of several other attempts by North Korean hackers to target software developers, maintainers, and software libraries with significant download volume." In a report published in April 2026, Arctic Wolf said the targeted social engineering campaign had targeted over 400 victims across more than 20 countries, with most of them concentrated in the U.S., Singapore, the U.K., Hong Kong, South Korea, and the U.A.E. "A full 80% of identified targets operate directly in cryptocurrency/blockchain finance (54%) or adjacent finance and investment sectors (26%)," the cybersecurity company noted at the time. "CEOs and founders alone account for 45% of the target set – nearly half. This underscores BlueNoroff's singular operational focus: individuals with access to cryptocurrency assets, wallet infrastructure, exchange platforms, or investment decision-making authority." The activity has since expanded in scope, with 677 targets identified across 58 countries. More than 80% of the targets are founders and C-suite executives. Besides introducing new lure themes such as a fake Chrome PDF Viewer update, the campaign incorporates generative AI technology from ChatGPT, Google, SpaceXAI Grok, and Wondershare AI Content Generator (AIGC) to supply the attackers with artwork, avatars, and convincing synthetic participant videos. "Upstream, reconnaissance has both widened and become more deliberate," the company added . "Lure material has been scraped not just from profile photos and prior victims' webcam streams, but from YouTube interviews and conference talks, which are screen-recorded by the actor. This allows them to capture a specific person's likeness and voice – a founder perhaps, or a CEO – and then create fake meeting footage without having to directly compromise the target themselves." Each new victim offers a pathway to further the attack. The cyclic modus operandi still remains the beating heart of the social engineering operation. "Combined with their new fake media generation capabilities to produce varied and credible lure content, this presents a significant escalation in BlueNoroff's efforts to compromise high-value individuals who control funds, signing keys, sensitive information, authenticated communications, and trusted professional relationships," Arctic Wolf said. It's worth emphasizing here that the FaceStealer campaign is distinct from ClickFake Interview , an iteration of Contagious Interview that also employs ClickFix-style tactics to trigger the execution of malware as part of recruitment-themed campaigns. Like FaceStealer, this involves the attackers approaching prospective targets by posing as recruiters on platforms like LinkedIn and sharing a "technical assessment" designed to run malware. In a post shared on LinkedIn, Alina Krasavina, an engineering manager at Delivery Hero, detailed how she was targeted in October 2026 by two fake recruiters on the same day, 13 minutes apart. "The first one sent a 'technical assessment': a Next.js project of 113 files. At the end of next.config.js, after 204 spaces, there was a backdoor," Krasavina said . "The second one didn't send any ZIP. On a video call, a 'Member of Technical Staff' asked me to share my whole screen, download a repo, and run it. When I said no, he told me it was 'a requirement to continue.' After the call, I wrote to the recruiter and asked for another interview format. About a minute later she blocked me." "The two attacks were built in opposite ways. The first one put the effort into the code and almost none into the recruiter. The second one put it into the people, and I never even saw its code." According to a joint cybersecurity advisory published by cybersecurity and intelligence agencies from Japan, the U.S., Australia, and Germany in late September 2026, the long-running campaign is estimated to have compromised at least 30,000 devices located in 100 countries. The attacks experiment with multiple delivery methods to convince victims to run malicious code - Last month, Sophos disclosed that an employee's corporate macOS device had been compromised in mid-September 2026 after they cloned a public code repository presented as a job interview coding assignment and opened it as a workspace in VS Code. "The repository contained a weaponized VS Code workspace settings file that replaced the editor's integrated terminal profile," the cybersecurity company said . "When a terminal opened in the workspace, the modified profile silently downloaded and ran a multi-stage payload." The payload in question is BeaverTail, a JavaScript loader that's used to deliver a Python backdoor referred to as InvisibleFerret. Both malware families are attributed to Contagious Interview. Sophos said the malware ran in memory on the device for about 26 hours, right from its execution on September 14, 2026, until it was rebooted a day later. The incident did not affect any of its products or services, or customer data or their systems, it added. What's more, recent research from JFrog has uncovered that the threat actors linked to the campaign have even set up a decoy company named AccuraSoftHire, complete with a careers site, client testimonials, a LinkedIn page, job ads on mainstream boards, and verified recruiters in an attempt to lend credibility and ultimately deceive candidates into running malware through a rigged take-home test and a video verification step. "Our research shows these lures are built to pass the checks people rely on: a professional website, a LinkedIn page, job ads on mainstream boards and recruiters with LinkedIn's verified badge," Guy Korolevski, senior security researcher at JFrog Security Research, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News. "Developers and other employees with system access can't be expected to catch that on their own, so employers need to set the rules. Interview assignments with downloads should only ever run in a disposable virtual machine, never on a work laptop. Security teams should also warn employees about downloading unknown files, even from a source they think they can trust. Developers can also check when a recruiter’s profile was created and whether the company's location is the same on every page." The United States Justice Department said Thursday it had seized cloud infrastructure used by North Korean hackers in a video-call scam that has stolen more than $400 million (€361 million) in cryptocurrency over 18 months. It also said it had court approval to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion taken in the recent Binance hack. The Federal Bureau of Investigation calls the scam "FaceStealer." According to the Justice Department, hackers sent meeting invitations from accounts taken over from earlier victims. Once a target joins, the hackers record their webcam video and play a prerecorded clip of a previous victim the target knows, so trusted contacts appear to be present. The FBI says hackers are also starting to use AI-generated deepfakes of well-known crypto figures. The hackers then stage a fake technical error and offer a link to "fix" it, which installs malware, the department said. In some cases, they waited months, or over a year, before stealing funds. After that, they use the victim's contacts to find new targets. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Most targets work in crypto and other internet-related fields, and the hackers are increasingly going after open-source software developers, apparently to enable supply-chain attacks, the department said. Under a federal warrant, the FBI seized more than 900 webcam videos of victims. "If you can't imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough," said Patrick Grandy, who heads the FBI's Los Angeles field office. The FBI ties FaceStealer to a hacking cluster known as Sapphire Sleet or UNC1069. It is separate from the North Korean military hackers blamed for the Binance theft. In the Binance case, the FBI said the group known as TraderTraitor stole more than $6 billion (5.4 billion euros) on or around October 29. AP put the figure at about $6.3 billion (5.7 billion euros) and called it the biggest crypto heist on record. US agencies and private firms have since frozen more than $2.7 billion (2.44 billion euros), the department said. Authorities usually file a forfeiture claim in court, after which a judge decides who has a rightful claim to the recovered funds, AP reported. Scott Proctor, the department's principal deputy assistant attorney general for national security. North Korea has denied involvement in the Binance hack.

extraction.body: State-sponsored hackers from North Korea have taken more than $400 million in cryptocurrency by using fake video calls to steal people's identities, US authorities say. More than 900 victims have fallen prey to the scheme, which the FBI refers to as FaceStealer, in the last 18 months, according to the bureau. "The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," says FBI cyber director Brett Leatherman. This comes a week after the world's largest crypto exchange Binance revealed that hackers had used fake job interviews to steal a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from the company. US law enforcement agencies attributed the Binance hack, thought to be the largest crypto hack to date, to North Korea-linked actors. Pyongyang has denied this claim. Authorities say FaceStealer, the latest scheme, "aggressively targets" those who work in the cryptocurrency and web3 sectors, particularly those who are involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software. According to the FBI and US Justice Department, FaceStealer hackers use fake or hijacked social media accounts to invite potential victims into video calls hosted over "imposter versions" of Zoom, Microsoft Teams, and Google Meet. Next, the hackers play pre-recorded videos of previous victims the target is acquainted with to simulate a legitimate call – except that the audio would appear to malfunction. A message then pops up on the target's screen, asking them to "fix" the audio by clicking on a link. This "fix" would eventually download malware onto the target's device, which allows hackers to access their contact lists and apps, widening their pool of potential victims. Hackers would secretly record these calls and use the recordings as material to scam their new victims, according to the US authorities. The FBI has described FaceStealer as "a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user". "It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships," Patrick Grandy, assistant director in charge of the bureau's Los Angeles field office, said in a statement on Thursday. "If you can't imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough." Police say people are being targeted on WhatsApp with messages pretending to be from Lloyds Bank. Robert Barr directed Sean Favier and Iain Doyle to steal the funds from two houses in Midlothian in 2024. The Jersey Cyber Security Centre boss is "challenging whether everyone needs a connected fridge". Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. extraction.body: The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has established that threat actors tied to the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK aka North Korea) have stolen more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency as part of a social engineering scheme codenamed FaceStealer in the last 18 months. As part of a coordinated set of actions announced by the U.S. government, the cloud-based infrastructure used to pull off the "hard-to-detect" campaign has been seized. In tandem, the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) has announced the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen by the North Korea-linked TraderTraitor actors following the hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance. The plundered digital assets are used to fund Pyongyang's illicit weapons program, the DoJ added. "The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman in a statement. "North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months." According to the Justice Department, FaceStealer relies on surreptitiously recorded videos and deepfakes to facilitate cryptocurrency theft. Some aspects of the activity dovetail with a campaign documented by Kaspersky under the name GhostCall in October 2025. The activity is linked to a prolific North Korea-linked financially motivated threat cluster tracked as BlueNoroff , which is also known by the cryptonyms APT38, CageyChameleon, CryptoCore, DangerousPassword, Nickel Gladstone, Sapphire Sleet, Stardust Chollima, and UNC1069. The campaign involves luring targets with invitations to video meetings delivered from stolen accounts belonging to prior victims. Targets who join the meeting have their video stream recorded, while simultaneously serving an authentic, prerecorded webcam video of a previous victim or victims known to the target to build trust. "The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective," the DoJ said. "Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target's trust." A few seconds into the meeting, a mock technical error is presented to the victim, claiming that they cannot be heard, and they are provided a link to address the non-existent issue. The fix is a ClickFix-style lure that's designed to install malware on the victim's workstation and steal cryptocurrency, as well as abuse the target's privileges to other computer infrastructure. In an extensive report shared with The Hacker News in July 2026, JUMPSEC revealed how the social engineering operation is built atop a phishing kit designed to impersonate videoconferencing platforms like Zoom and Microsoft Teams. The cybersecurity company has characterized FaceStealer as a victim acquisition platform that involves using compromised trusted contacts as a pathway to fuel a self-propagating attack chain via Telegram. This includes hijacking social media and communications accounts such as Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack, and Discord for extended periods of time, and then accessing the victim's contact list to target the victim's personal and professional circles. The goal is to obtain access to the developers' devices and the software repository accounts they control to facilitate software supply chain attacks. Notably, the FaceStealer scheme was put to use in targeting the maintainer of the popular Axios npm package earlier this year to push a trojanized version that delivered a cross-platform remote access trojan (RAT). More than 900 victim webcam video recordings used by the threat actors to impersonate victims in follow-on attacks have been seized by the FBI. The agency said it's "aware of several other attempts by North Korean hackers to target software developers, maintainers, and software libraries with significant download volume." In a report published in April 2026, Arctic Wolf said the targeted social engineering campaign had targeted over 400 victims across more than 20 countries, with most of them concentrated in the U.S., Singapore, the U.K., Hong Kong, South Korea, and the U.A.E. "A full 80% of identified targets operate directly in cryptocurrency/blockchain finance (54%) or adjacent finance and investment sectors (26%)," the cybersecurity company noted at the time. "CEOs and founders alone account for 45% of the target set – nearly half. This underscores BlueNoroff's singular operational focus: individuals with access to cryptocurrency assets, wallet infrastructure, exchange platforms, or investment decision-making authority." The activity has since expanded in scope, with 677 targets identified across 58 countries. More than 80% of the targets are founders and C-suite executives. Besides introducing new lure themes such as a fake Chrome PDF Viewer update, the campaign incorporates generative AI technology from ChatGPT, Google, SpaceXAI Grok, and Wondershare AI Content Generator (AIGC) to supply the attackers with artwork, avatars, and convincing synthetic participant videos. "Upstream, reconnaissance has both widened and become more deliberate," the company added . "Lure material has been scraped not just from profile photos and prior victims' webcam streams, but from YouTube interviews and conference talks, which are screen-recorded by the actor. This allows them to capture a specific person's likeness and voice – a founder perhaps, or a CEO – and then create fake meeting footage without having to directly compromise the target themselves." Each new victim offers a pathway to further the attack. The cyclic modus operandi still remains the beating heart of the social engineering operation. "Combined with their new fake media generation capabilities to produce varied and credible lure content, this presents a significant escalation in BlueNoroff's efforts to compromise high-value individuals who control funds, signing keys, sensitive information, authenticated communications, and trusted professional relationships," Arctic Wolf said. It's worth emphasizing here that the FaceStealer campaign is distinct from ClickFake Interview , an iteration of Contagious Interview that also employs ClickFix-style tactics to trigger the execution of malware as part of recruitment-themed campaigns. Like FaceStealer, this involves the attackers approaching prospective targets by posing as recruiters on platforms like LinkedIn and sharing a "technical assessment" designed to run malware. In a post shared on LinkedIn, Alina Krasavina, an engineering manager at Delivery Hero, detailed how she was targeted in October 2026 by two fake recruiters on the same day, 13 minutes apart. "The first one sent a 'technical assessment': a Next.js project of 113 files. At the end of next.config.js, after 204 spaces, there was a backdoor," Krasavina said . "The second one didn't send any ZIP. On a video call, a 'Member of Technical Staff' asked me to share my whole screen, download a repo, and run it. When I said no, he told me it was 'a requirement to continue.' After the call, I wrote to the recruiter and asked for another interview format. About a minute later she blocked me." "The two attacks were built in opposite ways. The first one put the effort into the code and almost none into the recruiter. The second one put it into the people, and I never even saw its code." According to a joint cybersecurity advisory published by cybersecurity and intelligence agencies from Japan, the U.S., Australia, and Germany in late September 2026, the long-running campaign is estimated to have compromised at least 30,000 devices located in 100 countries. The attacks experiment with multiple delivery methods to convince victims to run malicious code - Last month, Sophos disclosed that an employee's corporate macOS device had been compromised in mid-September 2026 after they cloned a public code repository presented as a job interview coding assignment and opened it as a workspace in VS Code. "The repository contained a weaponized VS Code workspace settings file that replaced the editor's integrated terminal profile," the cybersecurity company said . "When a terminal opened in the workspace, the modified profile silently downloaded and ran a multi-stage payload." The payload in question is BeaverTail, a JavaScript loader that's used to deliver a Python backdoor referred to as InvisibleFerret. Both malware families are attributed to Contagious Interview. Sophos said the malware ran in memory on the device for about 26 hours, right from its execution on September 14, 2026, until it was rebooted a day later. The incident did not affect any of its products or services, or customer data or their systems, it added. What's more, recent research from JFrog has uncovered that the threat actors linked to the campaign have even set up a decoy company named AccuraSoftHire, complete with a careers site, client testimonials, a LinkedIn page, job ads on mainstream boards, and verified recruiters in an attempt to lend credibility and ultimately deceive candidates into running malware through a rigged take-home test and a video verification step. "Our research shows these lures are built to pass the checks people rely on: a professional website, a LinkedIn page, job ads on mainstream boards and recruiters with LinkedIn's verified badge," Guy Korolevski, senior security researcher at JFrog Security Research, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News. "Developers and other employees with system access can't be expected to catch that on their own, so employers need to set the rules. Interview assignments with downloads should only ever run in a disposable virtual machine, never on a work laptop. Security teams should also warn employees about downloading unknown files, even from a source they think they can trust. Developers can also check when a recruiter’s profile was created and whether the company's location is the same on every page." It also said it had court approval to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion taken in the recent Binance hack. The Federal Bureau of Investigation calls the scam "FaceStealer." According to the Justice Department, hackers sent meeting invitations from accounts taken over from earlier victims. Once a target joins, the hackers record their webcam video and play a prerecorded clip of a previous victim the target knows, so trusted contacts appear to be present. The FBI says hackers are also starting to use AI-generated deepfakes of well-known crypto figures. The hackers then stage a fake technical error and offer a link to "fix" it, which installs malware, the department said. In some cases, they waited months, or over a year, before stealing funds. After that, they use the victim's contacts to find new targets. "If you can't imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough," said Patrick Grandy, who heads the FBI's Los Angeles field office. AP put the figure at about $6.3 billion (5.7 billion euros) and called it the biggest crypto heist on record. US agencies and private firms have since frozen more than $2.7 billion (2.44 billion euros), the department said. extraction.body: A new entity tied to Alice Huang, the Chinese executive at the heart of the scandal that led to the resignation of NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang, disclosed banned NVIDIA GPUs as part of collateral offered by the holding company for financing in 2025, according to a new report from Bloomberg. The new details share another link with Alice Huang, whose firm Megaspeed has already been probed for supplying banned NVIDIA AI chips to China. While reports suggest that the US intelligence community is unconvinced that Alice Huang, the associate of NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang, was a spy, her links to transporting banned GPUs to China are nevertheless present in Bloomberg's analysis of filings with Chinese regulators. In a report , the publication shares that a holding company called Shanghai Longteng Intelligent Computing Data Group Co. ended up gaining access to servers purchased by Aperia Cloud from Dell. Aperia's CEO is facing charges for fraud related to the smuggling of NVIDIA GPUs to China. A Longteng unit (Shanghai Longjie Yaoteng) then used these servers as part of a group of equipment as collateral for financing, says the report, which adds that Alice founded Longteng in 2016 and relinquished shares in 2017. The details about the holding company, which is tied to a Shanghai data center with links to Megaspeed, come as the Southeast Asian nation of Malaysia further tightens GPU rules. Amidst the firestorm created by the former NVIDIA CEO, Minister of Investment, Trade and Industry Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani shared earlier today that his country was evaluating current laws to determine whether they could target GPU re-exports to comply with the US sanctions. US lawmakers are also advancing legislation to prevent Chinese AI companies from accessing restricted chips remotely, with 'footprints' of the banned Blackwell GPUs discovered in forensic analysis of leading Chinese AI models. While Bloomberg also claims that servers manufactured by Super Micro, using the H100 or H200 chips, were also part of the regulatory disclosure, the firm asserted that it did not directly make any such sales. Super Micro has long faced scrutiny for similar shipments. Individuals tied to the firm were charged by the Justice Department in March for diverting restricted chips to China. However, the firm's statement claimed that the actions of the indicted were against its rules and policies and in line with US law. The new details share another link with Alice Huang, whose firm Megaspeed has already been probed for supplying banned NVIDIA AI chips to China. While reports suggest that the US intelligence community is unconvinced that Alice Huang, the associate of NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang, was a spy, her links to transporting banned GPUs to China are nevertheless present in Bloomberg's analysis of filings with Chinese regulators. In a report , the publication shares that a holding company called Shanghai Longteng Intelligent Computing Data Group Co. ended up gaining access to servers purchased by Aperia Cloud from Dell. Aperia's CEO is facing charges for fraud related to the smuggling of NVIDIA GPUs to China. A Longteng unit (Shanghai Longjie Yaoteng) then used these servers as part of a group of equipment as collateral for financing, says the report, which adds that Alice founded Longteng in 2016 and relinquished shares in 2017. The details about the holding company, which is tied to a Shanghai data center with links to Megaspeed, come as the Southeast Asian nation of Malaysia further tightens GPU rules. Amidst the firestorm created by the former NVIDIA CEO, Minister of Investment, Trade and Industry Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani shared earlier today that his country was evaluating current laws to determine whether they could target GPU re-exports to comply with the US sanctions. US lawmakers are also advancing legislation to prevent Chinese AI companies from accessing restricted chips remotely, with 'footprints' of the banned Blackwell GPUs discovered in forensic analysis of leading Chinese AI models. While Bloomberg also claims that servers manufactured by Super Micro, using the H100 or H200 chips, were also part of the regulatory disclosure, the firm asserted that it did not directly make any such sales. Super Micro has long faced scrutiny for similar shipments. Individuals tied to the firm were charged by the Justice Department in March for diverting restricted chips to China. However, the firm's statement claimed that the actions of the indicted were against its rules and policies and in line with US law. extraction.body: Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has drawn a range of responses across Asia, with some governments moving to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations. On Sunday, November 8, Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation after reports that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation; Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed. Nvidia’s influence extends far beyond the United States. The chip giant has built close ties with companies worldwide, particularly in Asia, where many of its key partners play important roles in the global AI industry. China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing. On Friday , a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang. Huang’s exit has also raised uncertainty over more than $3 billion in Chinese AI computing projects reliant on Nvidia’s restricted processors, according to Reuters. Many of these chips are subject to U.S. export controls, making them difficult for Chinese companies to obtain. In Singapore, authorities seized the passport of Alice Huang, former CEO of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, in June 2025 as part of an investigation into possible false declarations regarding server purchases, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs. The Singapore ministry said police took her passport to ensure she remained available for questioning, as she was not based in Singapore. The investigation examined whether servers shipped from Singapore to Malaysia were later sent to other countries without proper declaration. In February 2026, police found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang had committed offenses related to the suspected false declarations, according to the ministry. However, authorities said she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed. She was issued a warning and barred from re-entering Singapore. Her passport was returned that month. Singapore also said it received limited assistance from U.S. authorities despite repeated requests for information about U.S. server maker Supermicro. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said its investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals remains ongoing. The ministry did not identify the six individuals or specify their alleged roles in the case. South Korea has close ties to Nvidia, with major chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix playing important roles in supplying memory chips used in its AI processors. Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects. Apart from that, South Korea’s government AI strategy council held an emergency meeting on Friday to assess the potential impact of Huang’s departure on the country’s AI industry, per a local media report. Taiwan’s Economy Minister Kung Ming-shin said Huang’s departure was unlikely to significantly change the growth of the global AI industry, according to local media . Meanwhile, Taipei’s city government said Nvidia’s planned overseas headquarters in the city remained on track despite the leadership change. The company has met its contractual obligations so far, and officials said they would continue to support the project. In Japan, the Industry Ministry said the government would closely monitor Nvidia following Huang’s resignation, describing the chipmaker as an important player in Japan’s AI semiconductor industry, Reuters reported. Deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki said it was too early to assess the impact on the global AI industry, while stressing Japan’s commitment to ensuring a stable supply of semiconductors. passages: [BEIJING] Nvidia has said US export controls have effectively shut it out of China’s artificial intelligence data centre market, but a Reuters review has identified more than US$3 billion in Chinese computing projects built around the American chipmaker’s restricted processors.

The findings come a day after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive amid a scandal over his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by US authorities of intelligence ties to Beijing .
Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation , saying it had no reason to believe company secrets or US national security were compromised.
There has been no public finding that Jensen Huang violated export-control laws.
But an IDC report cited by Reuters in October estimated Nvidia still accounted for 34 per cent of Chinese AI-accelerator shipments in the first half of 2026.
Huang, a vocal advocate of easing export restrictions, said in 2025 Nvidia’s market share in China had fallen from 95 per cent to zero.
Inside Jensen Huang’s last hours as Nvidia CEO

The projects, stretching from China’s wealthy coastal technology hubs to remote western provinces, reveal the scale of continuing demand for Nvidia hardware even as Washington seeks to curb Beijing’s access to the technology powering the global AI boom .
The estimate includes planned investments and signed contracts as well as completed installations.
It covers buildings, power systems and other infrastructure, and does not reflect spending on Nvidia chips alone.
Huang’s departure could deepen these vulnerabilities by weakening Nvidia’s lobbying leverage as US lawmakers press for tighter controls.

The scrutiny has intensified since Huang’s resignation on Thursday (Nov 12), following allegations involving Alice Huang, a former executive associated with Singapore-based Nvidia cloud partner Megaspeed .
Across China, developers and institutions are advancing billions of dollars in AI data centre projects designed around restricted Nvidia H100, H200, and H800 processors.

These range from massive regional computing hubs to retrofitted commercial sites – such as a facility in northwestern Gansu province that was expected to install thousands of Nvidia chips before end-2026, though it remains unclear if those processors ever arrived.
Washington began restricting Nvidia’s advanced AI processors in 2022 and subsequently tightened controls on modified chips developed for China, including the H800.
Megaspeed has denied illegally diverting Nvidia chips to China.
The Chinese projects identified by Reuters have not been linked to Megaspeed or the allegations involving Huang.
The findings paint a detailed picture of how deeply Nvidia technology remains embedded in China’s AI expansion.
China’s commerce ministry and Nvidia did not immedietely respond to Reuters request for comment.

Last year, Nvidia wrote off about $4.5 billion in Chinese-tuned AI chips.

The Nvidia spokesperson pushed back on the story in a statement to CNBC, saying that Singapore-based Megaspeed is another one of the company's regional cloud customers, and that Jensen Huang's interactions with its officials are not unusual, because he speaks with thousands of customers every year.
Earlier this year the U.S. government cleared Nvidia's H200 chip to be shipped to China, but Chinese regulators prevented their imports.
H200s are Nvidia's Hopper generation chip, not the current faster Blackwell generation currently used by American AI developers.

Nvidia has had to walk a tightrope in Washington as its AI chips have become a powerful tool for all AI developers and a bargaining chip in economic competition with China.
China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing.

On Friday , a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang.
Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects.

Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has drawn a range of responses across Asia, with some governments moving to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations.
Meanwhile, Taipei’s city government said Nvidia’s planned overseas headquarters in the city remained on track despite the leadership change.

[BEIJING] Nvidia has said US export controls have effectively shut it out of China’s artificial intelligence data centre market, but a Reuters review has identified more than US$3 billion in Chinese computing projects built around the American chipmaker’s restricted processors.

The findings come a day after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive amid a scandal over his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by US authorities of intelligence ties to Beijing .
Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation , saying it had no reason to believe company secrets or US national security were compromised.
There has been no public finding that Jensen Huang violated export-control laws.
But an IDC report cited by Reuters in October estimated Nvidia still accounted for 34 per cent of Chinese AI-accelerator shipments in the first half of 2026.
Huang, a vocal advocate of easing export restrictions, said in 2025 Nvidia’s market share in China had fallen from 95 per cent to zero.

The projects, stretching from China’s wealthy coastal technology hubs to remote western provinces, reveal the scale of continuing demand for Nvidia hardware even as Washington seeks to curb Beijing’s access to the technology powering the global AI boom .
The estimate includes planned investments and signed contracts as well as completed installations.
It covers buildings, power systems and other infrastructure, and does not reflect spending on Nvidia chips alone.
Huang’s departure could deepen these vulnerabilities by weakening Nvidia’s lobbying leverage as US lawmakers press for tighter controls.

The scrutiny has intensified since Huang’s resignation on Thursday (Nov 12), following allegations involving Alice Huang, a former executive associated with Singapore-based Nvidia cloud partner Megaspeed .
Across China, developers and institutions are advancing billions of dollars in AI data centre projects designed around restricted Nvidia H100, H200, and H800 processors.

These range from massive regional computing hubs to retrofitted commercial sites – such as a facility in northwestern Gansu province that was expected to install thousands of Nvidia chips before end-2026, though it remains unclear if those processors ever arrived.
Washington began restricting Nvidia’s advanced AI processors in 2022 and subsequently tightened controls on modified chips developed for China, including the H800.
Megaspeed has denied illegally diverting Nvidia chips to China.
The Chinese projects identified by Reuters have not been linked to Megaspeed or the allegations involving Huang.
The findings paint a detailed picture of how deeply Nvidia technology remains embedded in China’s AI expansion.
China’s commerce ministry and Nvidia did not immedietely respond to Reuters request for comment.

The intersection of Jensen Huang's sudden resignation as Nvidia's CEO, intense U.S. regulatory scrutiny, and fresh investigative findings regarding restricted semiconductor flows has created a massive compliance and political crisis for the tech giant.

A comprehensive investigation by Reuters revealed a pipeline of over $3 billion in Chinese computing projects—embedded across local government-backed ventures, regional cloud data centers, state-owned engineering groups, and universities—that rely directly on restricted Nvidia processors (such as the H100 and H200 series).

The Reuters review examined more than 150 Chinese procurement notices, investment plans, construction contracts and corporate disclosures, identifying projects and equipment agreements with a combined reported value exceeding 23 billion yuan ($3.2 billion).

The projects, stretching from China's wealthy coastal technology hubs to remote western provinces, reveal the scale of continuing demand for Nvidia hardware even as Washington seeks to curb Beijing's access to the technology powering the global artificial-intelligence (AI) boom.
The exposure of these projects coincides with unprecedented turbulence at the top of Nvidia:

Industry estimates (including IDC data) show Nvidia maintaining a notable presence via secondary or indirect routes, highlighting how difficult it is for Washington to completely sever high-end computing supply chains.

While Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation concluding that no company secrets or national security parameters were compromised, and no legal finding of export-control violations has been leveled against Huang directly, the political shockwaves are immense.

extraction.body: An Nvidia spokesperson on Thursday pushed back on a New York Times report that detailed American intelligence agencies surveilling a person close to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang because they thought she could be a Chinese intelligence asset. According to the Times report , which cited people briefed on intelligence surveillance, Alice Huang, who is linked to the Singapore-based cloud Megaspeed, developed a close relationship with Nvidia's Jensen Huang. Intelligence agencies worried that she was a spy, helping the Chinese government gain information from Nvidia and Jensen Huang, and fretted that Nvidia's CEO had access to President Donald Trump. The Nvidia spokesperson pushed back on the story in a statement to CNBC, saying that Singapore-based Megaspeed is another one of the company's regional cloud customers, and that Jensen Huang's interactions with its officials are not unusual, because he speaks with thousands of customers every year. The spokesperson added that customers don't get access to Nvidia trade secrets or relevant national security information. The report also alleged that Megaspeed was previously suspected of helping companies evade U.S. export controls on Nvidia's AI chips, which aren't allowed to be shipped to China. Nvidia said that Megaspeed had already been investigated for evading export controls. "The diversion allegations against this regional cloud were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year," the spokesperson said in a statement. Nvidia implied that the U.S. government had not briefed Nvidia on Alice Huang. "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know," the spokesperson said. Nvidia has had to walk a tightrope in Washington as its AI chips have become a powerful tool for all AI developers and a bargaining chip in economic competition with China. Politicians and analysts say that Nvidia's AI chips could be used to create Chinese military AI models, or commercial AI models that could compete and eventually surpass American technology. As AI has become more important to the government, Nvidia's Huang has befriended Trump and has given pro-American speeches about building U.S. AI infrastructure. Huang has appeared with Trump at state dinners, AI summits, and international trips, all while pushing for certain Nvidia chips to get a green light to be shipped to China. Earlier this year the U.S. government cleared Nvidia's H200 chip to be shipped to China, but Chinese regulators prevented their imports. H200s are Nvidia's Hopper generation chip, not the current faster Blackwell generation currently used by American AI developers. The Nvidia spokesperson said the Chinese government is not looking for Nvidia products from regional clouds like Megaspeed. "Instead, the PRC government blocked U.S. AI chips, protecting its own industry and resulting in the largest write-offs in U.S. tech history," the Nvidia spokesperson said. extraction.body: Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has drawn a range of responses across Asia, with some governments moving to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations. On Sunday, November 8, Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation after reports that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation; Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed. Nvidia’s influence extends far beyond the United States. The chip giant has built close ties with companies worldwide, particularly in Asia, where many of its key partners play important roles in the global AI industry. China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing. On Friday , a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang. Huang’s exit has also raised uncertainty over more than $3 billion in Chinese AI computing projects reliant on Nvidia’s restricted processors, according to Reuters. Many of these chips are subject to U.S. export controls, making them difficult for Chinese companies to obtain. In Singapore, authorities seized the passport of Alice Huang, former CEO of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, in June 2025 as part of an investigation into possible false declarations regarding server purchases, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs. The Singapore ministry said police took her passport to ensure she remained available for questioning, as she was not based in Singapore. The investigation examined whether servers shipped from Singapore to Malaysia were later sent to other countries without proper declaration. In February 2026, police found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang had committed offenses related to the suspected false declarations, according to the ministry. However, authorities said she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed. She was issued a warning and barred from re-entering Singapore. Her passport was returned that month. Singapore also said it received limited assistance from U.S. authorities despite repeated requests for information about U.S. server maker Supermicro. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said its investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals remains ongoing. The ministry did not identify the six individuals or specify their alleged roles in the case. South Korea has close ties to Nvidia, with major chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix playing important roles in supplying memory chips used in its AI processors. Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects. Apart from that, South Korea’s government AI strategy council held an emergency meeting on Friday to assess the potential impact of Huang’s departure on the country’s AI industry, per a local media report. Taiwan’s Economy Minister Kung Ming-shin said Huang’s departure was unlikely to significantly change the growth of the global AI industry, according to local media . Meanwhile, Taipei’s city government said Nvidia’s planned overseas headquarters in the city remained on track despite the leadership change. The company has met its contractual obligations so far, and officials said they would continue to support the project. In Japan, the Industry Ministry said the government would closely monitor Nvidia following Huang’s resignation, describing the chipmaker as an important player in Japan’s AI semiconductor industry, Reuters reported. Deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki said it was too early to assess the impact on the global AI industry, while stressing Japan’s commitment to ensuring a stable supply of semiconductors. extraction.body: Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security. U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported. The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up. By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. More reports continue to roll out that illustrate the shock and severity of Huang’s resignation from Nvidia. Bloomberg reported that Huang looked “broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted” by the time he surrendered his role on Wednesday night, uttering phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care.” Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported that Huang had been critical of his CFO and current interim CEO, Colette Kress. Huang is said to have described Kress as “a deer in the headlights” during a presentation this summer, and he had described Kress as someone who could not help him steer strategy or decision-making. In a scathing letter sent to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Representative Richard Neal (D-MA) and Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) said they will investigate how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China, especially after Trump was briefed about Huang’s relationship with a purported Chinese spy. “Although [Lutnick] and President Trump were reportedly briefed on this intelligence, the Administration did not appear to acknowledge this evident national security threat. On the contrary: despite reportedly learning of Mr. Huang’s compromising relationship last fall, President Trump granted Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales,” the letter states. Nvidia said its board had accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. The company’s current CFO, Colette Kress , will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang. Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia’s board since 1993. Later in the day, Huang confirmed that he would testify in Congress at some point before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26. “Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.” The testimony is expected to take place behind closed doors, but Mast believes the briefing will be recorded and transcribed. After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per The Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days. Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said . The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO. According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year. Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressmen to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China Committee Chairman John Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed . The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum. Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported . The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips. Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported . Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang. An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary. “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.” U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times. Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo. Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service. Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born. These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. Jensen Huang leads Nvidia; Alice Huang ran operations at a firm built on Nvidia’s technology. Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has led it since.
