extraction.body: Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security. U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported. The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up. By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. More reports continue to roll out that illustrate the shock and severity of Huang’s resignation from Nvidia. Bloomberg reported that Huang looked “broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted” by the time he surrendered his role on Wednesday night, uttering phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care.” Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported that Huang had been critical of his CFO and current interim CEO, Colette Kress. Huang is said to have described Kress as “a deer in the headlights” during a presentation this summer, and he had described Kress as someone who could not help him steer strategy or decision-making. In a scathing letter sent to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Representative Richard Neal (D-MA) and Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) said they will investigate how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China, especially after Trump was briefed about Huang’s relationship with a purported Chinese spy. “Although [Lutnick] and President Trump were reportedly briefed on this intelligence, the Administration did not appear to acknowledge this evident national security threat. On the contrary: despite reportedly learning of Mr. Huang’s compromising relationship last fall, President Trump granted Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales,” the letter states. Nvidia said its board had accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. The company’s current CFO, Colette Kress , will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang. Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia’s board since 1993. Later in the day, Huang confirmed that he would testify in Congress at some point before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26. “Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.” The testimony is expected to take place behind closed doors, but Mast believes the briefing will be recorded and transcribed. After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per The Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days. Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said . The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO. According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year. Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressmen to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China Committee Chairman John Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed . The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum. Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported . The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips. Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported . Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang. An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary. “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.” U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times. Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo. Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service. Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born. These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. extraction.body: For more on Jensen Huang’s resignation and the fallout from Nvidia’s leadership crisis, follow Terrence O’Brien. How it started On October 29th, The New York Times reported that Nvidia co-founder and showman CEO Jensen Huang appeared to be the target of a Chinese spy plot. Any major tech CEO potentially being compromised by the Chinese government is concerning — especially Jensen Huang. “If you could draw the network diagram of the entire US AI ecosystem, Nvidia would be at the center of that,” Kyle Chan, a foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. “If you could draw the diagram of the entire Nvidia ecosystem, a single man is standing at the heart of all of that.” The Times reported that Jensen Huang had developed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. Alice Huang had been on the American government’s radar for some time, perhaps as early as 2024. Her company was investigated by the US Commerce Department over suspicions it was illegally smuggling Nvidia’s AI chips into China in violation of US government trade restrictions. Singapore authorities confiscated her passport back in June of 2025, eventually barring her from the country, after she reportedly gave “inaccurate information” to police. And perhaps more concerningly, some US officials believed she was passing information, possibly about Nvidia’s designs or the White House’s deliberations over trade restrictions, directly back to Beijing. This made her relationship with Jensen Huang concerning for multiple reasons. Nvidia’s chips are considered crucial to America’s AI superiority and a matter of national security by the White House. The government has restricted the sale of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China since the Biden administration. But Jensen Huang has routinely pushed to loosen those trade restrictions. On Friday, November 6th, the Times reported that Alice Huang was specifically recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia’s CEO. Though, there is some disagreement among US intelligence officials over the strength of evidence tying Alice Huang to Beijing. While the paper did not confirm it at the time, rumors suggested the “close relationship” between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang was romantic in nature. On Sunday, November 8th, Jensen Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair, but did not name the Megaspeed exec and alleged Chinese spy specifically. Nvidia’s board announced that it was launching an investigation into its CEO shortly after. Many believed that Jensen Huang would survive the scandal. His company’s importance to America’s booming AI industry and his crucial role at the company seemed to make him nearly untouchable. He was, after all, the only CEO the company had ever known with no clear and obvious succession plan in place, and he sat atop an unusual corporate structure with around 60 direct reports. (These numbers are slightly outdated, but according to the Harvard Business Review, 10 to 20 is far more common among Fortune 500 companies, and Tim Cook reportedly had 17 in 2015, which was deemed “a lot” by Business Insider.) Then on Wednesday, November 11th, The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had a second affair — this one with one of his direct reports, Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care. Whether that was the last straw or if they were afraid it would be merely the tip of the iceberg, the board was ready to push Jensen Huang out, according to reports circulating that evening. According to Bloomberg, he had accepted his fate Wednesday evening reportedly looking “broken and shattered” and telling people, “I’m a piece of shit.” On Thursday, November 12th, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang had resigned as CEO of Nvidia. How it’s going CFO Colette Kress was immediately named interim CEO, and acknowledged to employees that this has been an “extraordinarily difficult period.” Harvey Jones was also named the first board chair in the company’s history, already signaling there would be some changes to the corporate structure. In a memo to employees, Jones said the company would “search for a permanent successor looking at both internal and external candidates.” But the destabilizing impact was immediate. Nvidia’s stock closed at an all-time high of $239.24 on October 6th. It’s hard to overstate the importance of Nvidia to the US’s AI arms race with China, and the industry in general. The company has invested $99 billion in various AI labs, startups, and neo clouds. Plus has announced plans to mobilize over $500 billion in financing for building out AI data centers and other infrastructure. Even before Jensen Huang had resigned, Nvidia was already facing a shareholder lawsuit claiming the company had deceived investors. Jensen Huang and the company’s spokespeople insisted that the relationship with Alice Huang and Megaspeed was “completely normal and not unusual.” Only days later, Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair that raised “national security concerns” without naming anyone specifically. According to Reuters, Jensen Huang misled several Nvidia leaders, “including general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld” about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang. Many in the AI industry and Silicon Valley jumped to Jensen Huang’s defense. Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney called it a “sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity,” in a particularly hyperbolic post. Elon Musk said on X that it would “be an honor” to hire Jensen Huang. Many of Nvidia’s employees even voiced their support to “bring back THE boss,” on an internal post.

extraction.body: We’re getting some extraordinary reporting on what it has been like inside Nvidia during Huang’s last days. Before his forced resignation, Huang had given up, Bloomberg says , and was heard saying things like “whatever,” “I don’t care,” and referring to himself as a “piece of sh--.” That, of course, was in stark contrast to how Huang historically ran the company. Huang had “imperial control,” and ran it like a “feudal system,” according to the FT . “I can’t tell you what a cult this place is,” a source told the paper. General counsel Tim Teter wore a leather jacket just like Huang’s, the source said: “Jensen is a god, and that’s how he’s worshipped.” Noteworthy: In addition to having no board chair, the company also did not have a compliance officer, the FT says. Interim CEO Colette Kress and whoever replaces her as permanent CEO will have messy office politics to deal with, according to the FT . Huang’s daughter Madison Huang is a senior director of marketing at the company, but she acts like her father’s de facto chief of staff, the FT says. Nvidia also employs her husband Nico Caprez and Huang’s son Spencer. Kress, meanwhile, sometimes did not get Huang’s respect, the WSJ reported . He once called her “a deer in the headlights” and a “reporting CFO” (as opposed to a strategic leader) during a meeting in which they were discussing Nvidia’s agreements “to provide billions of dollars of guarantees to companies that couldn’t afford its chips,” the WSJ said. Kress struggled to rein in Caprez, who had made multiple offers of financing to cloud providers and data-center builders in return for shares of revenue. Lenders relied on the Huang family's backing for AI financing when structuring deals with AI providers. Without Huang at the top, “that Nvidia guarantee is not worth what it was worth a week ago, that puts those neocloud businesses at risk,” Joe Kaiser of Switchyard Partners, an AI financing company, told Fortune’s Catherina Gioino . Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and commerce secretary Howard Lutnick have been called by Sen. Tim Scott (R-South Carolina) to testify in front of the Senate Banking Committee, the NYT reports . The hearing will be conducted next month. “Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology,” Scott said. That’s a reference to Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy who ran a company that bought Nvidia chips and is suspected of smuggling them into China in violation of U.S. export controls. As for Lutnick, Republicans are furious at what they perceive was the special treatment he gave Nvidia in terms of its access to the Chinese market and in his foot-dragging on the enforcement of export bans to China, the FT says . Lutnick shielded Nvidia from the White House’s attempts to restrict export of the U.S.’s best technology to China, the NYT reported . All matters related to Nvidia were routed through a deputy to Lutnick, Jeff Kessler, who rarely took action without Lutnick’s approval, the NYT said . Inside the White House, senior Trump administration figures largely blame Lutnick for being asleep at the wheel in terms of the threat Nvidia posed to national security, given its ties to Chinese importers, the WSJ reported . ​​Alice Huang: Those concerns will get extra momentum on the news that Jensen Huang’s affair partner, suspected spy Alice Huang (no relation) of Megaspeed, had a relationship with Huawei, China’s biggest competitor in China, according to CNBC . Alice Huang allegedly ran a complicated network of companies to do deals with Nvidia that resulted in its chips ending up at Chinese companies, per Bloomberg . extraction.body: For more on Jensen Huang’s resignation and the fallout from Nvidia’s leadership crisis, follow Terrence O’Brien. How it started On October 29th, The New York Times reported that Nvidia co-founder and showman CEO Jensen Huang appeared to be the target of a Chinese spy plot. Any major tech CEO potentially being compromised by the Chinese government is concerning — especially Jensen Huang. “If you could draw the network diagram of the entire US AI ecosystem, Nvidia would be at the center of that,” Kyle Chan, a foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. “If you could draw the diagram of the entire Nvidia ecosystem, a single man is standing at the heart of all of that.” The Times reported that Jensen Huang had developed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. Alice Huang had been on the American government’s radar for some time, perhaps as early as 2024. Her company was investigated by the US Commerce Department over suspicions it was illegally smuggling Nvidia’s AI chips into China in violation of US government trade restrictions. Singapore authorities confiscated her passport back in June of 2025, eventually barring her from the country, after she reportedly gave “inaccurate information” to police. And perhaps more concerningly, some US officials believed she was passing information, possibly about Nvidia’s designs or the White House’s deliberations over trade restrictions, directly back to Beijing. This made her relationship with Jensen Huang concerning for multiple reasons. Nvidia’s chips are considered crucial to America’s AI superiority and a matter of national security by the White House. The government has restricted the sale of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China since the Biden administration. But Jensen Huang has routinely pushed to loosen those trade restrictions. On Friday, November 6th, the Times reported that Alice Huang was specifically recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia’s CEO. Though, there is some disagreement among US intelligence officials over the strength of evidence tying Alice Huang to Beijing. While the paper did not confirm it at the time, rumors suggested the “close relationship” between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang was romantic in nature. On Sunday, November 8th, Jensen Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair, but did not name the Megaspeed exec and alleged Chinese spy specifically. Nvidia’s board announced that it was launching an investigation into its CEO shortly after. Many believed that Jensen Huang would survive the scandal. His company’s importance to America’s booming AI industry and his crucial role at the company seemed to make him nearly untouchable. He was, after all, the only CEO the company had ever known with no clear and obvious succession plan in place, and he sat atop an unusual corporate structure with around 60 direct reports. (These numbers are slightly outdated, but according to the Harvard Business Review, 10 to 20 is far more common among Fortune 500 companies, and Tim Cook reportedly had 17 in 2015, which was deemed “a lot” by Business Insider.) Then on Wednesday, November 11th, The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had a second affair — this one with one of his direct reports, Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care. Whether that was the last straw or if they were afraid it would be merely the tip of the iceberg, the board was ready to push Jensen Huang out, according to reports circulating that evening. According to Bloomberg, he had accepted his fate Wednesday evening reportedly looking “broken and shattered” and telling people, “I’m a piece of shit.” On Thursday, November 12th, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang had resigned as CEO of Nvidia. How it’s going CFO Colette Kress was immediately named interim CEO, and acknowledged to employees that this has been an “extraordinarily difficult period.” Harvey Jones was also named the first board chair in the company’s history, already signaling there would be some changes to the corporate structure. In a memo to employees, Jones said the company would “search for a permanent successor looking at both internal and external candidates.” But the destabilizing impact was immediate. Nvidia’s stock closed at an all-time high of $239.24 on October 6th. It’s hard to overstate the importance of Nvidia to the US’s AI arms race with China, and the industry in general. The company has invested $99 billion in various AI labs, startups, and neo clouds. Plus has announced plans to mobilize over $500 billion in financing for building out AI data centers and other infrastructure. Even before Jensen Huang had resigned, Nvidia was already facing a shareholder lawsuit claiming the company had deceived investors. Jensen Huang and the company’s spokespeople insisted that the relationship with Alice Huang and Megaspeed was “completely normal and not unusual.” Only days later, Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair that raised “national security concerns” without naming anyone specifically. According to Reuters, Jensen Huang misled several Nvidia leaders, “including general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld” about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang. Many in the AI industry and Silicon Valley jumped to Jensen Huang’s defense. Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney called it a “sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity,” in a particularly hyperbolic post. Elon Musk said on X that it would “be an honor” to hire Jensen Huang. Many of Nvidia’s employees even voiced their support to “bring back THE boss,” on an internal post.

(These numbers are slightly outdated, but according to the Harvard Business Review, 10 to 20 is far more common among Fortune 500 companies, and Tim Cook reportedly had 17 in 2015, which was deemed “a lot” by Business Insider.) Then on Wednesday, November 11th, The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had a second affair — this one with one of his direct reports, Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care.
Whether that was the last straw or if they were afraid it would be merely the tip of the iceberg, the board was ready to push Jensen Huang out, according to reports circulating that evening.

According to Bloomberg, he had accepted his fate Wednesday evening reportedly looking “broken and shattered” and telling people, “I’m a piece of shit.” On Thursday, November 12th, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang had resigned as CEO of Nvidia.

How it’s going CFO Colette Kress was immediately named interim CEO, and acknowledged to employees that this has been an “extraordinarily difficult period.” Harvey Jones was also named the first board chair in the company’s history, already signaling there would be some changes to the corporate structure.
In a memo to employees, Jones said the company would “search for a permanent successor looking at both internal and external candidates.” But the destabilizing impact was immediate.
Nvidia’s stock closed at an all-time high of $239.24 on October 6th.
It’s hard to overstate the importance of Nvidia to the US’s AI arms race with China, and the industry in general.
The company has invested $99 billion in various AI labs, startups, and neo clouds.
Plus has announced plans to mobilize over $500 billion in financing for building out AI data centers and other infrastructure.
Even before Jensen Huang had resigned, Nvidia was already facing a shareholder lawsuit claiming the company had deceived investors.

Jensen Huang and the company’s spokespeople insisted that the relationship with Alice Huang and Megaspeed was “completely normal and not unusual.” Only days later, Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair that raised “national security concerns” without naming anyone specifically.

According to Reuters, Jensen Huang misled several Nvidia leaders, “including general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld” about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang.
Many in the AI industry and Silicon Valley jumped to Jensen Huang’s defense.
Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney called it a “sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity,” in a particularly hyperbolic post.
Elon Musk said on X that it would “be an honor” to hire Jensen Huang.
Many of Nvidia’s employees even voiced their support to “bring back THE boss,” on an internal post.

extraction.body: We’re getting some extraordinary reporting on what it has been like inside Nvidia during Huang’s last days. Before his forced resignation, Huang had given up, Bloomberg says , and was heard saying things like “whatever,” “I don’t care,” and referring to himself as a “piece of sh--.” That, of course, was in stark contrast to how Huang historically ran the company. Huang had “imperial control,” and ran it like a “feudal system,” according to the FT . “I can’t tell you what a cult this place is,” a source told the paper. General counsel Tim Teter wore a leather jacket just like Huang’s, the source said: “Jensen is a god, and that’s how he’s worshipped.” Noteworthy: In addition to having no board chair, the company also did not have a compliance officer, the FT says. Interim CEO Colette Kress and whoever replaces her as permanent CEO will have messy office politics to deal with, according to the FT . Huang’s daughter Madison Huang is a senior director of marketing at the company, but she acts like her father’s de facto chief of staff, the FT says. Nvidia also employs her husband Nico Caprez and Huang’s son Spencer. Kress, meanwhile, sometimes did not get Huang’s respect, the WSJ reported . He once called her “a deer in the headlights” and a “reporting CFO” (as opposed to a strategic leader) during a meeting in which they were discussing Nvidia’s agreements “to provide billions of dollars of guarantees to companies that couldn’t afford its chips,” the WSJ said. Kress struggled to rein in Caprez, who had made multiple offers of financing to cloud providers and data-center builders in return for shares of revenue. Lenders relied on the Huang family's backing for AI financing when structuring deals with AI providers. Without Huang at the top, “that Nvidia guarantee is not worth what it was worth a week ago, that puts those neocloud businesses at risk,” Joe Kaiser of Switchyard Partners, an AI financing company, told Fortune’s Catherina Gioino . Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and commerce secretary Howard Lutnick have been called by Sen. Tim Scott (R-South Carolina) to testify in front of the Senate Banking Committee, the NYT reports . The hearing will be conducted next month. “Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology,” Scott said. That’s a reference to Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy who ran a company that bought Nvidia chips and is suspected of smuggling them into China in violation of U.S. export controls. As for Lutnick, Republicans are furious at what they perceive was the special treatment he gave Nvidia in terms of its access to the Chinese market and in his foot-dragging on the enforcement of export bans to China, the FT says . Lutnick shielded Nvidia from the White House’s attempts to restrict export of the U.S.’s best technology to China, the NYT reported . All matters related to Nvidia were routed through a deputy to Lutnick, Jeff Kessler, who rarely took action without Lutnick’s approval, the NYT said . Inside the White House, senior Trump administration figures largely blame Lutnick for being asleep at the wheel in terms of the threat Nvidia posed to national security, given its ties to Chinese importers, the WSJ reported . ​​Alice Huang: Those concerns will get extra momentum on the news that Jensen Huang’s affair partner, suspected spy Alice Huang (no relation) of Megaspeed, had a relationship with Huawei, China’s biggest competitor in China, according to CNBC . Alice Huang allegedly ran a complicated network of companies to do deals with Nvidia that resulted in its chips ending up at Chinese companies, per Bloomberg . Congress needs to catch up - Andrew M. Cuomo One central question about the Anthropic IPO is: how can this company grow revenue if its product prices—as measured via tokens—are in a race to the bottom? Turns out that piling it high and selling it cheap works in AI the same way it works in groceries, as these charts from Alpine Macro’s Noah Ramos show. “While token prices have declined dramatically, overall customer spending continues to scale. This reflects both users extracting more intelligence per unit of compute and inference optimizations that make it economically viable to consume substantially more tokens. Lower token prices are expanding consumption rather than reducing spending,” he said in a note. —Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives, expressing the head-spinning pace at which Jensen Huang went from indispensable founder to excess baggage at his own company, Nvidia. “The old Jensen, the black leather jacket, the Godfather of AI, the rock star viewed as the face of the AI boom, is over and in the past; his value to the company pre and post this week is dramatically different, and the board did what we said it needed to do, which is rip off the band-aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter without him after this dark moment for Jensen and Nvidia.” Ives also has an eyebrow-raising suggestion for who could replace Huang as CEO: Apple’s Tim Cook. He could be “a dark horse candidate in our view given the global importance of Nvidia to the overall U.S. tech industry.” The proposal makes sense given that Cook just retired as CEO of Apple, and although he is now its chairman, he does, in theory, have time on his hands. And frankly, who knows more than Cook about stewarding the most important tech company of its day to further success following the loss of an “irreplaceable” founder? It goes without saying that the stakes are high. Remember what happened at HP and Intel, warn Wedbush’s Matt Bryson and Tuo Ma: “Both [HP’s] Mark Hurd and [Intel’s] Brian Krzanich departed their posts relatively abruptly following affairs with no clear successors in place. And for both Intel and HP, we believe these transitions played some role in disastrous periods that saw the companies lose their respective leadership positions in technology, with HP eventually breaking apart and Intel still struggling to prove it can regain the fab and chip design expertise it seemingly lost during its failed 10nm transition.” Ouch! Nscale warns it needs more cash ahead of $35bn IPO - FT Van Hollen Says He Will Challenge Schumer for Senate Majority Leader - NYT Fanatics CEO Michael Rubin engaged to model girlfriend Camille Fishel after 10 years of dating - NY Post For decades, the markers of extreme wealth were easy to spot: the second home, the fancy cars, the Ivy League education. New analysis of Federal Reserve data points to a subtler one: a third child. Lawmakers from both parties are scrutinizing past remarks from Jensen, who was the most influential voice pushing US officials to curb export controls on Nvidia chips — even as they assess whether his affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang compromised national security.

Meanwhile, Bloomberg reported Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter directly called Kessler, who oversees chip export controls, in the summer of 2025 to ask about the department’s investigation into Megaspeed.

Ousting Huang himself, the source added, would be a “massive earthquake” during a fragile moment for the AI sector, which is already facing questions on Wall Street over whether it’s a giant bubble ready to burst.

However, there are real concerns about Huang’s ability to remain at the helm of Nvidia – despite the fact that many consider him irreplaceable to the company and the lack of any obvious successor within its ranks.
That argument seems unlikely to satisfy key lawmakers who were already concerned about China gaining access to Nvidia’s best hardware – even before Huang’s embarrassing misstep.

Some DC sources believe the scandal will result in a bipartisan push for even stronger curbs on chip sales — with proponents concerned that Nvidia’s cutting-edge chips will fuel greater inroads into AI by Chinese companies.

One key loophole currently under the microscope is China’s well-documented practice of accessing high-end Nvidia hardware housed in data centers based in Southeast Asia.

extraction.body: See more of our coverage in your search results. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy has sparked fears of a major clampdown on the AI industry – pitting China hawks against those who warn that an overreaction will put the US at a disadvantage versus Beijing, The Post has learned. Lawmakers from both parties are scrutinizing past remarks from Jensen, who was the most influential voice pushing US officials to curb export controls on Nvidia chips — even as they assess whether his affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang compromised national security. Some DC sources believe the scandal will result in a bipartisan push for even stronger curbs on chip sales — with proponents concerned that Nvidia’s cutting-edge chips will fuel greater inroads into AI by Chinese companies. At the same time, some of them warn that ordering such a crackdown – for example banning a loophole allowing Chinese companies to rent access to Nvidia’s high-end hardware through data centers located in Southeast Asia – would play right into China’s hands, a source close to the situation said. “If they do that, it will just drive those foreign clouds to Huawei,” the source told The Post, referring to the Chinese telecom giant that is aggressively pursuing AI business. “Ultimately, over time, those clouds will choose what’s available to them. It becomes an economic question – do you want foreign clouds to have American technology or Huawei technology?” Ousting Huang himself, the source added, would be a “massive earthquake” during a fragile moment for the AI sector, which is already facing questions on Wall Street over whether it’s a giant bubble ready to burst. “Nvidia is at the center of the AI buildout and he’s the central figure in the company,” the source said of Jensen Huang. That argument seems unlikely to satisfy key lawmakers who were already concerned about China gaining access to Nvidia’s best hardware – even before Huang’s embarrassing misstep. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) said he “strongly supports” adding tougher chip controls to an annual year-end defense spending bill, while Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) called for legislation targeting “various pathways through which China accesses advanced chips.” “Republican chairs are reaching out to speak to Jensen and get some more details,” a Senate Democratic aide told The Post. “This is not, at this point, a partisan mud fight. This is bipartisan. We need answers about what happened here, what the FBI is looking into or already knew . We are in a bipartisan gathering phase.” One key loophole currently under the microscope is China’s well-documented practice of accessing high-end Nvidia hardware housed in data centers based in Southeast Asia. US officials have suspected Singapore-based Megaspeed – and alleged Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang – of exploiting the loophole to smuggle AI chips to China. Nvidia has long resisted efforts to crack down on so-called “remote access,” while key Commerce Department figures like Howard Lutnick and undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler, who oversees the Bureau of Industry and Security, have been reluctant to take action. Rush Doshi, a China policy expert and Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, expects Democrats to push hard to close the “remote access” loophole. “If the reporting is right, it potentially reveals corruption and compromise in American China policy on one of the most important issues of our time, including in ways that undermine AI safety for Americans,” Doshi said. “Democrats and Republicans alike are going to want to investigate what they see as the decision to sell off American national security and economic advantage and AI safety for profit.” In October, White House officials nudged Congressional staffers to tack on a provision that would direct the Commerce Department to close the loophole as part of the AI Overwatch Act, a measure cosponsored by Warren and Banks and set to be included in the year-end defense bill, The Information reported. Nvidia declined to comment. Representatives for the White House and Commerce Department did not immediately return questions for comment. Aside from pursuing answers about Huang’s personal conduct, lawmakers from both parties are sure to seek answers about the Trump administration’s handling of the situation – specifically, its delay in taking action despite warnings months ago that the Nvidia boss was tangled up with an alleged Chinese spy, and the Commerce Department’s dealings with Nvidia, Doshi added. Last year, US officials grew concerned that Megaspeed, the largest buyer of Nvidia chips in southeast Asia, was involved in chip smuggling and asked Nvidia to audit its dealings with the firm. Nvidia initially replied that all of its chip sales were accurately recorded – even though Megaspeed had imported 50,000 more computer chips than what Nvidia linked to its data centers, Bloomberg reported. Meanwhile, Bloomberg reported Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter directly called Kessler, who oversees chip export controls, in the summer of 2025 to ask about the department’s investigation into Megaspeed. The report added that Commerce staffers were subsequently “muzzled in their ability to look into the company” and told to route requests on the matter through Kessler. “BIS conducts all enforcement strictly by the book,” a spokesperson told the outlet. “BIS enforces aggressively across the board, including with respect to chip smuggling, and enforcement is at an all-time high.” While the scandal is a major black eye for Nvidia, it’s unlikely to completely upend the company’s role as the linchpin of the AI movement, according to Daniel Newman, CEO of Futurum Group. The company’s deal roadmap is already largely set through 2028, and companies can’t easily find a replacement for Nvidia’s advanced hardware even if they were inclined to. However, there are real concerns about Huang’s ability to remain at the helm of Nvidia – despite the fact that many consider him irreplaceable to the company and the lack of any obvious successor within its ranks. “The big question is on the continuum of, is he a CEO that committed infidelity? I think he can survive that. That doesn’t mean it’s good,” Newman said. “All the risks around intelligence stuff is not survivable. If any line was crossed beyond him just having an affair, the board is going to have to move.”

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy has sparked fears of a major clampdown on the AI industry – pitting China hawks against those who warn that an overreaction will put the US at a disadvantage versus Beijing, The Post has learned.

Lawmakers from both parties are scrutinizing past remarks from Jensen, who was the most influential voice pushing US officials to curb export controls on Nvidia chips — even as they assess whether his affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang compromised national security.

Some DC sources believe the scandal will result in a bipartisan push for even stronger curbs on chip sales — with proponents concerned that Nvidia’s cutting-edge chips will fuel greater inroads into AI by Chinese companies.

At the same time, some of them warn that ordering such a crackdown – for example banning a loophole allowing Chinese companies to rent access to Nvidia’s high-end hardware through data centers located in Southeast Asia – would play right into China’s hands, a source close to the situation said.
“If they do that, it will just drive those foreign clouds to Huawei,” the source told The Post, referring to the Chinese telecom giant that is aggressively pursuing AI business.
“Ultimately, over time, those clouds will choose what’s available to them. It becomes an economic question – do you want foreign clouds to have American technology or Huawei technology?”

Ousting Huang himself, the source added, would be a “massive earthquake” during a fragile moment for the AI sector, which is already facing questions on Wall Street over whether it’s a giant bubble ready to burst.
“Nvidia is at the center of the AI buildout and he’s the central figure in the company,” the source said of Jensen Huang.
That argument seems unlikely to satisfy key lawmakers who were already concerned about China gaining access to Nvidia’s best hardware – even before Huang’s embarrassing misstep.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) said he “strongly supports” adding tougher chip controls to an annual year-end defense spending bill, while Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) called for legislation targeting “various pathways through which China accesses advanced chips.”

“Republican chairs are reaching out to speak to Jensen and get some more details,” a Senate Democratic aide told The Post. “This is not, at this point, a partisan mud fight. This is bipartisan. We need answers about what happened here, what the FBI is looking into or already knew . We are in a bipartisan gathering phase.”

One key loophole currently under the microscope is China’s well-documented practice of accessing high-end Nvidia hardware housed in data centers based in Southeast Asia. US officials have suspected Singapore-based Megaspeed – and alleged Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang – of exploiting the loophole to smuggle AI chips to China.

Nvidia has long resisted efforts to crack down on so-called “remote access,” while key Commerce Department figures like Howard Lutnick and undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler, who oversees the Bureau of Industry and Security, have been reluctant to take action.
Rush Doshi, a China policy expert and Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, expects Democrats to push hard to close the “remote access” loophole.

“If the reporting is right, it potentially reveals corruption and compromise in American China policy on one of the most important issues of our time, including in ways that undermine AI safety for Americans,” Doshi said.
“Democrats and Republicans alike are going to want to investigate what they see as the decision to sell off American national security and economic advantage and AI safety for profit.”

In October, White House officials nudged Congressional staffers to tack on a provision that would direct the Commerce Department to close the loophole as part of the AI Overwatch Act, a measure cosponsored by Warren and Banks and set to be included in the year-end defense bill, The Information reported.
Nvidia declined to comment. Representatives for the White House and Commerce Department did not immediately return questions for comment.

Aside from pursuing answers about Huang’s personal conduct, lawmakers from both parties are sure to seek answers about the Trump administration’s handling of the situation – specifically, its delay in taking action despite warnings months ago that the Nvidia boss was tangled up with an alleged Chinese spy, and the Commerce Department’s dealings with Nvidia, Doshi added.

Last year, US officials grew concerned that Megaspeed, the largest buyer of Nvidia chips in southeast Asia, was involved in chip smuggling and asked Nvidia to audit its dealings with the firm. Nvidia initially replied that all of its chip sales were accurately recorded – even though Megaspeed had imported 50,000 more computer chips than what Nvidia linked to its data centers, Bloomberg reported.

Meanwhile, Bloomberg reported Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter directly called Kessler, who oversees chip export controls, in the summer of 2025 to ask about the department’s investigation into Megaspeed.
The report added that Commerce staffers were subsequently “muzzled in their ability to look into the company” and told to route requests on the matter through Kessler.

“BIS conducts all enforcement strictly by the book,” a spokesperson told the outlet. “BIS enforces aggressively across the board, including with respect to chip smuggling, and enforcement is at an all-time high.”

While the scandal is a major black eye for Nvidia, it’s unlikely to completely upend the company’s role as the linchpin of the AI movement, according to Daniel Newman, CEO of Futurum Group. The company’s deal roadmap is already largely set through 2028, and companies can’t easily find a replacement for Nvidia’s advanced hardware even if they were inclined to.

However, there are real concerns about Huang’s ability to remain at the helm of Nvidia – despite the fact that many consider him irreplaceable to the company and the lack of any obvious successor within its ranks.

“The big question is on the continuum of, is he a CEO that committed infidelity? I think he can survive that. That doesn’t mean it’s good,” Newman said. “All the risks around intelligence stuff is not survivable. If any line was crossed beyond him just having an affair, the board is going to have to move.”

extraction.body: The chip-smuggling controversy swirling around Nvidia centers on one company : Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing provider that, according to several media reports, is suspected of funneling advanced AI processors to Chinese companies. While details of what Megaspeed is alleged to have done remain murky, experts say the case shows how Chinese firms rely on Southeast Asia to skirt U.S. trade controls. “Chinese firms can access data centers in Singapore and Malaysia—and their computing capacity—without having to import restricted semiconductors,” Ja Ian Chong, a political science expert from the National University of Singapore (NUS), tells Fortune . “But the ease of shipping [chips] through Singapore and Malaysia also makes them attractive for firms and people who wish to circumvent U.S. controls.” Washington restricts the export of Nvidia’s top-end Blackwell and Rubin chips to China, out of fear Beijing could use them to supercharge its AI ambitions . According to The Information , Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, used her personal relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to move at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips through Megaspeed and its Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix. Singapore says it is investigating Megaspeed for “suspected breaches of our domestic laws,” but it separately rejected reports that its authorities were investigating Alice Huang over the espionage allegations. U.S. officials had also been investigating Megaspeed for potential export-control violations. Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing; Nvidia has previously claimed that it found no evidence of illicit chip transfers. Nvidia’s board said in a Nov. 8 statement that it was initiating an independent investigation into whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, though it added it had no reason to believe “either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” The board said it “prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders.” Following reports that Huang conducted a second affair, this time with an Nvidia executive, the chipmaker’s board is now considering removing Huang as CEO, the Wall Street Journal reports. Megaspeed is a Singapore-based neocloud that supplies AI computing power. Originally incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International, a Chinese gaming firm with ties to state-backed investors, the company changed its name to Megaspeed in early 2023, the same year that Alice Huang joined the company. Another Singapore-registered firm, Swiftdata, acquired Megaspeed in November 2023. Alice Huang stepped down as Megaspeed’s managing director, while Singaporean businessman Tan Yong Pong—who owns Swiftdata —became its sole director. (Tan owns another Singapore-registered company, Monster Investment.) In 2024, Tan established Speedmatrix, a Malaysia-based subsidiary of Megaspeed, which was reportedly used to receive shipments of Nvidia chips. According to the New York Times , between June 2024 and June 2025, Speedmatrix received over 200 shipments of restricted Nvidia technology. These chips—which are subject to U.S. restrictions on sales to China—were eventually used to power data centers built by Shanghai Century Litong, a Chinese firm in which Alice’s younger sister, Huang Yu, is a founding shareholder, according to The Information . The firm, which builds data centers in the Chinese cities of Shanghai and Shenzhen, then provides high-performance AI computing capacity to Chinese tech giants including Alibaba and Tencent . “AI chip distributors and resellers often spend too little effort vetting customers, usually relying on paperwork the customer provides,” notes Erich Grunewald, a senior researcher at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy (IAPS), a U.S. nonpartisan think tank. Malaysia has been one of Southeast Asia’s biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom, drawing $94 billion in data center investments between 2021 and mid-2026, including from global tech hyperscalers like Google, AWS and Microsoft . “Malaysia has ample land and relatively cheap electricity and water, at least for now,” Chong notes. “The fact that it sits next to key submarine cables also makes it attractive as a spot for data centers.” Singapore, on the other hand, is favored by multinationals for its open economy, stable political environment and business-friendly policies. Many AI firms, including U.S. firms Anthropic and OpenAI , have chosen to house their APAC headquarters there. Companies like Megaspeed typically offer two routes to restricted silicon. The first is renting out chips already housed in data centers in Singapore and Malaysia—which, under current rules, is legal. The second is buying chips through front companies and shipping them to China, potentially in violation of U.S. export controls. (Megaspeed reportedly did both: it set up data center operations in Sedenak Tech Park in the Malaysian state of Johor , and according to the reports , also shuttled chips to Shanghai Century Litong’s facilities in China.) Under current U.S. export rules, it is legal to give Chinese companies access to AI processors housed outside of China—though previous deals have invited regulatory scrutiny. On Nov. 3, The Financial Times reported that Oracle had canceled a $7 billion deal to grant Tencent access to 100,000 AI chips in data centers across Southeast Asia after U.S. officials raised concerns. The FT also reported that Nvidia is telling cloud computing clients they must sell at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese companies. The U.S. House of Representatives passed a law—the Remote Access Security Act —that would close the loophole allowing Chinese companies to use AI processors housed in other countries; the bill is now before the U.S. Senate. Both Singapore and Malaysia have cracked down on chip smuggling. In addition to its investigation of Megaspeed, the Singaporean government last year charged three individuals with fraud after they diverted AI servers bound for Singapore to Malaysia instead. In October, Malaysian customs officials seized $12.1 million worth of advanced AI chips at Kuala Lumpur International Airport. Initial investigations found the 30 servers—falsely declared as electronic components—were being transferred from one Asian country to another, though officials declined to say which. Megaspeed, however, has denied the allegations . “There has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities, and this demonstrates that we are a compliant and legitimate company,” it wrote in a statement last December. “We operate fully within the bounds of all applicable export control regulations and maintain the highest standards of legal and ethical conduct.” Chong says the escalating AI arms race between the U.S. and China means both Beijing and Washington will subject third parties like Singapore and Malaysia to deeper scrutiny to keep their own technology from leaking. “Both Singapore and Malaysia will want to continue to benefit from trust by Beijing and Washington for as long as they can,” concludes Chong. “But they may face greater suspicion, scrutiny, restrictions and even punishment from one or both major powers going forward, and perceptions that they are unreliable or duplicitous partners will only increase such pressure.” Angelica Ang is a Singapore-based journalist who covers the Asia-Pacific region.

coreStoryFacts.text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy has sparked fears of a major clampdown on the AI industry – pitting China hawks against those who warn that an overreaction will put the US at a disadvantage versus Beijing, The Post has learned.

Lawmakers from both parties are scrutinizing past remarks from Jensen, who was the most influential voice pushing US officials to curb export controls on Nvidia chips — even as they assess whether his affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang compromised national security.

Meanwhile, Bloomberg reported Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter directly called Kessler, who oversees chip export controls, in the summer of 2025 to ask about the department’s investigation into Megaspeed.

Ousting Huang himself, the source added, would be a “massive earthquake” during a fragile moment for the AI sector, which is already facing questions on Wall Street over whether it’s a giant bubble ready to burst.

However, there are real concerns about Huang’s ability to remain at the helm of Nvidia – despite the fact that many consider him irreplaceable to the company and the lack of any obvious successor within its ranks.
That argument seems unlikely to satisfy key lawmakers who were already concerned about China gaining access to Nvidia’s best hardware – even before Huang’s embarrassing misstep.

Some DC sources believe the scandal will result in a bipartisan push for even stronger curbs on chip sales — with proponents concerned that Nvidia’s cutting-edge chips will fuel greater inroads into AI by Chinese companies.
“Republican chairs are reaching out to speak to Jensen and get some more details,” a Senate Democratic aide told The Post.
One key loophole currently under the microscope is China’s well-documented practice of accessing high-end Nvidia hardware housed in data centers based in Southeast Asia.

Nvidia initially replied that all of its chip sales were accurately recorded – even though Megaspeed had imported 50,000 more computer chips than what Nvidia linked to its data centers, Bloomberg reported.
Rush Doshi, a China policy expert and Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, expects Democrats to push hard to close the “remote access” loophole.

“Chinese firms can access data centers in Singapore and Malaysia—and their computing capacity—without having to import restricted semiconductors,” Ja Ian Chong, a political science expert from the National University of Singapore (NUS), tells Fortune .

According to The Information , Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, used her personal relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to move at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips through Megaspeed and its Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix.

The chip-smuggling controversy swirling around Nvidia centers on one company : Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing provider that, according to several media reports, is suspected of funneling advanced AI processors to Chinese companies.
Companies like Megaspeed typically offer two routes to restricted silicon.
The second is buying chips through front companies and shipping them to China, potentially in violation of U.S. export controls.
3, The Financial Times reported that Oracle had canceled a $7 billion deal to grant Tencent access to 100,000 AI chips in data centers across Southeast Asia after U.S. officials raised concerns.
In addition to its investigation of Megaspeed, the Singaporean government last year charged three individuals with fraud after they diverted AI servers bound for Singapore to Malaysia instead.

Originally incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International, a Chinese gaming firm with ties to state-backed investors, the company changed its name to Megaspeed in early 2023, the same year that Alice Huang joined the company.

“But they may face greater suspicion, scrutiny, restrictions and even punishment from one or both major powers going forward, and perceptions that they are unreliable or duplicitous partners will only increase such pressure.”
“Malaysia has ample land and relatively cheap electricity and water, at least for now,” Chong notes.
“The fact that it sits next to key submarine cables also makes it attractive as a spot for data centers.”

Singapore says it is investigating Megaspeed for “suspected breaches of our domestic laws,” but it separately rejected reports that its authorities were investigating Alice Huang over the espionage allegations.
Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing; Nvidia has previously claimed that it found no evidence of illicit chip transfers.

While details of what Megaspeed is alleged to have done remain murky, experts say the case shows how Chinese firms rely on Southeast Asia to skirt U.S. trade controls. “Chinese firms can access data centers in Singapore and Malaysia—and their computing capacity—without having to import restricted semiconductors,” Ja Ian Chong, a political science expert from the National University of Singapore (NUS), tells Fortune . “But the ease of shipping [chips] through Singapore and Malaysia also makes them attractive for firms and people who wish to circumvent U.S. controls.” Washington restricts the export of Nvidia’s top-end Blackwell and Rubin chips to China, out of fear Beijing could use them to supercharge its AI ambitions . According to The Information , Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, used her personal relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to move at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips through Megaspeed and its Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix. Singapore says it is investigating Megaspeed for “suspected breaches of our domestic laws,” but it separately rejected reports that its authorities were investigating Alice Huang over the espionage allegations. U.S. officials had also been investigating Megaspeed for potential export-control violations. Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing; Nvidia has previously claimed that it found no evidence of illicit chip transfers. Nvidia’s board said in a Nov. 8 statement that it was initiating an independent investigation into whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, though it added it had no reason to believe “either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” The board said it “prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders.” Following reports that Huang conducted a second affair, this time with an Nvidia executive, the chipmaker’s board is now considering removing Huang as CEO, the Wall Street Journal reports. Megaspeed is a Singapore-based neocloud that supplies AI computing power. Originally incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International, a Chinese gaming firm with ties to state-backed investors, the company changed its name to Megaspeed in early 2023, the same year that Alice Huang joined the company. Another Singapore-registered firm, Swiftdata, acquired Megaspeed in November 2023. Alice Huang stepped down as Megaspeed’s managing director, while Singaporean businessman Tan Yong Pong—who owns Swiftdata —became its sole director. (Tan owns another Singapore-registered company, Monster Investment.) In 2024, Tan established Speedmatrix, a Malaysia-based subsidiary of Megaspeed, which was reportedly used to receive shipments of Nvidia chips. According to the New York Times , between June 2024 and June 2025, Speedmatrix received over 200 shipments of restricted Nvidia technology. These chips—which are subject to U.S. restrictions on sales to China—were eventually used to power data centers built by Shanghai Century Litong, a Chinese firm in which Alice’s younger sister, Huang Yu, is a founding shareholder, according to The Information . The firm, which builds data centers in the Chinese cities of Shanghai and Shenzhen, then provides high-performance AI computing capacity to Chinese tech giants including Alibaba and Tencent . “AI chip distributors and resellers often spend too little effort vetting customers, usually relying on paperwork the customer provides,” notes Erich Grunewald, a senior researcher at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy (IAPS), a U.S. nonpartisan think tank. Malaysia has been one of Southeast Asia’s biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom, drawing $94 billion in data center investments between 2021 and mid-2026, including from global tech hyperscalers like Google, AWS and Microsoft . “Malaysia has ample land and relatively cheap electricity and water, at least for now,” Chong notes. “The fact that it sits next to key submarine cables also makes it attractive as a spot for data centers.” Singapore, on the other hand, is favored by multinationals for its open economy, stable political environment and business-friendly policies. Many AI firms, including U.S. firms Anthropic and OpenAI , have chosen to house their APAC headquarters there. Companies like Megaspeed typically offer two routes to restricted silicon. The first is renting out chips already housed in data centers in Singapore and Malaysia—which, under current rules, is legal. The second is buying chips through front companies and shipping them to China, potentially in violation of U.S. export controls. (Megaspeed reportedly did both: it set up data center operations in Sedenak Tech Park in the Malaysian state of Johor , and according to the reports , also shuttled chips to Shanghai Century Litong’s facilities in China.) Under current U.S. export rules, it is legal to give Chinese companies access to AI processors housed outside of China—though previous deals have invited regulatory scrutiny. On Nov. 3, The Financial Times reported that Oracle had canceled a $7 billion deal to grant Tencent access to 100,000 AI chips in data centers across Southeast Asia after U.S. officials raised concerns. The FT also reported that Nvidia is telling cloud computing clients they must sell at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese companies. The U.S. House of Representatives passed a law—the Remote Access Security Act —that would close the loophole allowing Chinese companies to use AI processors housed in other countries; the bill is now before the U.S. Senate. Both Singapore and Malaysia have cracked down on chip smuggling. In addition to its investigation of Megaspeed, the Singaporean government last year charged three individuals with fraud after they diverted AI servers bound for Singapore to Malaysia instead. Washington restricts the export of Nvidia’s top-end Blackwell and Rubin chips to China, out of fear Beijing could use them to supercharge its AI ambitions .

Another Singapore-registered firm, Swiftdata, acquired Megaspeed in November 2023. Alice Huang stepped down as Megaspeed’s managing director, while Singaporean businessman Tan Yong Pong—who owns Swiftdata —became its sole director. (Tan owns another Singapore-registered company, Monster Investment.)

Malaysia has been one of Southeast Asia’s biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom, drawing $94 billion in data center investments between 2021 and mid-2026, including from global tech hyperscalers like Google, AWS and Microsoft . “Malaysia has ample land and relatively cheap electricity and water, at least for now,” Chong notes. “The fact that it sits next to key submarine cables also makes it attractive as a spot for data centers.”

Singapore, on the other hand, is favored by multinationals for its open economy, stable political environment and business-friendly policies. Many AI firms, including U.S. firms Anthropic and OpenAI , have chosen to house their APAC headquarters there.

Companies like Megaspeed typically offer two routes to restricted silicon. The first is renting out chips already housed in data centers in Singapore and Malaysia—which, under current rules, is legal. The second is buying chips through front companies and shipping them to China, potentially in violation of U.S. export controls.

Both Singapore and Malaysia have cracked down on chip smuggling. In addition to its investigation of Megaspeed, the Singaporean government last year charged three individuals with fraud after they diverted AI servers bound for Singapore to Malaysia instead.

In October, Malaysian customs officials seized $12.1 million worth of advanced AI chips at Kuala Lumpur International Airport. Initial investigations found the 30 servers—falsely declared as electronic components—were being transferred from one Asian country to another, though officials declined to say which.

Incredibly, Nvidia had no successor in place prior to the scandal that took down its leader because Huang didn’t believe in succession planning ; he was also apparently a micromanager with 60 direct reports and said last year that he reads thousands of employee emails a day. Which is all well and good if you’re planning to both (a) live that long and (b) not have an affair with an accused Chinese spy. Otherwise it’s pretty risky! On Wall Street, the company’s stock was down 11 percent on the news of his departure, which translates to a loss of roughly $1 trillion just this month. Trump has gushed in the past about “Tim Apple,” who visited the White House last year bearing gifts . “A Legend replaces a Legend!” the president wrote . If you’re just catching up to the sex-spy-AI scandal, here’s everything that’s happened so far. In a bombshell story, the New York Times reports that after concluding that Alice Huang (no relation), the chief executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed, was a “Chinese intelligence asset,” U.S. intelligence officials made an even more startling discovery: that Huang “had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang.” The Times story also reveals that Donald Trump had been “briefed about the intelligence findings” a year ago and “chose not to do anything with the information.” In fairness, the president may have been preoccupied with ballroom renovations; at the time, he was fighting with his architect . In an interview with Bloomberg, the CEO insists his interactions with Ms. Huang were strictly professional. “Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual,” Huang says . He will regret this statement ! GOP representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford — who lead the House’s Committee on Foreign Affairs, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the Select Committee on Intelligence, respectively — send a letter to Huang telling him they want a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Ms. Huang. “Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” they write. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk.” Democratic senator Chris Coons, who is expected to chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee come January, writes on X: “The more I learn about the insane relationship between the Trump Administration, Chinese spies, and AI billionaires, the more I’m convinced there is nothing this administration does that isn’t corrupt. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” He continues: “Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. The president of the United States continues: “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it … He’s done an amazing job for our country. You know, we have the hottest country anywhere in the world. We have the highest stock market.” Q: Is Jensen Huang coming with you on your trip to Asia? Trump: I’d certainly take him. I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong. (After Trump saw coverage about Huang not being included on the delegation, he wrote on social media that he was honored to have “the Great Jensen Huang” and other business executives “journeying to the Great Country of China where I will be asking President Xi, a Leader of extraordinary distinction, to ‘open up’ China so that these brilliant people can work their magic.” (Huang was picked up by Air Force One during a stop in Alaska .) In fact, he was told about it a year ago and chose not to do anything. I believe he is suffering greatly because of his family, his wife, who he loves, and his family. But he's… pic.twitter.com/XtODQmCpre The Times reports that a “monthslong investigation” into Megaspeed, and whether it was “smuggling Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips into China,” was suddenly paused “after Commerce Department investigators working on the case received an email from Nvidia’s general counsel seeking information about the inquiry.” Agents were reportedly alarmed when Nvidia’s general counsel said that a top Commerce official who reports directly to Secretary Howard Lutnick “had given Nvidia permission to reach out about the case.” The board of directors announces it has hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to run the investigation into Huang’s affair and whether company secrets were divulged or national security was breached. The probe will be run by Joon Kim, the former acting U.S. Attorney for the Southern District who was appointed in 2021 to investigate allegations of sexual harassment against then-governor Andrew Cuomo. As it turns out, the Nvidia CEO wasn’t just having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, he was also cheating on his wife with a subordinate named Kimberly Powell, according to the New York Times . And apparently he’d been hoping to keep that affair on the down low. Per the Times : In March, Ms. Powell appeared at GTC, Nvidia’s annual developer conference in San Jose, where she spoke about using A.I. to aid in breakthroughs in health care and biology. Her presentation used cartoon depictions of Mr. Huang. During the conference, Nvidia executives were at a nearby hotel for meetings. Mr. Huang and Ms. Powell were seen being affectionate at the hotel. One bystander captured the interaction on their phone, three people briefed on the incident said. Mr. Huang’s security workers witnessed the bystander with the phone and sequestered the person, the people said. The workers then asked the person to sign a nondisclosure agreement. When asked by a reporter about the relationship by phone, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” and hung up. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s bravado had evaporated this week by the time it became clear his scandalous affairs including one with an alleged Chinese spy would cost him his job — and he chastised himself as a “piece of s–t,” according to reports. On Wednesday, in his final hours in charge of the chipmaker he had grown into a $4 trillion giant, Huang had started using phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care,” and calling himself a “piece of s–t,” Bloomberg reported, citing unnamed sources. It was a quick fall from grace for the billionaire and face of the AI boom, who had repeatedly denied that his relationship with Alice Huang – an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed , who’s of no relation – was anything but an ordinary business relationship. After news outlets reported that the relationship with the suspected Chinese spy was a romantic one, Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, rushed to Huang’s house to confront him and Huang confessed, according to Bloomberg and The Information. The board was reportedly wary of taking action, but Teter urged them to make an announcement. On Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang had a second affair with Kimberly Powell , Nvidia’s vice president of health care. The board gathered for an emergency late-night meeting, and Huang was forced to resign, according to reports. On Thursday, Reuters reported that Huang had a third affair — with yet another Nvidia employee, who remains unidentified.
