extraction.body: Biographer Stephen Witt wonders whether the former tech chief can – or even wants to – lead again [SINGAPORE] At 63, Jensen Huang may no longer have it in him to start or lead another tech company, speculates Stephen Witt, who wrote Huang’s best-selling biography The Thinking Machine in 2025. Here for the Singapore Writers Festival, Witt says: “In the time that I was with him, I saw him slow down just a step. That’s just age. It’s time. It happens.” Witt worked on the book over several months, speaking with Huang as well as over 200 employees, customers, rivals and friends. The book built a picture of a brilliant, demanding workaholic who had made Nvidia the centre of his life. “But I just don’t know if he can be a CEO again or if he wants to be a CEO again,” Witt tells the festival audience in his keynote speech at Victoria Theatre. “I think his motivation might be shot after this.” Huang’s next task will probably be more personal: trying to save his marriage. Witt says: “I think he will beg his wife not to divorce him.” Although Huang had lovers, including businesswoman Alice Huang and Nvidia’s vice-president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, his love for his wife was genuine, Witt suggests. “Jensen talked about his wife all the time. All the time. He praised her constantly,” Witt says. “He never overlooked that sacrifice she made (leaving engineering to raise their two children). He acknowledged it constantly in conversation.” At the same time, “Nvidia consumed him, it was his life”, Witt adds. “I can see him having almost an identity crisis now… and he may reassess everything. I can see a world where Jensen leaves and just does philanthropic giving, believe it or not.” The biographer’s doubts about a comeback coexist with considerable admiration for the abilities that make Huang so difficult to replace . “Jensen’s a world-class computer scientist. He’s a world-class deal maker. And he’s a world-class ops guy.” Witt describes how Huang could draw an exploded diagram of a graphics chip from memory, explain what each component did and cost, and identify the various suppliers to call for a better price. “He didn’t know anything about business. He just knew about microchips. But he educated himself. He re-engineered himself to be the CEO of the company.” In an anecdote from Witt’s book, retold at the festival, Huang challenged an Nvidia executive with a Masters in Business Administration to name his three favourite books on pricing. The man could not name one, so Huang supplied three. “I want you to read these three books. And when you’re done, we’ll continue this conversation,” he told the executive. Even Huang’s public charisma, Witt suggests, had been painstakingly developed. He recalls watching Huang anxiously rock back and forth backstage before a small presentation, making bad jokes to those around him – despite already being able to command a stadium. “I can’t sleep at night whenever I have to go on stage,” Huang later told Witt, who tells the festival audience: “He uses that fear of failure and shame and guilt as fuel.” During a question-and-answer session moderated by tech writer Grace Chng, an audience member asks if Huang could work with Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX. According to news agency Anadolu, Musk had earlier responded to a suggestion that he should hire Huang by writing on X: “That would be an honour” – without actually announcing a formal offer. But Witt offers a bleakly comic forecast: “Those guys would last together about one week. That would be a titanic ego death match. It could be a reality show. They could sell tickets to it.” He adds: “Jensen temperamentally cannot work for another person. He cannot have Elon Musk be his boss. They have a long and contentious relationship.” In 2019, Tesla replaced its in-car driving computer developed by Nvidia with its own hardware. “I don’t think Jensen ever completely forgave him,” Witt says. Speaking candidly about Huang’s tendency to lose his temper with executives, Witt says: “He did it to me. He yelled at me for 20 minutes… And I was writing his biography. I don’t work for him.” Witt says Huang created different characters for himself to build the company: the scary boss, the charismatic showman, the generous employer who once tipped a waitress “ten US$100 bills or US$1,000”. “These characters that he played were taking over his identity,” Witt says. “And he no longer had any control over which one arrived or was present.” Witt says even Huang’s political ascent was the result of a character reinvention. “He can adapt himself to the needs of the moment in this chameleonic way, get what he needs, get what he wants.” He cultivated US President Donald Trump partly to preserve Nvidia’s access to China. But that access, in Witt’s view, antagonised administration officials who favoured tougher restrictions on China. Rubio had briefed Trump in May about the affair, but Trump didn’t act, says Witt. “So Marco Rubio took it to The New York Times and showed it to them instead. And that is how this story broke. The people who broke this story were the White House reporters at the Times . They did not cover Nvidia, like all of us Nvidia chumps over here trying to break the story. They got leaked classified intelligence.” Witt also thinks the revelations about Huang’s private life may extend beyond the three women reported so far: “I suspect there are more women. I’d be shocked if there weren’t.” In Witt’s reading, Nvidia’s directors had to weigh the value of keeping Huang – an undoubtedly formidable leader – against the prospect of further damaging disclosures. “I think the board knows that there’s more skeletons out there coming. It may be worse than it looks right now.” Singapore Writers Festival continues till Nov 22. extraction.body: We live in the age of artificial intelligence — an age that Jensen Huang, perhaps more than any other single person, has made possible. The systems we are building with Nvidia’s equipment will transform our society and culture in ways we can’t imagine. But Mr. Huang’s unraveling is not a technology story. It is a timeless tale of masculine hubris, of a man undone by reckless overconfidence. Some things never change. When I wrote my biography of Mr. Huang, I titled it “The Thinking Machine”. The name referred to the microchips that powered A.I., but also to Mr. Huang’s marauding, relentless intellect, which never slowed down or turned off. In the wake of his stunning departure, spurred by revelations that he carried on at least two affairs, one with a woman who U.S. intelligence determined is a Chinese spy and another with one of his direct reports, I should write a sequel: “The What-Were-You-Thinking?! Machine”. Let’s start with Mr. Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, an executive who managed a Singapore-based company that owns data centers in Southeast Asia. These data centers are suspected of helping Chinese A.I. developers circumvent U.S. restrictions on sales of Nvidia equipment. A recent report in The Information suggests they were used as a way station to illicitly smuggle some $7 billion of equipment into China. Since U.S. intelligence captured evidence of Mr. Huang in a romantic relationship with Ms. Huang, it’s hard to believe that he did not understand what was going on. Now consider Mr. Huang’s reported involvement with Kimberly Powell, an executive in the health care group at his company and his direct subordinate. A former Nvidia employee told me this affair was common knowledge in the company — the same company that employs both of Mr. Huang’s children in executive roles. It’s a stunning and disrespectful display of arrogance. I asked the former employee why Mr. Huang would behave this way, right in front of his kids. The former employee said that it got him high — a narcissist’s high. I started hearing rumors of Mr. Huang’s infidelities earlier but was unable to confirm them. Inside Nvidia, there was a culture of omertà that was difficult to break, and this enabled Mr. Huang to be his worst self. I sensed this deference, at times, in the sycophantic laughter of his subordinates when he was around, and the little things they muttered once he left the room. Ultimately, it took government intelligence to pierce Nvidia’s culture of silence — along with reporters at this newspaper. But now that containment is shattered, and I will not be surprised if more women come forward. No one will be surprised. Mr. Huang went to considerable lengths to cloak his arrogance. When I first met him in 2023, he and his handlers were pushing the idea that he was a humble man. In our conversations, Mr. Huang was constantly deflecting attention away from his success, always quick to assign credit to his employees and executive staff members. He also liked to glad-hand service people. He was a dishwasher once, a point he never let you forget. He loved visiting small, hole-in-the-wall restaurants and leaving extravagant tips. I’d met him for breakfast at Denny’s, and he tipped our waitress $1,000 in $100 bills. He didn’t make a show of it, either. I had to track her down to ask. Over time, though, I began to suspect that this was an act, one performed not for the observer but to flatter himself. In truth, Mr. Huang was quite arrogant. He had little tolerance for disagreement and almost no capacity for open discourse. When you contradicted him, even over the most trivial matter, it was like lighting a fuse. Stick to your position, and soon he exploded, screaming at you for your idiocy. A harangue from Mr. Huang could last an hour or more; his executive staff appeared genuinely afraid of him. Listening to their stories, I was reminded of the abusive music instructor from the movie “Whiplash”. Mr. Huang went to even greater lengths to present himself as a family man. Here, the act was harder to detect and must have involved a great deal of self-deception. He spoke of his wife, Lori, and his kids, Madison and Spencer, all the time. Unlike his flimsy man-of-the-people shtick, this affection for his family seemed genuine. He traveled with them often, all over the world. He encouraged his kids to leave careers in unrelated fields to join him at his microchip company. Several weeks ago, at a wedding in Hawaii, he gave away his daughter, Madison, to Nico Caprez, another Nvidia executive. Mr. Huang met his future wife when he was 17. The two were lab partners in an electrical engineering course, and Mr. Huang was so shy, it took him six months to ask her out. She was his first girlfriend, and they married in their early 20s. She left the work force to raise their kids so Mr. Huang could pursue his dream of founding a company. He has spoken often of the sacrifices she made for him. His betrayal of her is absolute. While reporting his biography, I spoke to some of the Huangs’ oldest friends. These were people they knew in their 20s, long before the money and the fame. I sometimes dropped little hints: Was there any chance of infidelity, perhaps? Any rumors of marital friction? Any arrangements? The response I got was that the Huangs’ marriage was happy, even ideal — something to be emulated. In a divorce, Lori Huang could become one of the richest women in America. It’s possible the Huangs signed a prenuptial agreement, or have some other agreement, but I doubt it. When they married, in the mid-1980s, neither had much in assets. The hundreds of millions of Nvidia shares they jointly own are held in family trusts. They recently donated $75 million toward a flagship building at Vanderbilt University’s new campus in San Francisco. Another building they helped fund at Oregon State University, where they met, is nearing completion. The hypocrisy is almost overwhelming. In the early days — the 1990s — Nvidia was a boys’ club. The staff played video games and drank beer in the office, and almost no women worked there. Their mascot, for a time, was Dawn, an underdressed, large-breasted C.G.I. pixie. Dawn was memory-holed in 2020, around the time Mr. Huang started to talk about empowering women within the company. In 2023, while at Nvidia’s campus, I saw Mr. Huang make an impassioned call for gender parity at Nvidia, where men still account for 80 percent of its employees. Maybe he had an ulterior motive. I was surprised — and, frankly, amazed — when Mr. Huang became President Trump’s close ally in 2025. He’d never shown much interest in politics and had limited Washington connections. He didn’t attend Mr. Trump’s inauguration. But soon, in a masterly display of social engineering, he’d gained the president’s trust, mostly by flattering him. By the time of the president’s tech summit at the White House this September, Mr. Huang was seated at Mr. Trump’s right arm. Mr. Trump and Mr. Huang have a fair amount in common — the bluster, the narcissism and, I suppose, the womanizing. But it was politics that triggered Mr. Huang’s downfall. He persuaded the president to lift export restrictions on Nvidia chips to China, and this put him in conflict with the more hawkish members of the president’s staff — especially Secretary of State Marco Rubio, whose sharp criticisms of China at one point got him barred from that country. It was Mr. Rubio who oversaw the memo that exposed Mr. Huang. Now Nvidia must find a successor. That’s going to be difficult: Mr. Huang never groomed one and has no second in command. Colette Kress will serve as interim chief executive, but she comes from the world of finance, not electrical engineering, so I don’t think she can provide a long-term solution. Whoever replaces Mr. Huang must be a world-class computer scientist, someone who can close deals with powerful customers and someone who can get on the phone to Taiwan and start screaming when the chips are delayed. Nvidia without Jensen Huang is like the Bulls without Michael Jordan. Mr. Huang built Nvidia from nothing, but through his arrogance and toxic self-regard, he has left an empty space that might be impossible to fill. passages: We live in the age of artificial intelligence — an age that Jensen Huang, perhaps more than any other single person, has made possible. The systems we are building with Nvidia’s equipment will transform our society and culture in ways we can’t imagine. But Mr. Huang’s unraveling is not a technology story. It is a timeless tale of masculine hubris, of a man undone by reckless overconfidence. Some things never change.

When I wrote my biography of Mr. Huang, I titled it “The Thinking Machine”. The name referred to the microchips that powered A.I., but also to Mr. Huang’s marauding, relentless intellect, which never slowed down or turned off. In the wake of his stunning departure, spurred by revelations that he carried on at least two affairs, one with a woman who U.S. intelligence determined is a Chinese spy and another with one of his direct reports, I should write a sequel: “The What-Were-You-Thinking?! Machine”.

Let’s start with Mr. Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, an executive who managed a Singapore-based company that owns data centers in Southeast Asia. These data centers are suspected of helping Chinese A.I. developers circumvent U.S. restrictions on sales of Nvidia equipment. A recent report in The Information suggests they were used as a way station to illicitly smuggle some $7 billion of equipment into China. Since U.S. intelligence captured evidence of Mr. Huang in a romantic relationship with Ms. Huang, it’s hard to believe that he did not understand what was going on.

Now consider Mr. Huang’s reported involvement with Kimberly Powell, an executive in the health care group at his company and his direct subordinate. A former Nvidia employee told me this affair was common knowledge in the company — the same company that employs both of Mr. Huang’s children in executive roles. It’s a stunning and disrespectful display of arrogance. I asked the former employee why Mr. Huang would behave this way, right in front of his kids. The former employee said that it got him high — a narcissist’s high.

I started hearing rumors of Mr. Huang’s infidelities earlier but was unable to confirm them. Inside Nvidia, there was a culture of omertà that was difficult to break, and this enabled Mr. Huang to be his worst self. I sensed this deference, at times, in the sycophantic laughter of his subordinates when he was around, and the little things they muttered once he left the room. Ultimately, it took government intelligence to pierce Nvidia’s culture of silence — along with reporters at this newspaper. But now that containment is shattered, and I will not be surprised if more women come forward. No one will be surprised.

Mr. Huang went to considerable lengths to cloak his arrogance. When I first met him in 2023, he and his handlers were pushing the idea that he was a humble man. In our conversations, Mr. Huang was constantly deflecting attention away from his success, always quick to assign credit to his employees and executive staff members. He also liked to glad-hand service people. He was a dishwasher once, a point he never let you forget. He loved visiting small, hole-in-the-wall restaurants and leaving extravagant tips. I’d met him for breakfast at Denny’s, and he tipped our waitress $1,000 in $100 bills. He didn’t make a show of it, either. I had to track her down to ask.

Over time, though, I began to suspect that this was an act, one performed not for the observer but to flatter himself. In truth, Mr. Huang was quite arrogant. He had little tolerance for disagreement and almost no capacity for open discourse. When you contradicted him, even over the most trivial matter, it was like lighting a fuse. Stick to your position, and soon he exploded, screaming at you for your idiocy. A harangue from Mr. Huang could last an hour or more; his executive staff appeared genuinely afraid of him. Listening to their stories, I was reminded of the abusive music instructor from the movie “Whiplash”.

Mr. Huang went to even greater lengths to present himself as a family man. Here, the act was harder to detect and must have involved a great deal of self-deception. He spoke of his wife, Lori, and his kids, Madison and Spencer, all the time. Unlike his flimsy man-of-the-people shtick, this affection for his family seemed genuine. He traveled with them often, all over the world. He encouraged his kids to leave careers in unrelated fields to join him at his microchip company. Several weeks ago, at a wedding in Hawaii, he gave away his daughter, Madison, to Nico Caprez, another Nvidia executive.

Mr. Huang met his future wife when he was 17. The two were lab partners in an electrical engineering course, and Mr. Huang was so shy, it took him six months to ask her out. She was his first girlfriend, and they married in their early 20s. She left the work force to raise their kids so Mr. Huang could pursue his dream of founding a company. He has spoken often of the sacrifices she made for him. His betrayal of her is absolute.

While reporting his biography, I spoke to some of the Huangs’ oldest friends. These were people they knew in their 20s, long before the money and the fame. I sometimes dropped little hints: Was there any chance of infidelity, perhaps? Any rumors of marital friction? Any arrangements? The response I got was that the Huangs’ marriage was happy, even ideal — something to be emulated.

In a divorce, Lori Huang could become one of the richest women in America. It’s possible the Huangs signed a prenuptial agreement, or have some other agreement, but I doubt it. When they married, in the mid-1980s, neither had much in assets. The hundreds of millions of Nvidia shares they jointly own are held in family trusts. They recently donated $75 million toward a flagship building at Vanderbilt University’s new campus in San Francisco. Another building they helped fund at Oregon State University, where they met, is nearing completion.

The hypocrisy is almost overwhelming. In the early days — the 1990s — Nvidia was a boys’ club. The staff played video games and drank beer in the office, and almost no women worked there. Their mascot, for a time, was Dawn, an underdressed, large-breasted C.G.I. pixie. Dawn was memory-holed in 2020, around the time Mr. Huang started to talk about empowering women within the company. In 2023, while at Nvidia’s campus, I saw Mr. Huang make an impassioned call for gender parity at Nvidia, where men still account for 80 percent of its employees. Maybe he had an ulterior motive.

I was surprised — and, frankly, amazed — when Mr. Huang became President Trump’s close ally in 2025. He’d never shown much interest in politics and had limited Washington connections. He didn’t attend Mr. Trump’s inauguration. But soon, in a masterly display of social engineering, he’d gained the president’s trust, mostly by flattering him. By the time of the president’s tech summit at the White House this September, Mr. Huang was seated at Mr. Trump’s right arm.

Mr. Trump and Mr. Huang have a fair amount in common — the bluster, the narcissism and, I suppose, the womanizing. But it was politics that triggered Mr. Huang’s downfall. He persuaded the president to lift export restrictions on Nvidia chips to China, and this put him in conflict with the more hawkish members of the president’s staff — especially Secretary of State Marco Rubio, whose sharp criticisms of China at one point got him barred from that country. It was Mr. Rubio who oversaw the memo that exposed Mr. Huang.

Now Nvidia must find a successor. That’s going to be difficult: Mr. Huang never groomed one and has no second in command. Colette Kress will serve as interim chief executive, but she comes from the world of finance, not electrical engineering, so I don’t think she can provide a long-term solution.

Whoever replaces Mr. Huang must be a world-class computer scientist, someone who can close deals with powerful customers and someone who can get on the phone to Taiwan and start screaming when the chips are delayed. Nvidia without Jensen Huang is like the Bulls without Michael Jordan. Mr. Huang built Nvidia from nothing, but through his arrogance and toxic self-regard, he has left an empty space that might be impossible to fill.
Stephen Witt is the author of The Thinking Machine , a biography of Jensen Huang.

coreStoryFacts.text: Less than two weeks ago, billionaire Jensen Huang was a gainfully employed CEO whose personal life the general public knew very little about; today, he’s out at Nvidia, the multitrillion-dollar company he co-founded in 1993, following revelations that he had an affair with (1) a woman accused of being a Chinese spy and (2) an Nvidia subordinate.

The stunning downfall will undoubtedly have reverberations far beyond Nvidia’s Silicon Valley campus, given Huang’s position as one of the most powerful, if not the most powerful, figures in the AI industry and his close proximity to Donald Trump.
On Wall Street, the company’s stock was down 11 percent on the news of his departure, which translates to a loss of roughly $1 trillion just this month.

In Washington, the New York Times notes that few tech executives “have had as much sway as Huang over Trump’s approach to A.I. and China.” He reportedly “persuaded the president to roll back a ban on chip sales to China and Nvidia has donated at least $20 million to a fund for Trump’s White House ballroom project.”

On Wednesday Nvidia’s board met for hours to decide Huang’s fate, and, despite the CEO reportedly “fighting hard to hang onto his role with the company he founded,” Huang resigned Thursday morning and chief financial officer Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO.

Incredibly, Nvidia had no successor in place prior to the scandal that took down its leader because Huang didn’t believe in succession planning ; he was also apparently a micromanager with 60 direct reports and said last year that he reads thousands of employee emails a day.
I support the investigation and will cooperate fully.
I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security.
Q: When were you first informed that there was an issue with Jensen Huang and the affair and what was presented to you at the time?
I believe he is suffering greatly because of his family, his wife, who he loves, and his family.
During the conference, Nvidia executives were at a nearby hotel for meetings.
Powell were seen being affectionate at the hotel.
One bystander captured the interaction on their phone, three people briefed on the incident said.
The board also says it has appointed its first-ever chairman, Harvey Jones, the former CEO of Synopsys.

The Times reports that a “monthslong investigation” into Megaspeed, and whether it was “smuggling Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips into China,” was suddenly paused “after Commerce Department investigators working on the case received an email from Nvidia’s general counsel seeking information about the inquiry.” Agents were reportedly alarmed when Nvidia’s general counsel said that a top Commerce official who reports directly to Secretary Howard Lutnick “had given Nvidia permission to reach out about the case.”
Powell appeared at GTC, Nvidia’s annual developer conference in San Jose, where she spoke about using A.I. to aid in breakthroughs in health care and biology.
Her presentation used cartoon depictions of Mr.
Q: Is Jensen Huang coming with you on your trip to Asia?

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s bravado had evaporated this week by the time it became clear his scandalous affairs including one with an alleged Chinese spy would cost him his job — and he chastised himself as a “piece of s–t,” according to reports.
On Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang had a second affair with Kimberly Powell , Nvidia’s vice president of health care.
Huang has been married to his wife Lori for over 40 years , and his two children and son-in-law work at Nvidia.
But reports later identified two more affairs with two executives at Nvidia.
On Sunday, Nvidia’s board announced it would investigate the reports.
The ousted Nvidia boss hasn’t been without defenders.

The board was reportedly wary of taking action, but Teter urged them to make an announcement. Huang had cultivated a close relationship with President Trump and was seen as somewhat of a celebrity in his native Taiwan. He typically responded to emails immediately at all times of day and night – but his responses had slowed, according to Bloomberg. His close hold on the company is part of the reason investors panicked that the firm might not survive without him – causing the stock to shed over $450 billion in market value. The ousted Nvidia boss hasn’t been without defenders. Trump has repeatedly praised Huang since news of the first affair. Most recently, Trump told Stephen A. Smith on Thursday that Huang should only step down if Alice was truly a Chinese spy, and that Huang is “going through hell” and “feels most badly [about] his wife and family.” In the meantime, Huang is gearing up to testify before Congress .

extraction.body: Biographer Stephen Witt wonders whether the former tech chief can – or even wants to – lead again [SINGAPORE] At 63, Jensen Huang may no longer have it in him to start or lead another tech company, speculates Stephen Witt, who wrote Huang’s best-selling biography The Thinking Machine in 2025. Here for the Singapore Writers Festival, Witt says: “In the time that I was with him, I saw him slow down just a step. That’s just age. It’s time. It happens.” Witt worked on the book over several months, speaking with Huang as well as over 200 employees, customers, rivals and friends. The book built a picture of a brilliant, demanding workaholic who had made Nvidia the centre of his life. “But I just don’t know if he can be a CEO again or if he wants to be a CEO again,” Witt tells the festival audience in his keynote speech at Victoria Theatre. “I think his motivation might be shot after this.” Huang’s next task will probably be more personal: trying to save his marriage. Witt says: “I think he will beg his wife not to divorce him.” Although Huang had lovers, including businesswoman Alice Huang and Nvidia’s vice-president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, his love for his wife was genuine, Witt suggests. “Jensen talked about his wife all the time. All the time. He praised her constantly,” Witt says. “He never overlooked that sacrifice she made (leaving engineering to raise their two children). He acknowledged it constantly in conversation.” At the same time, “Nvidia consumed him, it was his life”, Witt adds. “I can see him having almost an identity crisis now… and he may reassess everything. I can see a world where Jensen leaves and just does philanthropic giving, believe it or not.” The biographer’s doubts about a comeback coexist with considerable admiration for the abilities that make Huang so difficult to replace . “Jensen’s a world-class computer scientist. He’s a world-class deal maker. And he’s a world-class ops guy.” Witt describes how Huang could draw an exploded diagram of a graphics chip from memory, explain what each component did and cost, and identify the various suppliers to call for a better price. “He didn’t know anything about business. He just knew about microchips. But he educated himself. He re-engineered himself to be the CEO of the company.” In an anecdote from Witt’s book, retold at the festival, Huang challenged an Nvidia executive with a Masters in Business Administration to name his three favourite books on pricing. The man could not name one, so Huang supplied three. “I want you to read these three books. And when you’re done, we’ll continue this conversation,” he told the executive. Even Huang’s public charisma, Witt suggests, had been painstakingly developed. He recalls watching Huang anxiously rock back and forth backstage before a small presentation, making bad jokes to those around him – despite already being able to command a stadium. “I can’t sleep at night whenever I have to go on stage,” Huang later told Witt, who tells the festival audience: “He uses that fear of failure and shame and guilt as fuel.” During a question-and-answer session moderated by tech writer Grace Chng, an audience member asks if Huang could work with Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX. According to news agency Anadolu, Musk had earlier responded to a suggestion that he should hire Huang by writing on X: “That would be an honour” – without actually announcing a formal offer. But Witt offers a bleakly comic forecast: “Those guys would last together about one week. That would be a titanic ego death match. It could be a reality show. They could sell tickets to it.” He adds: “Jensen temperamentally cannot work for another person. He cannot have Elon Musk be his boss. They have a long and contentious relationship.” In 2019, Tesla replaced its in-car driving computer developed by Nvidia with its own hardware. “I don’t think Jensen ever completely forgave him,” Witt says. Speaking candidly about Huang’s tendency to lose his temper with executives, Witt says: “He did it to me. He yelled at me for 20 minutes… And I was writing his biography. I don’t work for him.” Witt says Huang created different characters for himself to build the company: the scary boss, the charismatic showman, the generous employer who once tipped a waitress “ten US$100 bills or US$1,000”. “These characters that he played were taking over his identity,” Witt says. “And he no longer had any control over which one arrived or was present.” Witt says even Huang’s political ascent was the result of a character reinvention. “He can adapt himself to the needs of the moment in this chameleonic way, get what he needs, get what he wants.” He cultivated US President Donald Trump partly to preserve Nvidia’s access to China. But that access, in Witt’s view, antagonised administration officials who favoured tougher restrictions on China. Rubio had briefed Trump in May about the affair, but Trump didn’t act, says Witt. “So Marco Rubio took it to The New York Times and showed it to them instead. And that is how this story broke. The people who broke this story were the White House reporters at the Times . They did not cover Nvidia, like all of us Nvidia chumps over here trying to break the story. They got leaked classified intelligence.” Witt also thinks the revelations about Huang’s private life may extend beyond the three women reported so far: “I suspect there are more women. I’d be shocked if there weren’t.” In Witt’s reading, Nvidia’s directors had to weigh the value of keeping Huang – an undoubtedly formidable leader – against the prospect of further damaging disclosures. “I think the board knows that there’s more skeletons out there coming. It may be worse than it looks right now.” Singapore Writers Festival continues till Nov 22. extraction.body: We live in the age of artificial intelligence — an age that Jensen Huang, perhaps more than any other single person, has made possible. The systems we are building with Nvidia’s equipment will transform our society and culture in ways we can’t imagine. But Mr. Huang’s unraveling is not a technology story. It is a timeless tale of masculine hubris, of a man undone by reckless overconfidence. Some things never change. When I wrote my biography of Mr. Huang, I titled it “The Thinking Machine”. The name referred to the microchips that powered A.I., but also to Mr. Huang’s marauding, relentless intellect, which never slowed down or turned off. In the wake of his stunning departure, spurred by revelations that he carried on at least two affairs, one with a woman who U.S. intelligence determined is a Chinese spy and another with one of his direct reports, I should write a sequel: “The What-Were-You-Thinking?! Machine”. Let’s start with Mr. Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, an executive who managed a Singapore-based company that owns data centers in Southeast Asia. These data centers are suspected of helping Chinese A.I. developers circumvent U.S. restrictions on sales of Nvidia equipment. A recent report in The Information suggests they were used as a way station to illicitly smuggle some $7 billion of equipment into China. Since U.S. intelligence captured evidence of Mr. Huang in a romantic relationship with Ms. Huang, it’s hard to believe that he did not understand what was going on. Now consider Mr. Huang’s reported involvement with Kimberly Powell, an executive in the health care group at his company and his direct subordinate. A former Nvidia employee told me this affair was common knowledge in the company — the same company that employs both of Mr. Huang’s children in executive roles. It’s a stunning and disrespectful display of arrogance. I asked the former employee why Mr. Huang would behave this way, right in front of his kids. The former employee said that it got him high — a narcissist’s high. I started hearing rumors of Mr. Huang’s infidelities earlier but was unable to confirm them. Inside Nvidia, there was a culture of omertà that was difficult to break, and this enabled Mr. Huang to be his worst self. I sensed this deference, at times, in the sycophantic laughter of his subordinates when he was around, and the little things they muttered once he left the room. Ultimately, it took government intelligence to pierce Nvidia’s culture of silence — along with reporters at this newspaper. But now that containment is shattered, and I will not be surprised if more women come forward. No one will be surprised. Mr. Huang went to considerable lengths to cloak his arrogance. When I first met him in 2023, he and his handlers were pushing the idea that he was a humble man. In our conversations, Mr. Huang was constantly deflecting attention away from his success, always quick to assign credit to his employees and executive staff members. He also liked to glad-hand service people. He was a dishwasher once, a point he never let you forget. He loved visiting small, hole-in-the-wall restaurants and leaving extravagant tips. I’d met him for breakfast at Denny’s, and he tipped our waitress $1,000 in $100 bills. He didn’t make a show of it, either. I had to track her down to ask. Over time, though, I began to suspect that this was an act, one performed not for the observer but to flatter himself. In truth, Mr. Huang was quite arrogant. He had little tolerance for disagreement and almost no capacity for open discourse. When you contradicted him, even over the most trivial matter, it was like lighting a fuse. Stick to your position, and soon he exploded, screaming at you for your idiocy. A harangue from Mr. Huang could last an hour or more; his executive staff appeared genuinely afraid of him. Listening to their stories, I was reminded of the abusive music instructor from the movie “Whiplash”. Mr. Huang went to even greater lengths to present himself as a family man. Here, the act was harder to detect and must have involved a great deal of self-deception. He spoke of his wife, Lori, and his kids, Madison and Spencer, all the time. Unlike his flimsy man-of-the-people shtick, this affection for his family seemed genuine. He traveled with them often, all over the world. He encouraged his kids to leave careers in unrelated fields to join him at his microchip company. Several weeks ago, at a wedding in Hawaii, he gave away his daughter, Madison, to Nico Caprez, another Nvidia executive. Mr. Huang met his future wife when he was 17. The two were lab partners in an electrical engineering course, and Mr. Huang was so shy, it took him six months to ask her out. She was his first girlfriend, and they married in their early 20s. She left the work force to raise their kids so Mr. Huang could pursue his dream of founding a company. He has spoken often of the sacrifices she made for him. His betrayal of her is absolute. While reporting his biography, I spoke to some of the Huangs’ oldest friends. These were people they knew in their 20s, long before the money and the fame. I sometimes dropped little hints: Was there any chance of infidelity, perhaps? Any rumors of marital friction? Any arrangements? The response I got was that the Huangs’ marriage was happy, even ideal — something to be emulated. In a divorce, Lori Huang could become one of the richest women in America. It’s possible the Huangs signed a prenuptial agreement, or have some other agreement, but I doubt it. When they married, in the mid-1980s, neither had much in assets. The hundreds of millions of Nvidia shares they jointly own are held in family trusts. They recently donated $75 million toward a flagship building at Vanderbilt University’s new campus in San Francisco. Another building they helped fund at Oregon State University, where they met, is nearing completion. The hypocrisy is almost overwhelming. In the early days — the 1990s — Nvidia was a boys’ club. The staff played video games and drank beer in the office, and almost no women worked there. Their mascot, for a time, was Dawn, an underdressed, large-breasted C.G.I. pixie. Dawn was memory-holed in 2020, around the time Mr. Huang started to talk about empowering women within the company. In 2023, while at Nvidia’s campus, I saw Mr. Huang make an impassioned call for gender parity at Nvidia, where men still account for 80 percent of its employees. Maybe he had an ulterior motive. I was surprised — and, frankly, amazed — when Mr. Huang became President Trump’s close ally in 2025. He’d never shown much interest in politics and had limited Washington connections. He didn’t attend Mr. Trump’s inauguration. But soon, in a masterly display of social engineering, he’d gained the president’s trust, mostly by flattering him. By the time of the president’s tech summit at the White House this September, Mr. Huang was seated at Mr. Trump’s right arm. Mr. Trump and Mr. Huang have a fair amount in common — the bluster, the narcissism and, I suppose, the womanizing. But it was politics that triggered Mr. Huang’s downfall. He persuaded the president to lift export restrictions on Nvidia chips to China, and this put him in conflict with the more hawkish members of the president’s staff — especially Secretary of State Marco Rubio, whose sharp criticisms of China at one point got him barred from that country. passages: We live in the age of artificial intelligence — an age that Jensen Huang, perhaps more than any other single person, has made possible. The systems we are building with Nvidia’s equipment will transform our society and culture in ways we can’t imagine. But Mr. Huang’s unraveling is not a technology story. It is a timeless tale of masculine hubris, of a man undone by reckless overconfidence. Some things never change.

When I wrote my biography of Mr. Huang, I titled it “The Thinking Machine”. The name referred to the microchips that powered A.I., but also to Mr. Huang’s marauding, relentless intellect, which never slowed down or turned off. In the wake of his stunning departure, spurred by revelations that he carried on at least two affairs, one with a woman who U.S. intelligence determined is a Chinese spy and another with one of his direct reports, I should write a sequel: “The What-Were-You-Thinking?! Machine”.

Let’s start with Mr. Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, an executive who managed a Singapore-based company that owns data centers in Southeast Asia. These data centers are suspected of helping Chinese A.I. developers circumvent U.S. restrictions on sales of Nvidia equipment. A recent report in The Information suggests they were used as a way station to illicitly smuggle some $7 billion of equipment into China. Since U.S. intelligence captured evidence of Mr. Huang in a romantic relationship with Ms. Huang, it’s hard to believe that he did not understand what was going on.

Now consider Mr. Huang’s reported involvement with Kimberly Powell, an executive in the health care group at his company and his direct subordinate. A former Nvidia employee told me this affair was common knowledge in the company — the same company that employs both of Mr. Huang’s children in executive roles. It’s a stunning and disrespectful display of arrogance. I asked the former employee why Mr. Huang would behave this way, right in front of his kids. The former employee said that it got him high — a narcissist’s high.

I started hearing rumors of Mr. Huang’s infidelities earlier but was unable to confirm them. Inside Nvidia, there was a culture of omertà that was difficult to break, and this enabled Mr. Huang to be his worst self. I sensed this deference, at times, in the sycophantic laughter of his subordinates when he was around, and the little things they muttered once he left the room. Ultimately, it took government intelligence to pierce Nvidia’s culture of silence — along with reporters at this newspaper. But now that containment is shattered, and I will not be surprised if more women come forward. No one will be surprised.

Mr. Huang went to considerable lengths to cloak his arrogance. When I first met him in 2023, he and his handlers were pushing the idea that he was a humble man. In our conversations, Mr. Huang was constantly deflecting attention away from his success, always quick to assign credit to his employees and executive staff members. He also liked to glad-hand service people. He was a dishwasher once, a point he never let you forget. He loved visiting small, hole-in-the-wall restaurants and leaving extravagant tips. I’d met him for breakfast at Denny’s, and he tipped our waitress $1,000 in $100 bills. He didn’t make a show of it, either. I had to track her down to ask.

Over time, though, I began to suspect that this was an act, one performed not for the observer but to flatter himself. In truth, Mr. Huang was quite arrogant. He had little tolerance for disagreement and almost no capacity for open discourse. When you contradicted him, even over the most trivial matter, it was like lighting a fuse. Stick to your position, and soon he exploded, screaming at you for your idiocy. A harangue from Mr. Huang could last an hour or more; his executive staff appeared genuinely afraid of him. Listening to their stories, I was reminded of the abusive music instructor from the movie “Whiplash”.

Mr. Huang went to even greater lengths to present himself as a family man. Here, the act was harder to detect and must have involved a great deal of self-deception. He spoke of his wife, Lori, and his kids, Madison and Spencer, all the time. Unlike his flimsy man-of-the-people shtick, this affection for his family seemed genuine. He traveled with them often, all over the world. He encouraged his kids to leave careers in unrelated fields to join him at his microchip company. Several weeks ago, at a wedding in Hawaii, he gave away his daughter, Madison, to Nico Caprez, another Nvidia executive.

Mr. Huang met his future wife when he was 17. The two were lab partners in an electrical engineering course, and Mr. Huang was so shy, it took him six months to ask her out. She was his first girlfriend, and they married in their early 20s. She left the work force to raise their kids so Mr. Huang could pursue his dream of founding a company. He has spoken often of the sacrifices she made for him. His betrayal of her is absolute.

While reporting his biography, I spoke to some of the Huangs’ oldest friends. These were people they knew in their 20s, long before the money and the fame. I sometimes dropped little hints: Was there any chance of infidelity, perhaps? Any rumors of marital friction? Any arrangements? The response I got was that the Huangs’ marriage was happy, even ideal — something to be emulated.

In a divorce, Lori Huang could become one of the richest women in America. It’s possible the Huangs signed a prenuptial agreement, or have some other agreement, but I doubt it. When they married, in the mid-1980s, neither had much in assets. The hundreds of millions of Nvidia shares they jointly own are held in family trusts. They recently donated $75 million toward a flagship building at Vanderbilt University’s new campus in San Francisco. Another building they helped fund at Oregon State University, where they met, is nearing completion.

The hypocrisy is almost overwhelming. In the early days — the 1990s — Nvidia was a boys’ club. The staff played video games and drank beer in the office, and almost no women worked there. Their mascot, for a time, was Dawn, an underdressed, large-breasted C.G.I. pixie. Dawn was memory-holed in 2020, around the time Mr. Huang started to talk about empowering women within the company. In 2023, while at Nvidia’s campus, I saw Mr. Huang make an impassioned call for gender parity at Nvidia, where men still account for 80 percent of its employees. Maybe he had an ulterior motive.

I was surprised — and, frankly, amazed — when Mr. Huang became President Trump’s close ally in 2025. He’d never shown much interest in politics and had limited Washington connections. He didn’t attend Mr. Trump’s inauguration. But soon, in a masterly display of social engineering, he’d gained the president’s trust, mostly by flattering him. By the time of the president’s tech summit at the White House this September, Mr. Huang was seated at Mr. Trump’s right arm.

He persuaded the president to lift export restrictions on Nvidia chips to China, and this put him in conflict with the more hawkish members of the president’s staff — especially Secretary of State Marco Rubio, whose sharp criticisms of China at one point got him barred from that country. It was Mr. Rubio who oversaw the memo that exposed Mr. Huang.

Now Nvidia must find a successor. That’s going to be difficult: Mr. Huang never groomed one and has no second in command. Colette Kress will serve as interim chief executive, but she comes from the world of finance, not electrical engineering, so I don’t think she can provide a long-term solution.

Whoever replaces Mr. Huang must be a world-class computer scientist, someone who can close deals with powerful customers and someone who can get on the phone to Taiwan and start screaming when the chips are delayed. Nvidia without Jensen Huang is like the Bulls without Michael Jordan. Mr. Huang built Nvidia from nothing, but through his arrogance and toxic self-regard, he has left an empty space that might be impossible to fill.

story.title: Jensen Huang Carried a Secret for More Than a Year. It Led to His Downfall. - The New York Times

facts.text: Less than two weeks ago, billionaire Jensen Huang was a gainfully employed CEO whose personal life the general public knew very little about; today, he’s out at Nvidia, the multitrillion-dollar company he co-founded in 1993, following revelations that he had an affair with (1) a woman accused of being a Chinese spy and (2) an Nvidia subordinate.

The stunning downfall will undoubtedly have reverberations far beyond Nvidia’s Silicon Valley campus, given Huang’s position as one of the most powerful, if not the most powerful, figures in the AI industry and his close proximity to Donald Trump.
On Wall Street, the company’s stock was down 11 percent on the news of his departure, which translates to a loss of roughly $1 trillion just this month.

In Washington, the New York Times notes that few tech executives “have had as much sway as Huang over Trump’s approach to A.I. and China.” He reportedly “persuaded the president to roll back a ban on chip sales to China and Nvidia has donated at least $20 million to a fund for Trump’s White House ballroom project.”

Incredibly, Nvidia had no successor in place prior to the scandal that took down its leader because Huang didn’t believe in succession planning ; he was also apparently a micromanager with 60 direct reports and said last year that he reads thousands of employee emails a day.
I support the investigation and will cooperate fully.
I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security.
Q: When were you first informed that there was an issue with Jensen Huang and the affair and what was presented to you at the time?
I believe he is suffering greatly because of his family, his wife, who he loves, and his family.
During the conference, Nvidia executives were at a nearby hotel for meetings.
Powell were seen being affectionate at the hotel.
One bystander captured the interaction on their phone, three people briefed on the incident said.
The board also says it has appointed its first-ever chairman, Harvey Jones, the former CEO of Synopsys.

The Times reports that a “monthslong investigation” into Megaspeed, and whether it was “smuggling Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips into China,” was suddenly paused “after Commerce Department investigators working on the case received an email from Nvidia’s general counsel seeking information about the inquiry.” Agents were reportedly alarmed when Nvidia’s general counsel said that a top Commerce official who reports directly to Secretary Howard Lutnick “had given Nvidia permission to reach out about the case.”
Powell appeared at GTC, Nvidia’s annual developer conference in San Jose, where she spoke about using A.I. to aid in breakthroughs in health care and biology.
Her presentation used cartoon depictions of Mr.
Q: Is Jensen Huang coming with you on your trip to Asia?

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s bravado had evaporated this week by the time it became clear his scandalous affairs including one with an alleged Chinese spy would cost him his job — and he chastised himself as a “piece of s–t,” according to reports.
On Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang had a second affair with Kimberly Powell , Nvidia’s vice president of health care.
Huang has been married to his wife Lori for over 40 years , and his two children and son-in-law work at Nvidia.
But reports later identified two more affairs with two executives at Nvidia.
On Sunday, Nvidia’s board announced it would investigate the reports.
The ousted Nvidia boss hasn’t been without defenders.
Days later, the Financial Times revealed that a secret, months-old government memo had found the relationship was a romantic one.
[SINGAPORE] At 63, Jensen Huang may no longer have it in him to start or lead another tech company, speculates Stephen Witt, who wrote Huang’s best-selling biography The Thinking Machine in 2025.
Witt worked on the book over several months, speaking with Huang as well as over 200 employees, customers, rivals and friends.
The book built a picture of a brilliant, demanding workaholic who had made Nvidia the centre of his life.
In an anecdote from Witt’s book, retold at the festival, Huang challenged an Nvidia executive with a Masters in Business Administration to name his three favourite books on pricing.
The man could not name one, so Huang supplied three.
In 2019, Tesla replaced its in-car driving computer developed by Nvidia with its own hardware.
“I don’t think Jensen ever completely forgave him,” Witt says.
Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang carried a secret for more than a year.
At the same time, “Nvidia consumed him, it was his life”, Witt adds.
“I can see him having almost an identity crisis now… and he may reassess everything.
“So Marco Rubio took it to The New York Times and showed it to them instead.
The people who broke this story were the White House reporters at the Times .
They did not cover Nvidia, like all of us Nvidia chumps over here trying to break the story.
Although Huang had lovers, including businesswoman Alice Huang and Nvidia’s vice-president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, his love for his wife was genuine, Witt suggests.
In Witt’s reading, Nvidia’s directors had to weigh the value of keeping Huang – an undoubtedly formidable leader – against the prospect of further damaging disclosures.
According to news agency Anadolu, Musk had earlier responded to a suggestion that he should hire Huang by writing on X: “That would be an honour” – without actually announcing a formal offer.
He cultivated US President Donald Trump partly to preserve Nvidia’s access to China.
We live in the age of artificial intelligence — an age that Jensen Huang, perhaps more than any other single person, has made possible.
Stephen Witt is the author of The Thinking Machine , a biography of Jensen Huang.
Nvidia without Jensen Huang is like the Bulls without Michael Jordan.
While reporting his biography, I spoke to some of the Huangs’ oldest friends.

extraction.body: The crypto market ended Thursday night with its steepest daily loss in weeks. At 07:30 UTC on November 13, 2026, bitcoin traded at about $69,000, down a little over 6% in 24 hours, after touching an intraday low of $67,922 according to CoinGecko. Total crypto market capitalization fell about 7% over the same period to roughly $2.35 trillion. If you are asking why is crypto down today, our running explainer tracks every sell-off of the year. This crypto news roundup sets out what is driving the move: forced selling of leveraged positions, outflows from US spot bitcoin ETFs, a strong dollar with rising Treasury yields, and thin order books. Our first report with key price levels is Bitcoin price falls below $70,000. Crypto news at a glance: bitcoin, ether, BNB and XRP this morning Losses run through the large caps, but not evenly. As of 07:30 UTC, per CoinGecko data: Bitcoin: about $69,000, down 6.2% in 24 hours. According to CoinDesk, ether fell below $2,000 for the first time since August; see Ethereum price below $2,000. BNB: about $634, down 5.9%; more in BNB falls below $650. XRP: about $1.03, down 1.3%, with an intraday low just under $1. XRP and Solana fell less than bitcoin and ether over the past day, but both had already lost more earlier in the week: over seven days XRP is down a little over 14% and Solana just over 10%, per CoinGecko. For medium-term scenarios, see our bitcoin price prediction and ethereum price prediction. Liquidations: more than $1.3 billion in leveraged bets wiped out in 24 hours A liquidation is the forced closing of a leveraged position by an exchange once the posted collateral no longer covers it. Based on CoinGlass data analysed by CoinDesk early Friday, more than $1.3 billion in crypto futures were liquidated within 24 hours, about $677 million of them on bitcoin. The largest single liquidation was a long bitcoin position worth more than $31 million on Hyperliquid, according to the same report. Later snapshots reported by KuCoin News and Bloomingbit reached up to $1.62 billion. The defensible range is therefore $1.3 billion to $1.6 billion, most of it from traders who had bet on rising prices. Bitcoin ETF outflows: why US funds are weighing on the price The second driver is US fund flows. According to Cointelegraph, BlackRock's IBIT recorded more than $2 billion in net outflows over nine consecutive sessions through Wednesday. Across all US spot bitcoin ETFs, nearly $1.44 billion left over five sessions. Preliminary Farside data showed a further $47.7 million in net outflows on Thursday, with BlackRock and Fidelity figures still pending. When investors redeem shares, the fund generally has to sell bitcoin, which adds to the pressure from liquidations. Dollar and Treasury yields: the macro pressure on crypto CoinDesk points to a strong US dollar: the Dollar Index rose above 103, its highest since April 2025. After a hotter-than-expected October CPI reading, markets also raised the odds of a Federal Reserve rate hike in December. Per Cointelegraph, data from 10x Research show bitcoin fell 5.9% between November 5 and 12, while the 10-year Treasury yield climbed above 5%. Order book depth: why the bitcoin price swings so hard Order book depth measures how many buy and sell orders sit close to the current price. The thinner it is, the further a large sale moves the market. According to Talos, cited by Cointelegraph, bitcoin order book depth across major exchanges stood at $72 million on November 9, roughly 33% below normal. Talos senior research associate Tanay Ved said liquidity remains thin while leverage stays elevated, leaving the market vulnerable to sharp moves in either direction. With few resting orders, even medium-sized sales trigger large price jumps. Fear and Greed Index at 20: extreme fear in the crypto market Sentiment matches the price action. The Crypto Fear and Greed Index from alternative.me reads 20 on Friday, which is "Extreme Fear", down from 28 the day before. Cointelegraph notes this is the lowest reading since July 8. How the market behaved after earlier spells of extreme fear is covered in our Fear and Greed Index history. CoinDesk also reported that the overnight sell-off accelerated on news of renewed military escalation in the Middle East.

passages: The crypto market downturn sent Bitcoin below $64K and left Ether, XRP and Solana down 22% in a week, with the December Fed decision in focus.
Bitcoin dropped to $63,863 on November 15, 2026—a 4.97% fall in 24 hours, according to CoinGecko.
The decline pushed BTC ▼ $65,498.00 to a three-month low just above $62,000, raising the question of where relief might come.
Bitcoin and several of the largest alternative cryptocurrencies suffered substantial weekly declines.
Bitcoin’s 17% loss was severe, while the three other tokens each surrendered more than a fifth of their value over the week.
The five-percentage-point gap shows how much harder those assets fell over the same interval.
Bitcoin and ether subsequently rebounded after another sharp drop.
Speaking with Anthony Pompliano on the Pomp Podcast, Wall Street veteran Jordi Visser argued that crypto investors had underestimated the bond market’s influence on Bitcoin.

Bitcoin dropped to $63,863 on November 15, 2026—a 4.97% fall in 24 hours, according to CoinGecko. The damage spread fast. Ether, XRP ▼ $0.9702 and solana each lost 22% over the week, while Bitcoin fell 17%, as bond yields climbed, investors locked in losses and margin calls from the AI selloff cascaded through portfolios. The decline pushed BTC ▼ $65,498.00 to a three-month low just above $62,000, raising the question of where relief might come. Analysts and strategists point to the December Fed decision as a potential turning point in this crypto market downturn. Bitcoin and several of the largest alternative cryptocurrencies suffered substantial weekly declines. Ether, XRP and solana each lost 22%, putting their weekly falls five percentage points beyond Bitcoin’s 17% decline. The token touched a fresh three-month low just above $62,000 as the selling continued. That brought BTC back into the broad price territory where analyst James Check said some investors had hesitated to buy during the summer. BTC fell below $73,000 on November 10. The break below $72,000 on November 12 marked another deterioration, followed by the later three-month low. Bitcoin and ether subsequently rebounded after another sharp drop. By November 15, however, BTC remained below $64,000 and its 24-hour change was still negative. The bounce occurred within a downturn that had already inflicted double-digit weekly losses across several major tokens. Speaking with Anthony Pompliano on the Pomp Podcast, Wall Street veteran Jordi Visser argued that crypto investors had underestimated the bond market’s influence on Bitcoin. He cited a weekly increase of 35 basis points in two-year yields and connected that move to BTC’s decline. Visser’s explanation centers on inflation fears and interest-rate expectations . He argued that those fears need to ease for the Fed to stop raising rates, and that a change in the liquidity backdrop would help Bitcoin recover. His outlook still included further tightening—at least two more rate increases, he said, with December’s size mattering enough to change Bitcoin’s direction. Check described the decline as the fourth capitulation event since Bitcoin’s all-time high. His assessment focused on investors who passed on BTC in the mid-to-high $60,000s during the summer, bought in the $80,000s in September and were now selling at a loss. Fundstrat’s Tom Lee offered another source of pressure: margin calls associated with the AI and Nvidia selloff, particularly among Asian retail investors. His explanation points to investors selling crypto while facing pressure elsewhere in their portfolios. Visser placed a different emphasis on that connection, saying the AI selloff had affected Bitcoin the previous week but considered the liquidity side of the market more relevant to its immediate direction. Check’s account traces a shift from hesitation to chasing higher prices and then realizing losses. Investors who wanted cheaper Bitcoin during the summer eventually entered after BTC moved into the $80,000s, only to sell when it returned to prices they had previously considered attractive. For that group, the November decline erased the benefit of waiting for stronger momentum before buying. Check’s explanation centers on the decisions of those late entrants and their willingness to exit after the market reversed. Check characterized Bitcoin’s position as a deep-value zone, comparing it with earlier periods in February and late June of 2026, as well as late 2022. That valuation judgment does not mean the bottom is in. His view that investors gradually entering at such levels could eventually become profitable remains a forward-looking assessment, with further losses still possible before any recovery. The weekly declines covered Bitcoin, ether, XRP and solana, spreading the damage across several of the market’s largest assets. Bitcoin’s 17% loss was severe, while the three other tokens each surrendered more than a fifth of their value over the week. The five-percentage-point gap shows how much harder those assets fell over the same interval. The September purchases described by Check occurred in the $80,000s. Selling in the $60,000s locks in a loss for those positions, adding an investor-behavior dimension to the discussion of yields and monetary policy. His assessment also explains why a return to an earlier price range can feel very different to different holders. The immediate recovery challenge therefore has both a macroeconomic and a holder component. Visser looks for relief from interest-rate fears, while Check identifies investors already abandoning positions after the reversal. Singapore-based, Nasdaq-listed miner BitFuFu held 1,454 BTC at October’s end, up from 1,388 BTC at September’s end. That 66-BTC increase represented 4.8% month-over-month growth. The company had increased its Bitcoin holdings for three consecutive months. Chairman and CEO Leo Lu reiterated its commitment to increasing those holdings, giving the operating update a longer-term treasury focus. These were October balances, preceding the later increase in November selling pressure. BitFuFu mined 137 BTC in October, down from 167 BTC in September—a decline of about 18%. Its production consisted of 67 BTC from self-mining and 70 BTC from cloud mining. The production reduction was attributed mainly to an approximately 11.8% increase in mining difficulty during October. Managed hashrate edged up to 19.5 exahashes per second from 19.4 EH/s in September, leaving the company’s mining power relatively stable despite lower output. For the miner, the challenge was maintaining accumulation as greater mining difficulty weighed on production. Visser’s bearish concern is that inflation fears keep interest-rate expectations elevated. He cited the rise in two-year yields as a force behind the decline and said the liquidity backdrop needed to improve for Bitcoin to turn around. His interpretation differs from Arthur Hayes’s view that higher interest rates could push wealthy investors toward Bitcoin and other assets. Check’s description of investors realizing losses highlights a continuing source of potential selling. Buyers who entered after the September advance may remain under pressure as Bitcoin trades back in the $60,000s. Lee’s margin-call suggestion raises a second possible vulnerability: stress in AI-related investments spilling into crypto holdings. A durable recovery would have to contend with those pressures after the initial rebound. The strongest bullish argument in Visser’s account is relief from rate fears; the clearest threat is that inflation concerns keep the tightening outlook in place. Visser said the next rally could find its catalyst in December if the Fed avoids a 50-basis-point increase. His scenario allows for another rate hike, with a smaller move providing enough relief to support Bitcoin. The policy backdrop included Fed Governor Christopher Waller’s statement that a 50-basis-point increase should be considered if October inflation came in hot. According to Visser’s interview, that inflation condition was met. Visser pointed to Brent crude returning to its March price and inflation swaps reaching their lows for the year. Those observations formed part of his argument that inflation fears could ease enough to improve the policy outlook. His scenario links a potential Bitcoin recovery to that easing in fears and a smaller December increase. For holders searching why crypto is crashing, the central explanations are rising-rate concerns, investors realizing losses and possible selling linked to pressure in AI stocks. What happens next depends in part on whether those forces ease as the December decision approaches. The break occurred on November 12, 2026. It followed the November 10 move below $73,000 and preceded the later three-month low just above $62,000. CoinGecko recorded that price at 08:20:10 UTC on November 15, 2026. Bitcoin’s accompanying 24-hour change was a decline of 4.97%. Visser points to the December rate decision. He expects further increases but believes a move smaller than 50 basis points could give Bitcoin room to rally. It means a half-percentage-point increase in the Fed’s policy rate. Visser’s potential recovery scenario involves a smaller December increase while his broader outlook still includes additional tightening. Check names February and late June of 2026, along with late 2022. He uses those periods as reference points for his assessment of Bitcoin after the decline. The balance is dated October 31, 2026. The production reduction was attributed mainly to an approximately 11.8% increase in mining difficulty during October. Managed hashrate edged up to 19.5 exahashes per second from 19.4 EH/s in September, leaving the company’s mining power relatively stable despite lower output. For the miner, the challenge was maintaining accumulation as greater mining difficulty weighed on production.

Visser’s bearish concern is that inflation fears keep interest-rate expectations elevated. He cited the rise in two-year yields as a force behind the decline and said the liquidity backdrop needed to improve for Bitcoin to turn around. His interpretation differs from Arthur Hayes’s view that higher interest rates could push wealthy investors toward Bitcoin and other assets.

Check’s description of investors realizing losses highlights a continuing source of potential selling. Buyers who entered after the September advance may remain under pressure as Bitcoin trades back in the $60,000s. Lee’s margin-call suggestion raises a second possible vulnerability: stress in AI-related investments spilling into crypto holdings. A durable recovery would have to contend with those pressures after the initial rebound. The strongest bullish argument in Visser’s account is relief from rate fears; the clearest threat is that inflation concerns keep the tightening outlook in place.

Visser said the next rally could find its catalyst in December if the Fed avoids a 50-basis-point increase. His scenario allows for another rate hike, with a smaller move providing enough relief to support Bitcoin. The policy backdrop included Fed Governor Christopher Waller’s statement that a 50-basis-point increase should be considered if October inflation came in hot. According to Visser’s interview, that inflation condition was met.

Visser pointed to Brent crude returning to its March price and inflation swaps reaching their lows for the year. Those observations formed part of his argument that inflation fears could ease enough to improve the policy outlook. His scenario links a potential Bitcoin recovery to that easing in fears and a smaller December increase. For holders searching why crypto is crashing, the central explanations are rising-rate concerns, investors realizing losses and possible selling linked to pressure in AI stocks. What happens next depends in part on whether those forces ease as the December decision approaches.

It means a half-percentage-point increase in the Fed’s policy rate. Visser’s potential recovery scenario involves a smaller December increase while his broader outlook still includes additional tightening.

From November 5 to November 11, the funds recorded five straight days of net outflows: That comes to about $1.44 billion in five sessions. BlackRock’s IBIT alone lost $269.7 million on November 11, its ninth outflow session in a row, which brings its total for the run to about $2 billion. The crypto sell-off is part of a wider pullback from risk: Bitcoin’s market value has fallen to about $1.38 trillion and it now sits about 46% below its record high of around $126,198, set in October 2025. extraction.body: The crypto market ended Thursday night with its steepest daily loss in weeks. At 07:30 UTC on November 13, 2026, bitcoin traded at about $69,000, down a little over 6% in 24 hours, after touching an intraday low of $67,922 according to CoinGecko. Total crypto market capitalization fell about 7% over the same period to roughly $2.35 trillion. If you are asking why is crypto down today, our running explainer tracks every sell-off of the year. This crypto news roundup sets out what is driving the move: forced selling of leveraged positions, outflows from US spot bitcoin ETFs, a strong dollar with rising Treasury yields, and thin order books. Our first report with key price levels is Bitcoin price falls below $70,000. Crypto news at a glance: bitcoin, ether, BNB and XRP this morning Losses run through the large caps, but not evenly. As of 07:30 UTC, per CoinGecko data: Bitcoin: about $69,000, down 6.2% in 24 hours. According to CoinDesk, ether fell below $2,000 for the first time since August; see Ethereum price below $2,000. BNB: about $634, down 5.9%; more in BNB falls below $650. XRP: about $1.03, down 1.3%, with an intraday low just under $1. XRP and Solana fell less than bitcoin and ether over the past day, but both had already lost more earlier in the week: over seven days XRP is down a little over 14% and Solana just over 10%, per CoinGecko. For medium-term scenarios, see our bitcoin price prediction and ethereum price prediction. Liquidations: more than $1.3 billion in leveraged bets wiped out in 24 hours A liquidation is the forced closing of a leveraged position by an exchange once the posted collateral no longer covers it. Based on CoinGlass data analysed by CoinDesk early Friday, more than $1.3 billion in crypto futures were liquidated within 24 hours, about $677 million of them on bitcoin. The largest single liquidation was a long bitcoin position worth more than $31 million on Hyperliquid, according to the same report. Later snapshots reported by KuCoin News and Bloomingbit reached up to $1.62 billion. The defensible range is therefore $1.3 billion to $1.6 billion, most of it from traders who had bet on rising prices. Bitcoin ETF outflows: why US funds are weighing on the price The second driver is US fund flows. According to Cointelegraph, BlackRock's IBIT recorded more than $2 billion in net outflows over nine consecutive sessions through Wednesday. Across all US spot bitcoin ETFs, nearly $1.44 billion left over five sessions. Preliminary Farside data showed a further $47.7 million in net outflows on Thursday, with BlackRock and Fidelity figures still pending. When investors redeem shares, the fund generally has to sell bitcoin, which adds to the pressure from liquidations. Dollar and Treasury yields: the macro pressure on crypto CoinDesk points to a strong US dollar: the Dollar Index rose above 103, its highest since April 2025. After a hotter-than-expected October CPI reading, markets also raised the odds of a Federal Reserve rate hike in December. Per Cointelegraph, data from 10x Research show bitcoin fell 5.9% between November 5 and 12, while the 10-year Treasury yield climbed above 5%. Order book depth: why the bitcoin price swings so hard Order book depth measures how many buy and sell orders sit close to the current price. The thinner it is, the further a large sale moves the market. According to Talos, cited by Cointelegraph, bitcoin order book depth across major exchanges stood at $72 million on November 9, roughly 33% below normal. Talos senior research associate Tanay Ved said liquidity remains thin while leverage stays elevated, leaving the market vulnerable to sharp moves in either direction. With few resting orders, even medium-sized sales trigger large price jumps. Fear and Greed Index at 20: extreme fear in the crypto market Sentiment matches the price action. The Crypto Fear and Greed Index from alternative.me reads 20 on Friday, which is "Extreme Fear", down from 28 the day before. Cointelegraph notes this is the lowest reading since July 8. How the market behaved after earlier spells of extreme fear is covered in our Fear and Greed Index history. CoinDesk also reported that the overnight sell-off accelerated on news of renewed military escalation in the Middle East.

Bitcoin dropped to $63,863 on November 15, 2026—a 4.97% fall in 24 hours, according to CoinGecko.
The decline pushed BTC ▼ $65,498.00 to a three-month low just above $62,000, raising the question of where relief might come.
Bitcoin and several of the largest alternative cryptocurrencies suffered substantial weekly declines.
Bitcoin’s 17% loss was severe, while the three other tokens each surrendered more than a fifth of their value over the week.

Bitcoin and ether subsequently rebounded after another sharp drop.
