Bitcoin dropped to $63,863 on November 15, 2026—a 4.97% fall in 24 hours, according to CoinGecko. The damage spread fast. Ether, XRP ▼ $0.9702 and solana each lost 22% over the week, while Bitcoin fell 17%, as bond yields climbed, investors locked in losses and margin calls from the AI selloff cascaded through portfolios. The decline pushed BTC ▼ $65,498.00 to a three-month low just above $62,000, raising the question of where relief might come. Analysts and strategists point to the December Fed decision as a potential turning point in this crypto market downturn. Bitcoin and several of the largest alternative cryptocurrencies suffered substantial weekly declines. Ether, XRP and solana each lost 22%, putting their weekly falls five percentage points beyond Bitcoin’s 17% decline. The token touched a fresh three-month low just above $62,000 as the selling continued. That brought BTC back into the broad price territory where analyst James Check said some investors had hesitated to buy during the summer. BTC fell below $73,000 on November 10. The break below $72,000 on November 12 marked another deterioration, followed by the later three-month low. Bitcoin and ether subsequently rebounded after another sharp drop. By November 15, however, BTC remained below $64,000 and its 24-hour change was still negative. The bounce occurred within a downturn that had already inflicted double-digit weekly losses across several major tokens. Speaking with Anthony Pompliano on the Pomp Podcast, Wall Street veteran Jordi Visser argued that crypto investors had underestimated the bond market’s influence on Bitcoin. He cited a weekly increase of 35 basis points in two-year yields and connected that move to BTC’s decline. Visser’s explanation centers on inflation fears and interest-rate expectations . He argued that those fears need to ease for the Fed to stop raising rates, and that a change in the liquidity backdrop would help Bitcoin recover. His outlook still included further tightening—at least two more rate increases, he said, with December’s size mattering enough to change Bitcoin’s direction. Check described the decline as the fourth capitulation event since Bitcoin’s all-time high. His assessment focused on investors who passed on BTC in the mid-to-high $60,000s during the summer, bought in the $80,000s in September and were now selling at a loss. Fundstrat’s Tom Lee offered another source of pressure: margin calls associated with the AI and Nvidia selloff, particularly among Asian retail investors. His explanation points to investors selling crypto while facing pressure elsewhere in their portfolios. Visser placed a different emphasis on that connection, saying the AI selloff had affected Bitcoin the previous week but considered the liquidity side of the market more relevant to its immediate direction. Check’s account traces a shift from hesitation to chasing higher prices and then realizing losses. Investors who wanted cheaper Bitcoin during the summer eventually entered after BTC moved into the $80,000s, only to sell when it returned to prices they had previously considered attractive. For that group, the November decline erased the benefit of waiting for stronger momentum before buying. Check’s explanation centers on the decisions of those late entrants and their willingness to exit after the market reversed. Check characterized Bitcoin’s position as a deep-value zone, comparing it with earlier periods in February and late June of 2026, as well as late 2022. That valuation judgment does not mean the bottom is in. His view that investors gradually entering at such levels could eventually become profitable remains a forward-looking assessment, with further losses still possible before any recovery. The weekly declines covered Bitcoin, ether, XRP and solana, spreading the damage across several of the market’s largest assets. Bitcoin’s 17% loss was severe, while the three other tokens each surrendered more than a fifth of their value over the week. The five-percentage-point gap shows how much harder those assets fell over the same interval. The September purchases described by Check occurred in the $80,000s. Selling in the $60,000s locks in a loss for those positions, adding an investor-behavior dimension to the discussion of yields and monetary policy. His assessment also explains why a return to an earlier price range can feel very different to different holders. The immediate recovery challenge therefore has both a macroeconomic and a holder component. Visser looks for relief from interest-rate fears, while Check identifies investors already abandoning positions after the reversal. Singapore-based, Nasdaq-listed miner BitFuFu held 1,454 BTC at October’s end, up from 1,388 BTC at September’s end. That 66-BTC increase represented 4.8% month-over-month growth. The company had increased its Bitcoin holdings for three consecutive months. Chairman and CEO Leo Lu reiterated its commitment to increasing those holdings, giving the operating update a longer-term treasury focus. These were October balances, preceding the later increase in November selling pressure. BitFuFu mined 137 BTC in October, down from 167 BTC in September—a decline of about 18%. Its production consisted of 67 BTC from self-mining and 70 BTC from cloud mining. The production reduction was attributed mainly to an approximately 11.8% increase in mining difficulty during October. Managed hashrate edged up to 19.5 exahashes per second from 19.4 EH/s in September, leaving the company’s mining power relatively stable despite lower output. For the miner, the challenge was maintaining accumulation as greater mining difficulty weighed on production. Visser’s bearish concern is that inflation fears keep interest-rate expectations elevated. He cited the rise in two-year yields as a force behind the decline and said the liquidity backdrop needed to improve for Bitcoin to turn around. His interpretation differs from Arthur Hayes’s view that higher interest rates could push wealthy investors toward Bitcoin and other assets. Check’s description of investors realizing losses highlights a continuing source of potential selling. Buyers who entered after the September advance may remain under pressure as Bitcoin trades back in the $60,000s. Lee’s margin-call suggestion raises a second possible vulnerability: stress in AI-related investments spilling into crypto holdings. A durable recovery would have to contend with those pressures after the initial rebound. The strongest bullish argument in Visser’s account is relief from rate fears; the clearest threat is that inflation concerns keep the tightening outlook in place. Visser said the next rally could find its catalyst in December if the Fed avoids a 50-basis-point increase. His scenario allows for another rate hike, with a smaller move providing enough relief to support Bitcoin. The policy backdrop included Fed Governor Christopher Waller’s statement that a 50-basis-point increase should be considered if October inflation came in hot. According to Visser’s interview, that inflation condition was met. Visser pointed to Brent crude returning to its March price and inflation swaps reaching their lows for the year. Those observations formed part of his argument that inflation fears could ease enough to improve the policy outlook. His scenario links a potential Bitcoin recovery to that easing in fears and a smaller December increase. For holders searching why crypto is crashing, the central explanations are rising-rate concerns, investors realizing losses and possible selling linked to pressure in AI stocks. What happens next depends in part on whether those forces ease as the December decision approaches. The break occurred on November 12, 2026. It followed the November 10 move below $73,000 and preceded the later three-month low just above $62,000. CoinGecko recorded that price at 08:20:10 UTC on November 15, 2026. Bitcoin’s accompanying 24-hour change was a decline of 4.97%. Visser points to the December rate decision. He expects further increases but believes a move smaller than 50 basis points could give Bitcoin room to rally. It means a half-percentage-point increase in the Fed’s policy rate. Visser’s potential recovery scenario involves a smaller December increase while his broader outlook still includes additional tightening. Check names February and late June of 2026, along with late 2022. He uses those periods as reference points for his assessment of Bitcoin after the decline. The balance is dated October 31, 2026. passages: The marks attained by the top scorer ⁠on South Korea’s national exam for aspiring tax accountants this year seemed too good to be true.
On Sunday, sceptics were ⁠proven right when he ⁠confessed to ​using generative AI to cheat.
His score of 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, with only one wrong answer out of 160 questions, had sparked accusations that he cheated using smart glasses, which he initially denied.
The scandal has followed months of speculation after he scored near-perfect marks on hundreds of questions over two exams ⁠taken in April and July.
He said he had cheated by ‌taking photos of the exam questions with a microcamera, sending them to an AI tool and checking the answers on a smartphone.

The Seoul metropolitan police agency said: “We received a written confession through the test taker’s lawyer this morning regarding cheating on the tax accountant exam,” adding that the case had been assigned to investigators.
It comes just days before Thursday’s annual national college entrance exam, ‌a high-pressure event for which many South ​Korean students will have spent much of their lives preparing.

passages: The top scorer in South Korea’s 2026 certified tax accountant exam admitted on Sunday, 15 November, to cheating in both rounds of the test using a miniature camera, a smartphone and generative AI, Yonhap reported.
In introductory tax law, one of four first-round papers sat in April, the candidate scored 100.
The 16,856 candidates averaged 30.18 points and 74% scored below the 40-point subject cut-off, according to HRD Korea scoring statistics reported by the Hankyoreh on 12 November.
By our arithmetic, only 34 candidates, or 0.2%, scored 70 or more on that paper.

HRD Korea said in a statement on 15 November that it would file a complaint against the candidate for obstruction of business , apologised for failing to prevent the cheating, and would work with the finance ministry and the National Tax Service on steps including cancelling the final pass, the Electric Times reported.

Its data submitted to the National Assembly counted five cases this year of cheating with smart glasses at written-test sites of national qualification exams, including the information processing engineer exam, the Hankyoreh reported.
Under the law, a person found to have cheated can have the exam invalidated and be barred from taking it for five years from the date the sanction is imposed.
As we read it, a licence is worth what its test filters out.

facts.text: The marks attained by the top scorer ⁠on South Korea’s national exam for aspiring tax accountants this year seemed too good to be true.
On Sunday, sceptics were ⁠proven right when he ⁠confessed to ​using generative AI to cheat.
His score of 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, with only one wrong answer out of 160 questions, had sparked accusations that he cheated using smart glasses, which he initially denied.
The scandal has followed months of speculation after he scored near-perfect marks on hundreds of questions over two exams ⁠taken in April and July.
He said he had cheated by ‌taking photos of the exam questions with a microcamera, sending them to an AI tool and checking the answers on a smartphone.

The Seoul metropolitan police agency said: “We received a written confession through the test taker’s lawyer this morning regarding cheating on the tax accountant exam,” adding that the case had been assigned to investigators.
It comes just days before Thursday’s annual national college entrance exam, ‌a high-pressure event for which many South ​Korean students will have spent much of their lives preparing.

The top scorer in South Korea’s 2026 certified tax accountant exam admitted on Sunday, 15 November, to cheating in both rounds of the test using a miniature camera, a smartphone and generative AI, Yonhap reported.
In introductory tax law, one of four first-round papers sat in April, the candidate scored 100.
The 16,856 candidates averaged 30.18 points and 74% scored below the 40-point subject cut-off, according to HRD Korea scoring statistics reported by the Hankyoreh on 12 November.
By our arithmetic, only 34 candidates, or 0.2%, scored 70 or more on that paper.

HRD Korea said in a statement on 15 November that it would file a complaint against the candidate for obstruction of business , apologised for failing to prevent the cheating, and would work with the finance ministry and the National Tax Service on steps including cancelling the final pass, the Electric Times reported.

Its data submitted to the National Assembly counted five cases this year of cheating with smart glasses at written-test sites of national qualification exams, including the information processing engineer exam, the Hankyoreh reported.
Under the law, a person found to have cheated can have the exam invalidated and be barred from taking it for five years from the date the sanction is imposed.

extraction.body: WASHINGTON — A White House security specialist has been suspended without pay for defying her supervisor Carl Kline, less than a week after NBC News reported Kline approved Jared Kushner for top secret clearance over the objections of career staff. The specialist, Tricia Newbold, had filed a discrimination complaint against Kline three months ago. Newbold's two-week suspension from the White House security office was for failure to supervise, failure to follow instructions and defiance of authority, according to the suspension decision notice obtained by NBC News. Security office chief Crede Bailey first proposed the suspension on Dec. Wednesday's notice is signed by Bailey and mentions that in Newbold's 18-year career she has not faced any "prior formal disciplinary action." The document also harshly criticizes Newbold for her "defiance" and notes that Newbold said she would "continue to do what is best for the Executive Office of the President." In the notice, the chief security officer denies that the suspension has anything to do with Newbold's Equal Employment Opportunity Commission complaint. Newbold's lawyer, Ed Passman, considers her a whistleblower and said he believes the administrative charges were brought as payback for her decision to file the complaint against Kline. "It's clearly reprisal for her whistleblowing," Passman said. "[It] has no basis in merit whatsoever." Newbold told NBC News, "I confidently feel that this is completely unwarranted and I am also confident that I have done nothing wrong, every decision I and my team have made have always been in the best interest of the United States," she said. "There is no compromise of personal identifiable information or sensitive information." Asked about Newbold's suspension, White House press secretary Sarah Sanders said, "We don't comment on personnel issues." Kline was the subject of an NBC News article last week that revealed he had approved Kushner's top-secret clearance after it was rejected by two career White House security specialists. The pair had made the decision to deny Kushner the clearance after an FBI background check raised concerns about potential foreign influence on him, two sources familiar with the matter told NBC News. On Thursday, two House Democrats wrote White House Chief of Staff Mick Mulvaney asking that Kushner's security clearance be revoked immediately. Don Beyer of Virginia and Ted Lieu of California said in their letter that in addition to Kushner, the White House has ignored similar questions about Ivanka Trump's security clearance despite her involvement in a Trump Tower Moscow project. In her EEOC complaint, Newbold, who has a rare form of dwarfism, accused Kline of discriminating against her because of her height. Her complaint states that, in December 2017, Kline moved security files to a new location that were too high and out of her reach. "You have people, have them get you the files you need; or you can ask me," he told Newbold, according to her complaint. Two sources who did not want to be identified confirmed that Kline had moved files out of Newbold's reach.

extraction.body: Few things are more unsettling for a security clearance holder than being told that their clearance has been suspended. One day, you are performing your regular duties on a classified contract or government assignment. The next, your security officer informs you that you can no longer access classified information. The immediate questions are understandable: Have I lost my clearance permanently? Will I be fired? How long will this last? Can I challenge the decision? The most important point is that a security clearance suspension is not necessarily a final denial or revocation. However, it can have serious employment consequences, and what happens during the following weeks or months can significantly affect the ultimate outcome. A suspension generally means that the government has temporarily restricted an individual’s eligibility or access while security concerns are evaluated. This can occur when information raises questions about an individual’s continued eligibility to access classified information. Common reasons may include financial problems , arrests or criminal allegations, drug involvement, foreign contacts, mishandling classified information, dishonesty, or other concerns under the National Security Adjudicative Guidelines in Security Executive Agent Directive 4 ( SEAD 4 ). Importantly, a suspension does not necessarily mean that the allegations have been proven. The government may need additional information before determining whether the individual should retain clearance eligibility. There is also an important distinction between an agency or employer temporarily suspending access to classified information and the government formally suspending clearance eligibility. These actions are not always identical, and the precise status matters. Possibly, but it depends on your position and employer. If your job requires access to classified information, a suspension may prevent you from performing some or all of your normal duties. A government contractor might be temporarily assigned to unclassified work, placed on leave, transferred to another project, or terminated if the company cannot accommodate the loss of clearance access. Unfortunately, an employer does not necessarily have to wait for a final clearance revocation before taking employment action, subject to applicable laws and policies. Federal employees may face similar practical problems, although their employment rights and the procedures governing reassignment, leave, or removal can differ. Only a few limited types of federal employee clearance appeals can be taken through the Merit Systems Protection Board ( MSPB ) appeals process. This is one reason a temporary suspension can become a significant career problem even if the government eventually restores eligibility. The next step usually involves further review of the information that led to the suspension. For Department of Defense contractors, the security office may report adverse information through the Defense Information System for Security ( DISS ). The government may then review the incident and determine whether additional investigation or adjudicative action is necessary. Depending on the circumstances, the individual may be asked to provide documents, complete an updated SF-86 , participate in an interview, or respond to specific security concerns. For example, if the suspension involves delinquent debts, the government may seek updated credit information, repayment agreements, or evidence that the financial problems are being resolved. If the issue involves criminal allegations, the government may seek police reports, court records, or information concerning the disposition of the case. The purpose is to determine whether the underlying security concerns can be resolved or mitigated. Not necessarily. A suspension does not automatically mean that an SOR will be issued. Some cases are resolved after additional information is reviewed, without proceeding to a formal adverse clearance determination. However, if the government determines that the concerns remain unresolved and proposes to deny or revoke eligibility, the individual may receive an SOR or another form of formal notice under the applicable agency procedures. Other cases may take months, particularly when they involve criminal investigations, disputed allegations, extensive financial issues, or additional background investigation. For the clearance holder, the uncertainty can be difficult because employment decisions may occur long before the security review is completed. The available options depend on the agency and the type of suspension. A temporary suspension generally does not carry the same administrative appeal rights as a final denial or revocation. For many clearance holders, the immediate priority is providing accurate information and documentation that addresses the government’s concerns. If the government later proposes an adverse eligibility determination, formal response and appeal procedures may become available. For many contractors, those proceedings can involve the Defense Office of Hearings and Appeals ( DOHA ). Federal employees, military personnel, and Intelligence Community personnel may follow different procedures. It is important not to assume that every suspension can immediately be appealed through the same process used to challenge a final clearance revocation. This can create another complication. Suppose a contractor’s clearance eligibility is under review, but the employer terminates the employee before the government completes its adjudication. Depending on the status of the case and the applicable procedures, the government may no longer have the necessary employment or sponsorship relationship to continue processing the matter. In some DoD cases, this can result in a Loss of Jurisdiction ( LOJ ) status. LOJ is not the same as a formal denial or revocation. However, it can create significant obstacles when the individual attempts to return to cleared employment. A new employer may need to establish the appropriate security affiliation and request additional government action before the individual can resume classified work. For this reason, individuals should pay close attention to the status of their eligibility if their employment ends during a pending security review. In some cases, providing accurate and persuasive mitigating evidence during the initial review can help resolve concerns before the matter reaches formal denial or revocation proceedings. Yes. A suspended clearance or access authorization may be restored when the responsible security authorities determine that the concerns have been sufficiently resolved and the applicable requirements for access are satisfied. For example, a financial issue may be resolved through documentation of repayment arrangements and improved financial stability. A disputed criminal allegation may be clarified through investigative records or other credible evidence. However, reinstatement is not automatic simply because an employee believes the allegations are unfounded or because an employer wants the individual to return to work. The responsible government agency must make the necessary determination, and the employer or agency must verify that the individual is authorized to resume access. extraction.body: WASHINGTON — A White House security specialist has been suspended without pay for defying her supervisor Carl Kline, less than a week after NBC News reported Kline approved Jared Kushner for top secret clearance over the objections of career staff. The specialist, Tricia Newbold, had filed a discrimination complaint against Kline three months ago. Newbold's two-week suspension from the White House security office was for failure to supervise, failure to follow instructions and defiance of authority, according to the suspension decision notice obtained by NBC News. Security office chief Crede Bailey first proposed the suspension on Dec. Wednesday's notice is signed by Bailey and mentions that in Newbold's 18-year career she has not faced any "prior formal disciplinary action." The document also harshly criticizes Newbold for her "defiance" and notes that Newbold said she would "continue to do what is best for the Executive Office of the President." In the notice, the chief security officer denies that the suspension has anything to do with Newbold's Equal Employment Opportunity Commission complaint. Newbold's lawyer, Ed Passman, considers her a whistleblower and said he believes the administrative charges were brought as payback for her decision to file the complaint against Kline. "It's clearly reprisal for her whistleblowing," Passman said. "[It] has no basis in merit whatsoever." Newbold told NBC News, "I confidently feel that this is completely unwarranted and I am also confident that I have done nothing wrong, every decision I and my team have made have always been in the best interest of the United States," she said. "There is no compromise of personal identifiable information or sensitive information." Asked about Newbold's suspension, White House press secretary Sarah Sanders said, "We don't comment on personnel issues." Kline was the subject of an NBC News article last week that revealed he had approved Kushner's top-secret clearance after it was rejected by two career White House security specialists. The pair had made the decision to deny Kushner the clearance after an FBI background check raised concerns about potential foreign influence on him, two sources familiar with the matter told NBC News. On Thursday, two House Democrats wrote White House Chief of Staff Mick Mulvaney asking that Kushner's security clearance be revoked immediately. Don Beyer of Virginia and Ted Lieu of California said in their letter that in addition to Kushner, the White House has ignored similar questions about Ivanka Trump's security clearance despite her involvement in a Trump Tower Moscow project. In her EEOC complaint, Newbold, who has a rare form of dwarfism, accused Kline of discriminating against her because of her height. Her complaint states that, in December 2017, Kline moved security files to a new location that were too high and out of her reach. "You have people, have them get you the files you need; or you can ask me," he told Newbold, according to her complaint. Two sources who did not want to be identified confirmed that Kline had moved files out of Newbold's reach.

extraction.body: Few things are more unsettling for a security clearance holder than being told that their clearance has been suspended. One day, you are performing your regular duties on a classified contract or government assignment. The next, your security officer informs you that you can no longer access classified information. The immediate questions are understandable: Have I lost my clearance permanently? Will I be fired? How long will this last? Can I challenge the decision? The most important point is that a security clearance suspension is not necessarily a final denial or revocation. However, it can have serious employment consequences, and what happens during the following weeks or months can significantly affect the ultimate outcome. A suspension generally means that the government has temporarily restricted an individual’s eligibility or access while security concerns are evaluated. This can occur when information raises questions about an individual’s continued eligibility to access classified information. Common reasons may include financial problems , arrests or criminal allegations, drug involvement, foreign contacts, mishandling classified information, dishonesty, or other concerns under the National Security Adjudicative Guidelines in Security Executive Agent Directive 4 ( SEAD 4 ). Importantly, a suspension does not necessarily mean that the allegations have been proven. The government may need additional information before determining whether the individual should retain clearance eligibility. There is also an important distinction between an agency or employer temporarily suspending access to classified information and the government formally suspending clearance eligibility. These actions are not always identical, and the precise status matters. Possibly, but it depends on your position and employer. If your job requires access to classified information, a suspension may prevent you from performing some or all of your normal duties. A government contractor might be temporarily assigned to unclassified work, placed on leave, transferred to another project, or terminated if the company cannot accommodate the loss of clearance access. Unfortunately, an employer does not necessarily have to wait for a final clearance revocation before taking employment action, subject to applicable laws and policies. Federal employees may face similar practical problems, although their employment rights and the procedures governing reassignment, leave, or removal can differ. Only a few limited types of federal employee clearance appeals can be taken through the Merit Systems Protection Board ( MSPB ) appeals process. This is one reason a temporary suspension can become a significant career problem even if the government eventually restores eligibility. The next step usually involves further review of the information that led to the suspension. For Department of Defense contractors, the security office may report adverse information through the Defense Information System for Security ( DISS ). The government may then review the incident and determine whether additional investigation or adjudicative action is necessary. Depending on the circumstances, the individual may be asked to provide documents, complete an updated SF-86 , participate in an interview, or respond to specific security concerns. For example, if the suspension involves delinquent debts, the government may seek updated credit information, repayment agreements, or evidence that the financial problems are being resolved. If the issue involves criminal allegations, the government may seek police reports, court records, or information concerning the disposition of the case. The purpose is to determine whether the underlying security concerns can be resolved or mitigated. Not necessarily. A Statement of Reasons (SOR) is a formal document identifying security concerns that may support a proposed denial or revocation of clearance eligibility. A suspension does not automatically mean that an SOR will be issued. Some cases are resolved after additional information is reviewed, without proceeding to a formal adverse clearance determination. However, if the government determines that the concerns remain unresolved and proposes to deny or revoke eligibility, the individual may receive an SOR or another form of formal notice under the applicable agency procedures. Other cases may take months, particularly when they involve criminal investigations, disputed allegations, extensive financial issues, or additional background investigation. For the clearance holder, the uncertainty can be difficult because employment decisions may occur long before the security review is completed. The available options depend on the agency and the type of suspension. A temporary suspension generally does not carry the same administrative appeal rights as a final denial or revocation. For many clearance holders, the immediate priority is providing accurate information and documentation that addresses the government’s concerns. If the government later proposes an adverse eligibility determination, formal response and appeal procedures may become available. For many contractors, those proceedings can involve the Defense Office of Hearings and Appeals ( DOHA ). Federal employees, military personnel, and Intelligence Community personnel may follow different procedures. It is important not to assume that every suspension can immediately be appealed through the same process used to challenge a final clearance revocation. This can create another complication. Suppose a contractor’s clearance eligibility is under review, but the employer terminates the employee before the government completes its adjudication. Depending on the status of the case and the applicable procedures, the government may no longer have the necessary employment or sponsorship relationship to continue processing the matter. In some DoD cases, this can result in a Loss of Jurisdiction ( LOJ ) status. LOJ is not the same as a formal denial or revocation. However, it can create significant obstacles when the individual attempts to return to cleared employment. A new employer may need to establish the appropriate security affiliation and request additional government action before the individual can resume classified work. For this reason, individuals should pay close attention to the status of their eligibility if their employment ends during a pending security review. In some cases, providing accurate and persuasive mitigating evidence during the initial review can help resolve concerns before the matter reaches formal denial or revocation proceedings. Yes. A suspended clearance or access authorization may be restored when the responsible security authorities determine that the concerns have been sufficiently resolved and the applicable requirements for access are satisfied. For example, a financial issue may be resolved through documentation of repayment arrangements and improved financial stability. A disputed criminal allegation may be clarified through investigative records or other credible evidence. However, reinstatement is not automatic simply because an employee believes the allegations are unfounded or because an employer wants the individual to return to work. The responsible government agency must make the necessary determination, and the employer or agency must verify that the individual is authorized to resume access. The answer depends on the nature of the allegations, the agency involved, the type of access, and whether the government needs additional information to resolve its concerns. A suspension is serious, but it is not necessarily permanent. Some suspensions are resolved without a formal denial or revocation. Others lead to additional investigation, a Statement of Reasons, or administrative appeal proceedings. A suspended clearance does not necessarily mean the end of a cleared career. But how you respond to the suspension can have a lasting impact on what happens next.

passages: It was the resignation heard across the world.
Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down .
“It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news.
Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures.

Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition.

If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.)
“When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said.
Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking.
“Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, founder of the hardware company Ghost, said.
Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang.

extraction.body: It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down . “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news. Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor , pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital. Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition. “Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch. Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term. Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes , especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out . Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street. “She’s much more conservative,” one investor said of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.” Nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, founder of the hardware company Ghost, said. facts.text: It was the resignation heard across the world.
Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down .
“It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news.
Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures.

Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition.

If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.)
“When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said.
Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking.
“Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, founder of the hardware company Ghost, said.
Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang.

extraction.body: It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down . “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news. Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor , pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital. Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition. “Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch. Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term. Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes , especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out . Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street. “She’s much more conservative,” one investor said of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.” Nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, founder of the hardware company Ghost, said. For instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe’s rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal . “Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya said of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.” It’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position. If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.) Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang. Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Big Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he said. CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs. While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did. Under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said. The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations. Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations. “When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said. Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking. Even so, few believe that Nvidia’s investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom. Though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, said that “founders and leaders must be held accountable,” and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. “That talent will, and must, continue to thrive.” Dominic-Madori Davis is a senior venture capital and startup reporter at TechCrunch. She is based in New York City. You can contact or verify outreach from Dominic by emailing [email protected] or via encrypted message at +1 646 831-7565 on Signal. Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations.

"When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe," Padval said. Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking.
Even so, few believe that Nvidia's investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom.

Though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, said that "founders and leaders must be held accountable," and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. "That talent will, and must, continue to thrive."

sources.title: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
passages: When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed.

In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.”
Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations.
In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations.
In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling.
The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling.
Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China.
A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia.
Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers.

It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.”
Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so.

Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China.

In the meantime, the controversy at Nvidia, Foster says, has fueled support among his colleagues for the rules in the bill: “There will be a lot of political pressure, in the wake of everything that’s happened, on the companies to actually do a very good job of the geographic validation of where the chip actually is.”

“They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public.
Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization.

Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy. When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.” But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them. “They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public. Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling. Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization. In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.” The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers. The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option. Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so. Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling. Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization. In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.” The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers. The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option. Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so. But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled. Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.”

Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.”
But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them.

“They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public.

Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling.
Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization.

In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.”

The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers.

The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option.
Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so.

But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled. Foster told MIT Technology Review he intends to introduce new, stricter legislation in the new year that would offer a workaround. The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified.

In the meantime, the controversy at Nvidia, Foster says, has fueled support among his colleagues for the rules in the bill: “There will be a lot of political pressure, in the wake of everything that’s happened, on the companies to actually do a very good job of the geographic validation of where the chip actually is.”
Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

Blackwell GPUs are banned from export to China or Chinese-owned firms, while the Trump administration allows Nvidia to export the H200, a less powerful chip, provided shipments take a circuitous shipping route that allows the U.S. to claim a 25% tariff.
The apparently widespread access to Blackwell GPUs among Chinese frontier labs shows the magnitude of the problem facing the leading chip designer.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang left the company this week after admitting to his affair with Alice Huang, executive of Megaspeed, a company implicated in smuggling Nvidia chips into China.
White House technology adviser Michael Kratsios said earlier this year that Moonshot had used export-banned Nvidia chips, citing U.S. intelligence sources.

In May, the short-selling research firm Culper published a report arguing that Nvidia had a “ China problem ” because a significant share of its revenue was driven by Chinese demand, either through remote data centers or smuggling in violation of U.S. law.

That doesn’t mean that these models were trained entirely on Nvidia chips, or that export control laws were necessarily violated; the chips could have been in an offshore data center, which has proven a popular way for Chinese firms to access compute and driven an industrial revolution in Malaysia.
Some 600,000 H200 chips are reportedly stockpiled in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment into China.
For now, U.S. companies have limited obligations to track what their customers do with controlled goods like AI chips.

extraction.body: The leading open-weight models developed by Chinese companies were trained on Nvidia chips that the U.S. government restricted from shipping to its largest geopolitical rival, a new research effort claims. The apparently widespread access to Blackwell GPUs among Chinese frontier labs shows the magnitude of the problem facing the leading chip designer. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang left the company this week after admitting to his affair with Alice Huang, executive of Megaspeed, a company implicated in smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Alice Huang has also been alleged to be an agent of China’s intelligence service. While Jensen Huang’s relationships with a customer and two employees have drawn the most public interest, Nvidia’s potential corporate liability for export control violations likely factored into its decision to part ways with Huang. U.S. export controls are intended to protect the country’s leadership in AI capabilities against China, but Huang has long sought to open up that market. Blackwell GPUs are banned from export to China or Chinese-owned firms, while the Trump administration allows Nvidia to export the H200, a less powerful chip, provided shipments take a circuitous shipping route that allows the U.S. to claim a 25% tariff. Will DePue, a former OpenAI researcher who leads the nonprofit research group Unemployment Labs, analyzed the weights — the unique structure — of large language models released openly by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, and Ant Group. The weights still reflect the configurations of the chips used to train them, and DePue was able to find compelling evidence that the most closely watched models, including Moonshot’s Kimi’s K3 releases and DeepSeek’s V4 models, bear fingerprints from training on Blackwell chips. White House technology adviser Michael Kratsios said earlier this year that Moonshot had used export-banned Nvidia chips, citing U.S. intelligence sources. Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization, estimates that about two million advanced chips entered China in 2024 and 2025 through schemes designed to hide their final destination. That doesn’t mean that these models were trained entirely on Nvidia chips, or that export control laws were necessarily violated; the chips could have been in an offshore data center, which has proven a popular way for Chinese firms to access compute and driven an industrial revolution in Malaysia. Epoch’s data estimates that 275,000 Nvidia AI accelerators were imported to Malaysia in 2024 and 2025. However, the ostensible goal of the export bans is to prevent exactly that: Chinese AI labs training on the most powerful chips. China hawks have long called for stronger controls on who uses chips, not just who owns them or where they are installed. “If we care about the U.S. tech edge, it doesn’t make any sense to me that you would not allow Chinese companies to access chips in mainland China or Hong Kong and Macau, but then say, actually, if you just go over to Malaysia, you can do whatever you want,” Sam Bresnick, a researcher at the Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology, told TechCrunch this summer. Megaspeed, the company led by Alice Huang, has been at the center of that trade for several years through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, and has been the subject of investigations by both the U.S. and S i ngaporean government. Friday, Bloomberg also reported that a company with links to Alice Huang was involved in smuggling banned Nvidia chips to a data center in Shanghai. In May, the short-selling research firm Culper published a report arguing that Nvidia had a “ China problem ” because a significant share of its revenue was driven by Chinese demand, either through remote data centers or smuggling in violation of U.S. law. It detailed Megaspeed’s relationship with Nvidia and alleged that Alice Huang’s companies are backed by Chinese firms that are barred from accessing U.S. chips. Ironically, short-seller Culper’s bet against Nvidia wasn’t driven by the expectation of a U.S. government crackdown. Instead, it was focused on the Chinese government’s response to the bans, which was to recommit to its domestic chip industry. If China succeeds, billions of dollars in Chinese demand for Nvidia chips could dry up. Some 600,000 H200 chips are reportedly stockpiled in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment into China. While Chinese companies might want the chips, observers have no consensus on why they haven’t been cleared for import. Graham Webster, a research scholar at Stanford who focuses on U.S.-China technology policy, said he doesn’t buy the idea that holding the chips back would drive domestic production, since demand for chips is so large. Other theories for the hold-up include preparation for a potential trade deal that would involve importing a large volume of U.S. goods, or concerns about potential surveillance technology in the chips. For now, U.S. companies have limited obligations to track what their customers do with controlled goods like AI chips. However, Jensen Huang’s personal and professional entanglements with Alice Huang create a much bigger problem for Nvidia if government investigators confirm that chip smuggling took place and that he was aware of it. Nvidia and Huang have both vouched for Megaspeed’s data centers, saying Nvidia officials had visited them to confirm they were legitimate. The U.S. government’s treatment of Nvidia and Megaspeed is also under scrutiny. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, who oversees the agencies that license chip exports, could reportedly lose his job after reports that his investigators failed to uncover suspicious chip buyers and were too cozy with Nvidia officials. passages: The leading open-weight models developed by Chinese companies were trained on Nvidia chips that the U.S. government restricted from shipping to its largest geopolitical rival, a new research effort claims.

The apparently widespread access to Blackwell GPUs among Chinese frontier labs shows the magnitude of the problem facing the leading chip designer. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang left the company this week after admitting to his affair with Alice Huang, executive of Megaspeed, a company implicated in smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Alice Huang has also been alleged to be an agent of China’s intelligence service.

While Jensen Huang’s relationships with a customer and two employees have drawn the most public interest, Nvidia’s potential corporate liability for export control violations likely factored into its decision to part ways with Huang.

U.S. export controls are intended to protect the country’s leadership in AI capabilities against China, but Huang has long sought to open up that market. Blackwell GPUs are banned from export to China or Chinese-owned firms, while the Trump administration allows Nvidia to export the H200, a less powerful chip, provided shipments take a circuitous shipping route that allows the U.S. to claim a 25% tariff.

Will DePue, a former OpenAI researcher who leads the nonprofit research group Unemployment Labs, analyzed the weights — the unique structure — of large language models released openly by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, and Ant Group. The weights still reflect the configurations of the chips used to train them, and DePue was able to find compelling evidence that the most closely watched models, including Moonshot’s Kimi’s K3 releases and DeepSeek’s V4 models, bear fingerprints from training on Blackwell chips.

White House technology adviser Michael Kratsios said earlier this year that Moonshot had used export-banned Nvidia chips, citing U.S. intelligence sources. Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization, estimates that about two million advanced chips entered China in 2024 and 2025 through schemes designed to hide their final destination.

That doesn’t mean that these models were trained entirely on Nvidia chips, or that export control laws were necessarily violated; the chips could have been in an offshore data center, which has proven a popular way for Chinese firms to access compute and driven an industrial revolution in Malaysia. Epoch’s data estimates that 275,000 Nvidia AI accelerators were imported to Malaysia in 2024 and 2025.

However, the ostensible goal of the export bans is to prevent exactly that: Chinese AI labs training on the most powerful chips. China hawks have long called for stronger controls on who uses chips, not just who owns them or where they are installed.

“If we care about the U.S. tech edge, it doesn’t make any sense to me that you would not allow Chinese companies to access chips in mainland China or Hong Kong and Macau, but then say, actually, if you just go over to Malaysia, you can do whatever you want,” Sam Bresnick, a researcher at the Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology, told TechCrunch this summer.

Megaspeed, the company led by Alice Huang, has been at the center of that trade for several years through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, and has been the subject of investigations by both the U.S. and S i ngaporean government. Friday, Bloomberg also reported that a company with links to Alice Huang was involved in smuggling banned Nvidia chips to a data center in Shanghai.

In May, the short-selling research firm Culper published a report arguing that Nvidia had a “ China problem ” because a significant share of its revenue was driven by Chinese demand, either through remote data centers or smuggling in violation of U.S. law. It detailed Megaspeed’s relationship with Nvidia and alleged that Alice Huang’s companies are backed by Chinese firms that are barred from accessing U.S. chips.

Ironically, short-seller Culper’s bet against Nvidia wasn’t driven by the expectation of a U.S. government crackdown. Instead, it was focused on the Chinese government’s response to the bans, which was to recommit to its domestic chip industry.

If China succeeds, billions of dollars in Chinese demand for Nvidia chips could dry up. Some 600,000 H200 chips are reportedly stockpiled in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment into China. While Chinese companies might want the chips, observers have no consensus on why they haven’t been cleared for import.

Graham Webster, a research scholar at Stanford who focuses on U.S.-China technology policy, said he doesn’t buy the idea that holding the chips back would drive domestic production, since demand for chips is so large. Other theories for the hold-up include preparation for a potential trade deal that would involve importing a large volume of U.S. goods, or concerns about potential surveillance technology in the chips.

For now, U.S. companies have limited obligations to track what their customers do with controlled goods like AI chips. However, Jensen Huang’s personal and professional entanglements with Alice Huang create a much bigger problem for Nvidia if government investigators confirm that chip smuggling took place and that he was aware of it. Nvidia and Huang have both vouched for Megaspeed’s data centers, saying Nvidia officials had visited them to confirm they were legitimate.

The U.S. government’s treatment of Nvidia and Megaspeed is also under scrutiny. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, who oversees the agencies that license chip exports, could reportedly lose his job after reports that his investigators failed to uncover suspicious chip buyers and were too cozy with Nvidia officials.

The outage also knocked out the company’s Copilot AI tools and Defender security screening software, and prevented system administrators from accessing their internal Intune dashboards and features.
Some users reportedly experienced issues with accessing their cloud-based Windows computers.
During that outage, Microsoft blamed a “core authentication configuration” issue that prevented users from accessing the service.

“We’re seeing encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure,” said Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president for Copilot, agents, and platform, in a statement on Friday. “Our teams are reviewing what happened and how we can prevent similar issues going forward.”

extraction.body: Microsoft is slowly recovering from its daylong outage after much of the company’s systems were hit by a cascading software issue. The problems, which started Thursday, were initially flagged as affecting the company’s services in the U.S. and the Americas, but quickly spread around the world, as engineers struggled to recover downed servers. What began as an Outlook email and Teams video conferencing outage soon developed into a full-blown meltdown affecting the company’s cloud services for both consumer and business email, files, and documents. The outage also knocked out the company’s Copilot AI tools and Defender security screening software, and prevented system administrators from accessing their internal Intune dashboards and features. Some users reportedly experienced issues with accessing their cloud-based Windows computers. Microsoft hasn’t yet said what caused the issues, only saying the outage involved “a large number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable.” The company said it continues to investigate the cause. The outage affected a broad range of industries, including TechCrunch’s own email. We’ve reached out to Microsoft for comment about the incident. As of Friday morning on the U.S. East Coast, Microsoft’s Outlook email service had begun to recover and some emails have been trickling in. The recovery comes after engineers initially could not find the cause of the issue that was causing servers in Microsoft’s data centers to fail. Doug Madory, the director of internet analysis at Kentik, a company that monitors internet traffic worldwide, said in a post on Bluesky that traffic was returning to Microsoft’s services after about 18 hours of downtime. Microsoft said in its latest status update on Friday that there was “no evidence of malicious activity associated with this incident,” and later noted that there was “not related to cyber or AI / agents.” That may be some solace for the millions who went without their email and online services yesterday, but the company is likely to face questions about its inability to swiftly recover from an outage of its own making. A Microsoft spokesperson did not respond to our questions asking if the company has the technical means to detect malicious activity, such as logs, or if Microsoft has a way to check what happened. “We’re seeing encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure,” said Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president for Copilot, agents, and platform, in a statement on Friday. “Our teams are reviewing what happened and how we can prevent similar issues going forward.” The last major incident affecting Microsoft services was in September , when a dayslong outage hit Microsoft’s cloud services. During that outage, Microsoft blamed a “core authentication configuration” issue that prevented users from accessing the service. This story was first published on November 12 and has been updated throughout. Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch. He also authors the weekly cybersecurity newsletter, this week in security . He can be reached via encrypted message at zackwhittaker.1337 on Signal. sources.title: ChatGPT’s new Wallet lets AI agents shop and check out for you
passages: On Friday, OpenAI launched a new wallet feature that lets its agents, called dots , help you decide what to buy and then complete the purchase on your behalf.
The option will initially be available to a limited number of U.S.
ChatGPT Pro subscribers, ages 18 and up, with a U.S.-issued Visa, Mastercard, or American Express.

To get started, ChatGPT subscribers add their eligible payment cards to the new ChatGPT Wallet, then ask their dot to help with a purchase. (This setup is a one-time thing; users don’t have to re-enter their payment information every time they buy.) When it’s time to transact, ChatGPT’s Wallet charges the selected card using a payment token, which is a substitute for the user’s actual card details, so that information isn’t shared with either the dot or the merchant.
The addition comes as consumer-facing AI tools are working to find the right product-market fit, in terms of how they can help people be more efficient as they complete various tasks.

While companies like DoorDash and Uber have so far reported low numbers of orders placed by AI agents, Meta’s Muse, which now has over 10 million users, has seen AI-assisted shopping become a top activity on its app.
Other personal AI agents, like Instinct, also support making purchases on users’ behalf.

OpenAI says that users are fully in control of the purchases, as they’re able to review the items, the total, and the payment card that will be used to complete the transaction before the checkout occurs.
In addition, users will approve the purchases directly with a security check like Face ID or a fingerprint, which creates a record of their transaction.
