extraction.body: ChatGPT can now shop for you. On Friday, OpenAI launched a new wallet feature that lets its agents, called dots , help you decide what to buy and then complete the purchase on your behalf. The option will initially be available to a limited number of U.S. ChatGPT Pro subscribers, ages 18 and up, with a U.S.-issued Visa, Mastercard, or American Express. OpenAI says that users are fully in control of the purchases, as they’re able to review the items, the total, and the payment card that will be used to complete the transaction before the checkout occurs. In addition, users will approve the purchases directly with a security check like Face ID or a fingerprint, which creates a record of their transaction. The addition comes as consumer-facing AI tools are working to find the right product-market fit, in terms of how they can help people be more efficient as they complete various tasks. While companies like DoorDash and Uber have so far reported low numbers of orders placed by AI agents, Meta’s Muse, which now has over 10 million users, has seen AI-assisted shopping become a top activity on its app. Other personal AI agents, like Instinct, also support making purchases on users’ behalf. It’s no surprise, then, that OpenAI would want to enter this space more with an agentic shopping feature of its own. To get started, ChatGPT subscribers add their eligible payment cards to the new ChatGPT Wallet, then ask their dot to help with a purchase. (This setup is a one-time thing; users don’t have to re-enter their payment information every time they buy.) When it’s time to transact, ChatGPT’s Wallet charges the selected card using a payment token, which is a substitute for the user’s actual card details, so that information isn’t shared with either the dot or the merchant. The merchant will automatically receive what it needs to fulfill the order from the dot, like the shipping address and contact information, OpenAI says. The company notes that customers who shop via their dots will still be able to earn their credit card rewards and be able to take advantage of protections that typically come with cards, like being able to dispute transactions. The limited availability at launch will allow OpenAI to test and improve the feature and its capabilities before rolling it out more broadly. In the future, the company plans to offer users more control over the feature by allowing them to set spending limits or configure other parameters around purchase categories or time periods, so they can pre-approve purchases that their agent can then handle more autonomously. It also aims to make the agentic shopping feature an option at a broader number of supported retailers. This could be a challenge in some areas, where retailers are blocking AI agents from using their site ; on the shopping front, the largest retailer to ban AI agents is Amazon, as it aims to steer users to its own AI agent, Alexa, instead. To help retailers adapt to agentic commerce, OpenAI also published a Commerce Partner Playbook that offers tools and guidance to sites that want to support customers using agents. extraction.body: ChatGPT can now shop for you. On Friday, OpenAI launched a new wallet feature that lets its agents, called dots , help you decide what to buy and then complete the purchase on your behalf. The option will initially be available to a limited number of U.S. ChatGPT Pro subscribers, ages 18 and up, with a U.S.-issued Visa, Mastercard, or American Express. OpenAI says that users are fully in control of the purchases, as they’re able to review the items, the total, and the payment card that will be used to complete the transaction before the checkout occurs. In addition, users will approve the purchases directly with a security check like Face ID or a fingerprint, which creates a record of their transaction. The addition comes as consumer-facing AI tools are working to find the right product-market fit, in terms of how they can help people be more efficient as they complete various tasks. While companies like DoorDash and Uber have so far reported low numbers of orders placed by AI agents, Meta’s Muse, which now has over 10 million users, has seen AI-assisted shopping become a top activity on its app. Other personal AI agents, like Instinct, also support making purchases on users’ behalf. It’s no surprise, then, that OpenAI would want to enter this space more with an agentic shopping feature of its own. To get started, ChatGPT subscribers add their eligible payment cards to the new ChatGPT Wallet, then ask their dot to help with a purchase. (This setup is a one-time thing; users don’t have to re-enter their payment information every time they buy.) When it’s time to transact, ChatGPT’s Wallet charges the selected card using a payment token, which is a substitute for the user’s actual card details, so that information isn’t shared with either the dot or the merchant. The merchant will automatically receive what it needs to fulfill the order from the dot, like the shipping address and contact information, OpenAI says. The company notes that customers who shop via their dots will still be able to earn their credit card rewards and be able to take advantage of protections that typically come with cards, like being able to dispute transactions. The limited availability at launch will allow OpenAI to test and improve the feature and its capabilities before rolling it out more broadly. In the future, the company plans to offer users more control over the feature by allowing them to set spending limits or configure other parameters around purchase categories or time periods, so they can pre-approve purchases that their agent can then handle more autonomously. It also aims to make the agentic shopping feature an option at a broader number of supported retailers. This could be a challenge in some areas, where retailers are blocking AI agents from using their site ; on the shopping front, the largest retailer to ban AI agents is Amazon, as it aims to steer users to its own AI agent, Alexa, instead. To help retailers adapt to agentic commerce, OpenAI also published a Commerce Partner Playbook that offers tools and guidance to sites that want to support customers using agents. extraction.body: Carpet making may be one of the oldest skilled jobs in the world, but even this traditional industry has begun to adopt the most modern of technologies – Artificial Intelligence (AI). Kukoon Rugs is a family-owned firm that sells online and through some of the biggest retail chains in the UK and Ireland. Chief Executive Paul Vallely says AI allows the business to be more competitive, allowing him to scale up parts of the firm that he previously wouldn't have been able to. "I think every department uses it extensively, pretty much daily. That's from finance through to commercial, marketing, supply chain, and product." While acknowledging the history of his family's business in Newry, he believes technology like AI can only enhance it. "Rug making has been around for thousands of years, and has been around in this area for a long, long time. "The product itself maybe doesn't change too much, but every single bit of the process as to how we design and create the product, market it to the customer, and then get it to the customer, that's fundamentally changing. And that's through AI." Artificial Intelligence has often been accused of having a negative impact on creative industries , but Vallely says this isn't the case. "AI is allowing us to do more accurate, more efficient, and far faster and more thoughtful work, and it's releasing the team's time to look at more analysis, more research, and actually produce more creative work." Vallely says the "biggest impact for us to adopting AI has been, first of all, the removal of some of the very worst and most boring tasks across office-based roles, and probably the excitement and engagement of the team". "I think as everyone started to adopt it and really buy into it, everyone can see opportunities to do work that they were never able to do before to a standard they were never able to do it, and they're really getting their time released to do more." Kukoon is not the only business to harness artificial intelligence in a bid to become more competitive. The manufacturing industry also has a long tradition in Northern Ireland, which became world famous for linen and shipbuilding in the wake of the industrial revolution in the 19th century. Their products are exported to healthcare facilities right across the globe including the US and Australia. Their seats have also featured in television dramas including Emmerdale and Coronation Street. For managing director Martin Tierney, AI has its strengths and weaknesses, but it is now an integrated part of his company's daily work. "AI is not going to replace your job, but someone who knows AI could replace your job, so we're very much embracing it, encouraging people to use it, and doing it within guardrails in a sensible way," Tierney says. While Tierney feels the technology is poor at customer service, it has revolutionised many of the back-office functions. "On all the laborious things like accounting and finance and data and pulling together information from 20 different sources, it's a really good tool to help you get there." Tierney says he likens the power of AI to that of a calculator. "Well, that didn't happen. It allowed the accountant to be more productive, and then Excel came along and made them more productive again. "AI is doing that again, but doing it on steroids." He says implementing AI across his business has not only improved productivity it has also led to new jobs being created. "We have more team members now than we did before, and AI is allowing those people to be more productive, to do more intelligent work, and less of the boring work. "No one likes going upstairs and into a filing cabinet to pull out a drawer and flick through your paper. You know that's not a good use of anyone's time." Tierney says one of the great things about AI is that he doesn't need to have an IT degree to make use of the software. "You just chat to it, say: 'Here's what I'm trying to do, could you help me flesh out this idea?'" While staff at Seating Matters are encouraged to use AI to help solve problems and speed up some of the more mundane tasks, they do operate within guardrails. "We're not putting patient information or financial information on here. "Yes, we can use it to sift through data to help us find an email from six years ago that might be relevant today, but we're doing it in a way that there's always a human at the wheel. It's always checked by someone." There's more on this story on the BBC's The View . The scandal has cast a spotlight on Singapore's success as a chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade. Scott Bessent told CNBC that several government agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months". Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. Kukoon Rugs is a family-owned firm that sells online and through some of the biggest retail chains in the UK and Ireland. Chief Executive Paul Vallely says AI allows the business to be more competitive, allowing him to scale up parts of the firm that he previously wouldn't have been able to. "I think every department uses it extensively, pretty much daily. That's from finance through to commercial, marketing, supply chain, and product." While acknowledging the history of his family's business in Newry, he believes technology like AI can only enhance it. "Rug making has been around for thousands of years, and has been around in this area for a long, long time. "The product itself maybe doesn't change too much, but every single bit of the process as to how we design and create the product, market it to the customer, and then get it to the customer, that's fundamentally changing. And that's through AI." Artificial Intelligence has often been accused of having a negative impact on creative industries , but Vallely says this isn't the case. "AI is allowing us to do more accurate, more efficient, and far faster and more thoughtful work, and it's releasing the team's time to look at more analysis, more research, and actually produce more creative work." Vallely says the "biggest impact for us to adopting AI has been, first of all, the removal of some of the very worst and most boring tasks across office-based roles, and probably the excitement and engagement of the team". "I think as everyone started to adopt it and really buy into it, everyone can see opportunities to do work that they were never able to do before to a standard they were never able to do it, and they're really getting their time released to do more." Kukoon is not the only business to harness artificial intelligence in a bid to become more competitive. The manufacturing industry also has a long tradition in Northern Ireland, which became world famous for linen and shipbuilding in the wake of the industrial revolution in the 19th century. Their products are exported to healthcare facilities right across the globe including the US and Australia. Their seats have also featured in television dramas including Emmerdale and Coronation Street. For managing director Martin Tierney, AI has its strengths and weaknesses, but it is now an integrated part of his company's daily work. "AI is not going to replace your job, but someone who knows AI could replace your job, so we're very much embracing it, encouraging people to use it, and doing it within guardrails in a sensible way," Tierney says. While Tierney feels the technology is poor at customer service, it has revolutionised many of the back-office functions. "On all the laborious things like accounting and finance and data and pulling together information from 20 different sources, it's a really good tool to help you get there." It allowed the accountant to be more productive, and then Excel came along and made them more productive again. "AI is doing that again, but doing it on steroids." He says implementing AI across his business has not only improved productivity it has also led to new jobs being created. "We have more team members now than we did before, and AI is allowing those people to be more productive, to do more intelligent work, and less of the boring work. "No one likes going upstairs and into a filing cabinet to pull out a drawer and flick through your paper. You know that's not a good use of anyone's time." Tierney says one of the great things about AI is that he doesn't need to have an IT degree to make use of the software. "You just chat to it, say: 'Here's what I'm trying to do, could you help me flesh out this idea?'" "We're not putting patient information or financial information on here. "Yes, we can use it to sift through data to help us find an email from six years ago that might be relevant today, but we're doing it in a way that there's always a human at the wheel. It's always checked by someone." There's more on this story on the BBC's The View . The scandal has cast a spotlight on Singapore's success as a chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade. extraction.body: Outsiders had little reason to notice when Nvidia’s longtime chief security officer and head of product security stepped down in August. Just two and a half months later, CEO Jensen Huang himself left the company over growing questions about his extramarital relationships — starting with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company that U.S. investigators suspect of funneling Nvidia chips to China, then widening to reports about two separate affairs with Nvidia employees. At the time, David Reber, who spent four years as CSO and seven at Nvidia overall, said he was leaving for health reasons. “This wasn’t a pivot I had planned. But I know what needs to come first: family and health,” he wrote on LinkedIn in late August, disclosing that he’d been diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson’s more than two years ago. Reber’s replacement, Saša Zdjelar, previously spent 17 years at ExxonMobil in Houston, leaving as a senior IT manager before spending one year at Salesforce and several years at the cybersecurity company ReversingLabs. Zdjelar didn’t respond to questions Thursday about the transition or what the security team knew. Nothing public connects Reber’s or Zdjelar’s role changes to the Megaspeed matter, but it seems fair to wonder what Nvidia’s security team knew about the government’s scrutiny of Megaspeed and about Huang’s relationships, and whether anyone raised concerns. Reber didn’t respond to questions Thursday. Nvidia also has not answered our related questions. Relationships between a CEO and his employees typically fall to HR, legal and the board, not security. But security specialists say any affair — even one inside the office — can give a foreign intelligence service leverage over an exec who wants it kept quiet. And Huang’s relationship with an executive at Megaspeed, a company under federal investigation, wasn’t an office matter at all. (Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.) Still, spotting the clues isn’t easy. The way intelligence services collect information, much of it through everyday conversation rather than hacking, makes it especially difficult for security teams to identify risks, according to retired senior intelligence officer Nicholas Eftimiades, who says he has trained more than 1,000 corporate security professionals. Some people inside Nvidia clearly knew parts of the picture. Nvidia’s top lawyer was engaged with the government’s Megaspeed inquiry more than a year ago, The New York Times reported earlier this week . (Nvidia has said it regularly contacts officials.) Reports about Huang’s relationships with employees suggest colleagues also knew of them, even if the behavior is not expressly forbidden by Nvidia’s code of conduct . The Times cited five Nvidia employees who said he was involved with a vice president who reported directly to him, and Reuters, citing two people, later reported a second relationship. What’s unclear is whether any of that reached security. Even if it had reached Nvidia’s security team, Eftimiades, who wrote Chinese Espionage Operations and Tactics in 2020, said a security team’s resources are often limited. For one thing, they’re often underfunded because, unlike some other cost centers, they don’t drive revenue. It’s astonishingly common for CEOs to answer a security team’s warnings with “not a nickel more than compliance,” he said. Many companies also define security overly narrowly, specialists say. In an opinion piece in The Hill , Don Aviv, CEO of the corporate investigations firm Interfor International, and author Jeremy Hurewitz, wrote, “Too many companies still approach security primarily as a matter of protecting facilities, preventing cyberattacks, and responding to physical threats.” The two argued that “[s]ecurity teams need to pay greater attention to insider threats, including the cultivation of executives and employees by foreign intelligence services, suspicious business relationships, conflicts of interest and attempts to obtain sensitive information through trusted personal contacts.” It would be surprising if Nvidia’s security team didn’t have a more expansive remit than most companies given its scale and business partners, but it’s possible. In fairness, some of it is simply beyond what any team can do. Speaking generally, not about Huang, Eftimiades offered a hypothetical in which a CEO complains that he can’t do something because “I’m fighting a board who doesn’t want to do this.” That tells an intelligence asset who the obstacle is. The service then asks, “Who’s the sticking point here?” and looks for ways into that person’s email and phone. What a rival intelligence service wants is often less technology than policy insight, including who’s pushing to change export rules and who the biggest blocker is. “Intel world tends to be like cancer,” he said. “Once it gets into the body, it looks to spread and looks to reach out.” The playbook isn’t new, Eftimiades added, “particularly for China.” Any executive dealing with the country “will tell you that they’ve been approached.” He said there are also “tons of diplomat stories” of U.S. diplomats walking into a hotel room to find a woman on the bed. He said what’s newer compared with Soviet era spying is the relationships these services cultivate now often last years, not weeks. Technology can augment that human intelligence, Eftimiades said, pointing to IMSI catchers as one example. The devices mimic a cell tower so that nearby phones connect to them. A basic version can cost about $1,000 and fit in a suitcase, he said, though government-grade models cost far more, and there were a couple of cases involving Chinese espionage where these factored in last year. Eftimiades says no one knows yet if the devices were used against Huang, whose phone was presumably hardened such that compromises could be detected, if not stopped altogether. But what Nvidia’s security team knew, and whether it could have acted on it, will only become clearer as the board’s independent investigation and federal inquiries proceed. In the meantime, Eftimiades said he hopes the whole episode is “a wake-up call” for U.S. industry, which he said is mostly “clueless” about China’s tactics. “We have lost trillions [of dollars] in intellectual property,” is his guess. “Whatever we think we’re doing isn’t working.” Get an Early Peek at the Next TechCrunch Disrupt Disrupt, Startup Battlefield, and more will return next year, and you can be at the front of the line. extraction.body: Outsiders had little reason to notice when Nvidia’s longtime chief security officer and head of product security stepped down in August. Just two and a half months later, CEO Jensen Huang himself left the company over growing questions about his extramarital relationships — starting with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company that U.S. investigators suspect of funneling Nvidia chips to China, then widening to reports about two separate affairs with Nvidia employees. At the time, David Reber, who spent four years as CSO and seven at Nvidia overall, said he was leaving for health reasons. “This wasn’t a pivot I had planned. But I know what needs to come first: family and health,” he wrote on LinkedIn in late August, disclosing that he’d been diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson’s more than two years ago. Reber’s replacement, Saša Zdjelar, previously spent 17 years at ExxonMobil in Houston, leaving as a senior IT manager before spending one year at Salesforce and several years at the cybersecurity company ReversingLabs. Zdjelar didn’t respond to questions Thursday about the transition or what the security team knew. Nothing public connects Reber’s or Zdjelar’s role changes to the Megaspeed matter, but it seems fair to wonder what Nvidia’s security team knew about the government’s scrutiny of Megaspeed and about Huang’s relationships, and whether anyone raised concerns. Reber didn’t respond to questions Thursday. Nvidia also has not answered our related questions. Relationships between a CEO and his employees typically fall to HR, legal and the board, not security. But security specialists say any affair — even one inside the office — can give a foreign intelligence service leverage over an exec who wants it kept quiet. And Huang’s relationship with an executive at Megaspeed, a company under federal investigation, wasn’t an office matter at all. (Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.) Still, spotting the clues isn’t easy. The way intelligence services collect information, much of it through everyday conversation rather than hacking, makes it especially difficult for security teams to identify risks, according to retired senior intelligence officer Nicholas Eftimiades, who says he has trained more than 1,000 corporate security professionals. Some people inside Nvidia clearly knew parts of the picture. Nvidia’s top lawyer was engaged with the government’s Megaspeed inquiry more than a year ago, The New York Times reported earlier this week . (Nvidia has said it regularly contacts officials.) Reports about Huang’s relationships with employees suggest colleagues also knew of them, even if the behavior is not expressly forbidden by Nvidia’s code of conduct . The Times cited five Nvidia employees who said he was involved with a vice president who reported directly to him, and Reuters, citing two people, later reported a second relationship. What’s unclear is whether any of that reached security. Even if it had reached Nvidia’s security team, Eftimiades, who wrote Chinese Espionage Operations and Tactics in 2020, said a security team’s resources are often limited. For one thing, they’re often underfunded because, unlike some other cost centers, they don’t drive revenue. It’s astonishingly common for CEOs to answer a security team’s warnings with “not a nickel more than compliance,” he said. Many companies also define security overly narrowly, specialists say. In an opinion piece in The Hill , Don Aviv, CEO of the corporate investigations firm Interfor International, and author Jeremy Hurewitz, wrote, “Too many companies still approach security primarily as a matter of protecting facilities, preventing cyberattacks, and responding to physical threats.” The two argued that “[s]ecurity teams need to pay greater attention to insider threats, including the cultivation of executives and employees by foreign intelligence services, suspicious business relationships, conflicts of interest and attempts to obtain sensitive information through trusted personal contacts.” It would be surprising if Nvidia’s security team didn’t have a more expansive remit than most companies given its scale and business partners, but it’s possible. In fairness, some of it is simply beyond what any team can do. Speaking generally, not about Huang, Eftimiades offered a hypothetical in which a CEO complains that he can’t do something because “I’m fighting a board who doesn’t want to do this.” That tells an intelligence asset who the obstacle is. The service then asks, “Who’s the sticking point here?” and looks for ways into that person’s email and phone. What a rival intelligence service wants is often less technology than policy insight, including who’s pushing to change export rules and who the biggest blocker is. “Intel world tends to be like cancer,” he said. “Once it gets into the body, it looks to spread and looks to reach out.” The playbook isn’t new, Eftimiades added, “particularly for China.” Any executive dealing with the country “will tell you that they’ve been approached.” He said there are also “tons of diplomat stories” of U.S. diplomats walking into a hotel room to find a woman on the bed. He said what’s newer compared with Soviet era spying is the relationships these services cultivate now often last years, not weeks. Technology can augment that human intelligence, Eftimiades said, pointing to IMSI catchers as one example. The devices mimic a cell tower so that nearby phones connect to them. A basic version can cost about $1,000 and fit in a suitcase, he said, though government-grade models cost far more, and there were a couple of cases involving Chinese espionage where these factored in last year. Eftimiades says no one knows yet if the devices were used against Huang, whose phone was presumably hardened such that compromises could be detected, if not stopped altogether. But what Nvidia’s security team knew, and whether it could have acted on it, will only become clearer as the board’s independent investigation and federal inquiries proceed. In the meantime, Eftimiades said he hopes the whole episode is “a wake-up call” for U.S. industry, which he said is mostly “clueless” about China’s tactics. “We have lost trillions [of dollars] in intellectual property,” is his guess. “Whatever we think we’re doing isn’t working.” Get an Early Peek at the Next TechCrunch Disrupt Disrupt, Startup Battlefield, and more will return next year, and you can be at the front of the line. extraction.body: Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman. That incident, now sometimes referred to as “the blip,” ended with Sam coming back as CEO, Helen resigning, and a new board of directors. But it’s worth remembering what Helen and the board were supposed to do: OpenAI’s nonprofit board existed specifically to make sure the company didn’t betray its mission to build safe AI by prioritizing profit and growth over safety. You can sign up here. --- Now, the question of AI safety is everywhere. This summer, AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic broke out of their testing environments and hacked real companies. The CEOs of these frontier labs have since called for a slowdown and asked Washington for help, but the White House’s answer was a voluntary accord — one that relies in part on the kind of board accountability that failed at OpenAI. Anthropic is also about to go public, which will put a whole new set of market pressures on OpenAI’s biggest competitor. Helen has seen up close what happens when safety commitments run headlong into commercial incentives. So we talked about what we might do instead: what the labs are actually trying to build, whether AI alignment is a problem that can be solved, and what a smarter approach to AI regulation might look like. That includes how to think about China, which is the issue that looms large in every policy conversation about AI right now — especially now after the Jensen Huang affair. Just for clarity, Helen and I talked before Nvidia opened its investigation and Jensen ultimately resigned, so you won’t hear us talk about that directly. Okay: Helen Toner, the executive director of CSET, on the future of AI safety. Helen Toner, you’re the executive director for the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. I have wanted to talk to you for 10 million years. You’ve been involved in a lot of AI safety and ethics ideas for a long time. You were obviously on the board of OpenAI during what everyone has come to call “the blip.” Now, you’re talking a lot about AI safety, about which I have 10 million questions. We have a big data team that helps us do our research. There’s a lot of polling that says the number one issue is corruption. The AI industry, and the tech industry, has flooded a bunch of money into politics. And then somewhere next to that is, “Oh, there’s a bunch of well-meaning researchers who are going to show up and tell you how it actually works and what the real risks are.” It just occurs to me that maybe people don’t believe that’s effective anymore, that the money and the corruption and the AI CEO standing next to Trump have completely outweighed the well-meaning, sincere, “here are the actual problems” research that you do. In this election, there were just unbelievable amounts of money being thrown at candidates, at messages, at opposition research. There was all kinds of astroturfing on Twitter, and some very strange things trying to get anyone who talked about AI governance, regulation, safety, any of those words thrown out or not elected. In DC, if you live and work here, you know that lobbyists in DC are not just people who go in and push their company’s position, though they do do that. A big reason that congressional staff and others want to have lobbyists come talk to them is because they’ll really help them understand the weeds of a given piece of legislation — what does it mean for that industry and so on and so forth. Also, we do lots in the executive branch, with different agencies — the White House, Department of War, Department of State, Department of Commerce, all across the board at different levels, depending on the topic and what’s happening at any given moment. There’s no way the government will ever catch up to the tech industry. In this election cycle, I’ve seen a number of candidate forum videos where someone was like, “I’ve tried Claude once.” There’s some huge gap, real or perceived. I’m just trying to understand how you see that gap, how big you think that gap is, because as we get into AI safety and regulation, it’s that gap that has to close. I know a lot of people from the tech industry who come over and start talking to congressional staff or staffers in executive branch offices. I saw after ChatGPT, there was a wave in 2023 of, “Oh, maybe Congress is going to get activated on AI, maybe they’re going to actually do something.” It didn’t really turn into anything actually happening, but it did turn into a real moment where a lot of members of Congress and other policymakers started to get smart on AI. It takes some time to learn what a language model is. I definitely don’t want to say there’s no gap or the government is super smart on AI across the board, but there are some champions who are really smart. In my mind, it’s much more a question of, “Can the institutions, in the state of functionality that they’re in, get anything significant across the line?” more than, “Are these people just too behind the eight ball?” We’re going to see. The reason I’m asking that is I feel like there’s a pretty huge gap in the AI tools and systems most people experience and the way this industry thinks about it. And their answer was, “You need blood.” And I looked at that and I was like, “Who was talking about blood?

extraction.body: An artificial intelligence trial has uncovered nearly 19,000 potential driving offences in two weeks, including a driver drinking from a bottle of wine and another inhaling from balloons. AI-powered cameras installed outside Ladywood fire station in Birmingham and Fallings Park in Wolverhampton also captured drivers holding mobile phones at the wheel and failing to wear seatbelts. Mat MacDonald, the West Midlands Road Safety Commissioner, described the findings highlighted a "huge problem" with driving behaviours in the region. He said another image, which showed a child "sitting unrestrained on a front passenger's lap", was "particularly shocking". He said the findings pointed to a "widespread culture" of dangerous driving behaviours. "What this trial has shown to me more than anything else, is we have a huge problem with these potentially lethal behaviours behind the wheel," he said. The AI cameras have been "trained to recognise certain patterns", such as drivers who appear to be using mobile phones Speaking about images that were captured during the two-week trial, which took place in March, MacDonald said he was not surprised by the number of drivers that were captured using mobile phones. "I was equally disturbed, but not entirely surprised by numbers around mobile phones, specifically," he said. "I travel by foot a lot, and it is almost impossible to get as far as the end of your street without seeing someone who is dialling and driving." MacDonald added: "There was one particularly galling photo of someone drinking from a bottle of wine." Simon Foster, West Midlands police and crime commissioner previously said the findings of the trial were "deeply concerning". "We are closely evaluating these trial results to consider how this advanced AI technology can be deployed for future police enforcement," he said. Road safety data from 2025 showed mobile phone use was linked to 32 deaths on UK roads while unfastened seatbelts were linked to 133 deaths, the WMCA said. MacDonald, former chairman of campaign group Better Streets for Birmingham and an NHS doctor, said he was hopeful of the potential to roll the AI cameras out more widely in the future. "I am working very hard to see what we can do to make this technology a reality on the roads in the West Midlands," he told the BBC. "Hopefully this is the first step towards something that will enable us to start getting a grip of these types of behaviours, which... can end lives and ruin people's futures." MacDonald said the trial was actually stopped earlier than planned because of how many possible road offences were being detected. The technology identified 11,045 potential seatbelt offences and 1,163 potential mobile phone offences at Ladywood, and 6,030 potential seatbelt offences and 757 potential mobile phone offences at Fallings Park. No enforcement was planned as a result of the trial, which was funded by the West Midlands Combined Authority (WMCA) working with the police and fire service. He said he was keen to ensure the technology became more than just an "interesting experiment" and believed it had the potential to help change driver behaviour if rolled out more widely. "We're currently in talks about what that looks like in terms of what resourcing we need to create to make this technology viable on our roads," he explained. The road safety commissioner added: "Ultimately, we don't want to fine anyone. Ultimately, we want the number of fines and activations on these cameras to be zero because then we know we've done our job." Dr Christophe Bastien, associate professor of Transport Safety at Coventry University, said the technology offered an objective way of understanding how motorists behaved on the roads. "The fact that 19,000 offences were identified during a relatively limited deployment suggests that actually, risky behaviour such as mobile phone use and seatbelt non-compliance, remain more common than many people think," he said. He said the technology could help to improve road safety and target action in the future. "These cameras provide an objective way to measure behaviour," he said. "I think they are a way to target intervention where they most need it." Dr Bastien, who has more than 25 years of experience in transport safety, added AI systems were not always perfect but could be used to support existing enforcement methods, rather than replacing them. "I think in some respects, you still need the police to make the call," he said. "The idea is not to punish people. It is the way people drive." Georgia's friend says the film is about celebrating her life and raising awareness of road safety. Take a look at these stunning images from across the West Midlands we have been sent this week. extraction.body: An artificial intelligence trial has uncovered nearly 19,000 potential driving offences in two weeks, including a driver drinking from a bottle of wine and another inhaling from balloons. AI-powered cameras installed outside Ladywood fire station in Birmingham and Fallings Park in Wolverhampton also captured drivers holding mobile phones at the wheel and failing to wear seatbelts. Mat MacDonald, the West Midlands Road Safety Commissioner, described the findings highlighted a "huge problem" with driving behaviours in the region. He said another image, which showed a child "sitting unrestrained on a front passenger's lap", was "particularly shocking". He said the findings pointed to a "widespread culture" of dangerous driving behaviours. "What this trial has shown to me more than anything else, is we have a huge problem with these potentially lethal behaviours behind the wheel," he said. The AI cameras have been "trained to recognise certain patterns", such as drivers who appear to be using mobile phones Speaking about images that were captured during the two-week trial, which took place in March, MacDonald said he was not surprised by the number of drivers that were captured using mobile phones. "I was equally disturbed, but not entirely surprised by numbers around mobile phones, specifically," he said. "I travel by foot a lot, and it is almost impossible to get as far as the end of your street without seeing someone who is dialling and driving." MacDonald added: "There was one particularly galling photo of someone drinking from a bottle of wine." Simon Foster, West Midlands police and crime commissioner previously said the findings of the trial were "deeply concerning". "We are closely evaluating these trial results to consider how this advanced AI technology can be deployed for future police enforcement," he said. Road safety data from 2025 showed mobile phone use was linked to 32 deaths on UK roads while unfastened seatbelts were linked to 133 deaths, the WMCA said. MacDonald, former chairman of campaign group Better Streets for Birmingham and an NHS doctor, said he was hopeful of the potential to roll the AI cameras out more widely in the future. "I am working very hard to see what we can do to make this technology a reality on the roads in the West Midlands," he told the BBC. "Hopefully this is the first step towards something that will enable us to start getting a grip of these types of behaviours, which... can end lives and ruin people's futures." MacDonald said the trial was actually stopped earlier than planned because of how many possible road offences were being detected. The technology identified 11,045 potential seatbelt offences and 1,163 potential mobile phone offences at Ladywood, and 6,030 potential seatbelt offences and 757 potential mobile phone offences at Fallings Park. No enforcement was planned as a result of the trial, which was funded by the West Midlands Combined Authority (WMCA) working with the police and fire service. He said he was keen to ensure the technology became more than just an "interesting experiment" and believed it had the potential to help change driver behaviour if rolled out more widely. "We're currently in talks about what that looks like in terms of what resourcing we need to create to make this technology viable on our roads," he explained. The road safety commissioner added: "Ultimately, we don't want to fine anyone. Ultimately, we want the number of fines and activations on these cameras to be zero because then we know we've done our job." Dr Christophe Bastien, associate professor of Transport Safety at Coventry University, said the technology offered an objective way of understanding how motorists behaved on the roads. "The fact that 19,000 offences were identified during a relatively limited deployment suggests that actually, risky behaviour such as mobile phone use and seatbelt non-compliance, remain more common than many people think," he said. He said the technology could help to improve road safety and target action in the future. "These cameras provide an objective way to measure behaviour," he said. "I think they are a way to target intervention where they most need it." Dr Bastien, who has more than 25 years of experience in transport safety, added AI systems were not always perfect but could be used to support existing enforcement methods, rather than replacing them. "I think in some respects, you still need the police to make the call," he said. "The idea is not to punish people. It is the way people drive." Georgia's friend says the film is about celebrating her life and raising awareness of road safety. Take a look at these stunning images from across the West Midlands we have been sent this week.
